Source: docs/guide/user/python.md

# PyForge (Python)

**PyForge** brings PyCharm's Python support to Forge. It has three plugins:

- **Python** (`forge.python`) — highlighting, scope-aware completion and syntax checks for
  `.py` files, pip requirements files, the Python language servers and Reformat Code. It is
  active in every project, so a lone script is still a Python file.
- **Python Interpreters and Packages** (`forge.python-env`) — interpreters, the Python
  Packages tool window, requirements inspections and the Python run configuration. It is
  active in [Python projects](docs/guide/getting-started/project-detection.md): `pyproject.toml`,
  `setup.py`, `setup.cfg`, `requirements*.txt`, `Pipfile`, `environment.yml`, Python files in
  the root, or two or more in a folder.
- **Python Tests, Debugger, Console and Profiler** (`forge.python-tools`) — pytest, unittest
  and tox in the test runner, debugging with debugpy, the Python Console and the profiler, in
  the same projects.

Django, Flask, FastAPI and Celery projects get more plugins: see
[Django, Flask, FastAPI and Celery](docs/guide/user/python-web-frameworks.md). Jupyter notebooks (`.ipynb`)
open in the notebook editor: see [Jupyter notebooks](docs/guide/user/jupyter.md).

![A Python file with basedpyright's errors and the requirements inspection](docs/screenshots/python-editor.png)

## Python interpreter

The status bar shows the project's interpreter, PyCharm style: **Python 3.12 (shop-api)**.
Click it (or run **Switch Python Interpreter…** from Find Action) to switch between the
configured interpreters, the project's environments and the Pythons found on this machine,
to add a new one, or to open the settings.

![The interpreter popup in the status bar](docs/screenshots/python-interpreter-popup.png)

Without a selection Forge uses the project's own environment (`.venv`, `venv` or the Poetry,
Pipenv or Hatch environment of the project) automatically.

### Settings | Project | Python Interpreter

The page selects the interpreter (`python.interpreter`: the path of a local `python`, or the
name of a configured interpreter) and lists its packages with the latest version on PyPI.
**Add Interpreter…** opens the **Add Python Interpreter** dialog.

![Settings | Project | Python Interpreter](docs/screenshots/python-interpreter-settings.png)

Forge finds, without running anything inside the project:

| Kind | Where |
| --- | --- |
| Virtualenv / venv | `.venv`, `venv`, `env` with a `pyvenv.cfg` (typed by `pyvenv.cfg`: uv and virtualenv write their own key) |
| uv | an environment created by `uv venv` / `uv sync`, or any project environment next to `uv.lock` |
| Poetry | `<cache>/pypoetry/virtualenvs/<name>-…`, else `poetry env info -p` |
| Pipenv | `~/.local/share/virtualenvs/<folder>-…` (`WORKON_HOME`), else `pipenv --venv` |
| Hatch | `<data>/hatch/env/virtual/<name>/…` |
| conda / mamba | `~/miniconda3`, `~/anaconda3`, `~/miniforge3`, `~/mambaforge`, `~/micromamba`, `/opt/conda` and their `envs/`, `~/.conda/environments.txt`; the version comes from `conda-meta` |
| pyenv | `~/.pyenv/versions/*` (`PYENV_ROOT`) |
| System | `python`, `python3`, `python3.X` on `PATH`, `/usr/bin`, `/usr/local/bin`, Homebrew; python.org installs on Windows (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Python`) |

Only system Pythons are asked for their version (`python --version`); environments report
theirs from their metadata. The tools (`poetry`, `pipenv`) are asked only outside
[Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md).

### Add Python Interpreter

![Add Python Interpreter](docs/screenshots/python-add-interpreter.png)

- **Local Interpreter | Generate new** creates an environment:
  - **Virtualenv**: `<base python> -m venv <location>`, then `pip install -r requirements.txt`.
  - **uv**: `uv venv <location> --python <base or version>`, then `uv sync` (with `uv.lock`)
    or `uv pip install -r requirements.txt`.
  - **Poetry**: `poetry env use <base python>`, then `poetry install`.
  - **Conda**: `conda create --yes --prefix <location> python=<version>`, then pip.

  The commands run one after another in the Run tool window; the new environment becomes the
  project's interpreter. "Install the project's dependencies" can be turned off.
- **Local Interpreter | Select existing** picks a detected interpreter or a path.
- **Docker**, **Docker Compose**, **SSH** and **WSL** work like PHP's
  [CLI interpreters](docs/guide/user/php.md): an image (the project is mounted at `/opt/project`), a compose
  service (`docker compose run` or `exec`), an SSH configuration of Settings | Tools | SSH
  Configurations, or a WSL distribution, plus the path of `python` there. Paths in arguments
  and the Run console are mapped both ways. Such interpreters are stored in
  `python.projectInterpreters` (or `python.interpreters` for every project).

## Python Packages tool window

**View | Tool Windows | Python Packages** lists the packages of the project's interpreter
with their versions; a newer release on PyPI is shown next to the version. Type in the search
field to filter them and to search PyPI. The right side shows the selected package: summary,
latest version, required Python, licence and home page, with **Install** (choose a version),
**Upgrade to …** and **Delete Package**.

![Python Packages](docs/screenshots/python-packages.png)

Packages are installed with the tool that manages the environment:

| Environment | Command |
| --- | --- |
| uv (or a venv next to `uv.lock`) | `uv pip install --python <python> …` / `uv pip uninstall` |
| Poetry | `poetry add` / `poetry remove` / `poetry update` (also changes `pyproject.toml`) |
| Pipenv | `pipenv install` / `uninstall` / `update` |
| anything else | `python -m pip install` / `uninstall --yes` / `install --upgrade` |

The commands run in the Run tool window and are refused in [Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md).
Installed packages are read with a small `importlib.metadata` script, so environments without
pip (uv's) work too.

PyPI answers are cached for 12 hours in `<cache dir>/forge/pypi` and the cache is used when
PyPI cannot be reached. Settings | Languages & Frameworks | Python | **Look up packages on
PyPI** (`python.packages.pypi`) turns the lookups off; **Package index**
(`python.packages.index`) points them at a mirror with PyPI's JSON API.

![Searching PyPI](docs/screenshots/python-packages-search.png)

## Requirements inspections

- **Package requirement 'X' is not satisfied**: a dependency in `requirements*.txt` or
  `pyproject.toml` (PEP 621 `dependencies` and `optional-dependencies`, PEP 735
  `dependency-groups`, Poetry's `tool.poetry.*dependencies`) is not installed, or the
  installed version does not match its specifiers. `Alt+Enter`: **Install requirement**,
  **Install all missing requirements**, **Ignore requirement**.
- **Package containing module 'x' is not listed in the project requirements**: an import of a
  third-party package that no dependency file declares. `Alt+Enter`: **Add requirement 'x' to
  pyproject.toml** (or `requirements.txt` when the project has no PEP 621 / Poetry
  dependencies), **Install package x** when it is not installed, **Ignore requirement**.
  The distribution name is taken from the installed packages (`import yaml` → `PyYAML`).

![Install requirement in requirements-dev.txt](docs/screenshots/python-requirements.png)

Versions are compared with PEP 440 rules (`~=`, `==1.4.*`, pre-releases, local versions,
Poetry's `^` and `~`). Dependencies with environment markers are not checked. **Install
Requirements** (Find Action) installs everything that is not satisfied. Settings | Languages &
Frameworks | Python | Inspections turns the two inspections off and lists ignored packages
(`python.inspections.ignoredPackages`).

Requirements files are highlighted (names, extras, specifiers, markers, options, URLs) and
complete package names (installed ones and PyPI) and versions; so do the dependency strings
of `pyproject.toml`.

## Language servers

Settings | Languages & Frameworks | Python lists the Python servers of the
[language server catalog](docs/guide/user/language-servers.md):

| Server | Role |
| --- | --- |
| **basedpyright** (default) | types, completion, navigation, hover; Forge installs it from npm with one click |
| **Pyright** | starts when basedpyright is missing or disabled |
| **ty** (preview) | Astral's type checker; off by default, enable it and disable basedpyright and Pyright |
| **Ruff** | `ruff server`: lint diagnostics and fixes next to the type checker |

Forge downloads ruff and ty itself, with your consent, as the official wheel of your platform
from PyPI, checked against the SHA-256 digest PyPI publishes, into
`<data dir>/forge/langservers/bin`. Nothing is bundled with Forge.

**Use language servers from the interpreter's environment**
(`python.lsp.useEnvironmentTools`, on by default): a basedpyright, ruff or ty installed in the
selected environment (or the project's `.venv`) is used before Forge's download and `PATH`.
basedpyright and Pyright get the interpreter as `python.pythonPath`, so imports resolve
against its site-packages.

## Reformat Code

`Ctrl+Alt+L` (and "Reformat code" in [Actions on Save](docs/guide/user/actions-on-save.md)) formats Python files
with the formatter of **Reformat Code with** (`python.formatter`): **ruff format** (default),
**Black**, **the language server** or **do not format**. Their settings in `pyproject.toml`,
`ruff.toml` or `.ruff.toml` apply. The executables come from `python.ruff.path` /
`python.black.path`, else the interpreter's environment, Forge's download (ruff) or `PATH`.

## Running Python code

The **Python** run configuration runs a **Script path** or a **Module name** (`python -m`) with
script parameters, interpreter options, environment variables and a working directory,
through the configuration's interpreter or the project's (local, Docker, Docker Compose, SSH or
WSL). `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1` keeps the output live. A ▶ in the gutter of
`if __name__ == "__main__":` runs the file, as does `Ctrl+Shift+F10` in a Python file.

Running scripts, modules, pip and environment tools is running project code: it is refused in
[Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md), like tests, debugging, the Python Console and Profile below.

## Testing with pytest, unittest and tox

Python tests run in the shared [test runner](docs/guide/user/testing.md): gutter icons, the test tree with
**Click to see difference**, Rerun Failed Tests, [Test History](docs/guide/user/testing.md) and
[Run with Coverage](docs/guide/user/coverage.md).

![pytest results with a failed parametrized case and its comparison](docs/screenshots/python-pytest.png)

- **Gutter icons** come from the source (no test run, no plugin needed): pytest's
  `test*` functions in `test_*.py` / `*_test.py` files, `Test*` classes without `__init__`
  (also nested ones) and their methods, and `unittest.TestCase` subclasses with their `test*`
  methods in any file. `@pytest.mark.parametrize` cases get icons of their own when each
  value is on its own line; their names are pytest's ids (`ids=`, `pytest.param(id=…)`, the
  values themselves, `argname0` otherwise; stacked decorators multiply). The icons show the
  last result, a failing case marks its test.
- **Default test runner** (Settings | Tools | Python Integrated Tools,
  `python.testing.runner`): *Autodetect* uses pytest when the project uses it
  (`pytest.ini`, `conftest.py`, `[tool.pytest.ini_options]`, `[tool:pytest]`, tox's
  `[pytest]` or a `pytest` dependency) and unittest for files with only test cases; or always
  pytest / always Unittests. Run Context Configuration (`Ctrl+Shift+F10`) runs the test at the
  caret, else the file; in a file without tests it runs the file as a Python script.
- **pytest** configurations run all tests, a directory, a **Script path**, a test (the node id
  after the file: `TestCart::test_add[one]`) or **Keywords** (`-k`), with additional
  arguments. Results come from pytest's JUnit XML (`--junitxml`, built in) or, with **pytest
  results** set to *Report log*, from the pytest-reportlog plugin. **Rerun Failed Tests** runs
  the failed tests' node ids, with their classes read from the files. **Run with Coverage**
  needs pytest-cov: it adds `--cov --cov-report=xml:…` and shows the Cobertura report in the
  Coverage tool window and the editor.
- **Unittests** configurations run discovery below the project or a directory (pattern
  `test*.py`), a file, a class or a test method with Forge's own runner: a small script that
  comes with Forge (standard library only, sent inline with `python -c`), reports every test as
  it runs and records `assertEqual` values for the comparison. **Run with Coverage** needs
  coverage.py in the interpreter: the runner measures with branch coverage and writes a
  Cobertura report. Rerun Failed Tests runs the
  failed tests' ids (`tests.test_cart.TestCart.test_total`).
- **tox** configurations run the environments you name (empty: tox's `env_list`) with
  `python -m tox`, or the program of **tox executable** (`python.tox.path`). Every
  environment is a test of the tree, with its output and its result (`OK`, `FAIL`, `SKIP`).
  **Run tox Environment…** (Tools menu, Find Action) lists the environments of `tox.ini`,
  `setup.cfg`, `tox.toml` or `pyproject.toml` (`[tool.tox]`), generative names such as
  `py{311,312}` expanded, and runs one.

All of them run through the configuration's or the project's interpreter, including Docker,
Docker Compose, SSH and WSL interpreters, and on a configuration's [run target](docs/guide/user/run-targets.md).
Report files go to the system temp folder, or to `.forge/test-reports/<run>` in the project
when the interpreter or target is remote, and are read and removed when the run ends.

## Debugging with debugpy

Debug (`Shift+F9`) on a Python, pytest or Unittests configuration, or **Debug** in a test's
gutter menu, debugs it with [debugpy](https://github.com/microsoft/debugpy) (MIT) in the
shared [debugger](docs/guide/user/debugging.md): breakpoints, conditions and logpoints, stepping, frames and
variables, watches, inline values, Set Value, exception breakpoints (raised, uncaught, user
uncaught) and the **Console** tab, which evaluates expressions in the selected frame.

![A pytest test paused in Cart.total with the debug console](docs/screenshots/python-debug.png)

- When the interpreter has no debugpy, Forge asks before it installs it with the
  environment's package manager (`pip install debugpy`, `uv pip install debugpy`, …); **Install
  debugpy without asking** turns the question off.
- The run starts in the Run tool window as `python [options] -m debugpy --listen
  127.0.0.1:<port> --wait-for-client …` and Forge attaches to it. Docker, SSH and WSL
  interpreters and run targets listen on every interface; the port is published or forwarded
  and the project's path mappings become debugpy's `pathMappings`, so breakpoints work in
  containers and on remote hosts.
- **Attach to Process** (`Ctrl+Alt+F5`) attaches debugpy to a running local Python process,
  with the adapter (`python -m debugpy.adapter`) started in the project's interpreter.
  **Attach to DAP Server** connects to a program started with
  `python -m debugpy --listen 5678 app.py`.
- Settings | Build, Execution, Deployment | Debugger | **Python Debugger**:
  **Step only through the project's code** (`python.debugger.justMyCode`, on) and
  **Attach to subprocesses automatically** (`python.debugger.subProcess`, on).

## Python Console

The **Python Console** tool window (Tools | Python Console) is an interactive REPL in the
project's interpreter, IPython when the interpreter has it (Settings | Build, Execution,
Deployment | Python Console, **Use IPython if available**).

![The Python Console with a variable expanded](docs/screenshots/python-console.png)

- Type at the prompt; `Enter` runs the input, an incomplete statement continues with `...`,
  `Shift+Enter` adds a line, `Up` / `Down` go through the command history (kept per project in
  Forge's state folder). A program's `input()` asks at the prompt.
- **Run Selection in Python Console** (`Alt+Shift+E`) runs the selection, or the caret's line,
  in the console and starts it when needed. **Run File in Python Console** runs the whole file
  in the console's namespace.
- **Show Variables** shows the console's variables with their types and values; lists, dicts,
  sets and objects expand.
- The toolbar reruns, stops and clears the console. It runs through Docker, SSH and WSL
  interpreters too and is refused in Safe Mode.

## Profiler

**Run | Profile** runs the selected Python configuration under cProfile (standard library):
`python [options] -m cProfile -o <snapshot> (<script> | -m <module>) …`. The snapshot
(`.pstats`) goes to Forge's cache folder (`<cache dir>/forge/profiles/<project>`; the newest
**Profiler snapshots to keep** stay); runs on remote interpreters write it into the project's
`.forge/test-reports` folder first, then Forge moves it out. Forge reads the file itself, no
Python is needed to view it.

![The Profiler's call tree](docs/screenshots/python-profiler.png)

The **Profiler** tool window shows a snapshot:

- **Call Tree**: what called what, with calls, total and own time and the share of the run;
  recursion shows once, cheap calls deep in the tree are left out.
- **Method List**: the hot spots — every function with its calls (`calls/primitive calls`
  for recursion), own time and share, and total time; sort by any column.

![The Profiler's method list](docs/screenshots/python-profiler-hot-spots.png)

Double-click a row to open the function's source. **Snapshots…** switches between the
project's snapshots, **Open Snapshot…** reads a `.pstats` file of the project, **Delete
Snapshot** removes one.

## Browser mode

`?project=python` opens the demo service `shop-api` (FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, a uv environment).
Its tests (pytest with a failing parametrized case, a unittest test case), `tox.ini`, a debug
session in `Cart.total`, the Python Console and a profile of `scripts/report.py` are simulated;
discovery, command lines, tox environments and the snapshot's call tree are computed by the
same Rust code (WebAssembly).

# Jupyter notebooks

`.ipynb` files open in the notebook editor, the way PyCharm shows them: cells with their
outputs, a toolbar to run them and a kernel that keeps the variables between runs. The
plugin **Jupyter** (`forge.jupyter`, pack PyForge) is on in every project; switch it off in
Settings | Plugins to open notebooks as JSON text again.

![A notebook with Markdown, code and a DataFrame table](docs/screenshots/jupyter-notebook.png)

Opening, editing, diffing and viewing notebooks never runs anything. Running a cell starts a
kernel, which runs the notebook's code with the project's interpreter, so it is refused in
[Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md) until you trust the project.

## The notebook editor

- **Cells**: code cells are editors with Python highlighting, bracket matching and the
  editor's color scheme; Markdown cells show their rendered text (double-click or `Enter` to
  edit them); raw cells are plain text. The gutter shows the run button and the execution
  count: `[3]` after a run, `[*]` while the cell runs or waits for the kernel.
- **Toolbar**: Run Cell and Select Below, Run All Cells, Interrupt Kernel, Restart Kernel,
  Clear All Outputs, Add Code Cell, Delete Cell and the cell type (Code, Markdown, Raw); on the
  right Show Variables, the kernel with its state (Not started, Starting…, Idle, Busy,
  Disconnected) and Shut Down Kernel.
- **Save** (`Ctrl+S`) writes the `.ipynb` file. Forge keeps everything it did not change:
  cell ids, metadata, the order of the keys, texts stored as one string or as a list of lines,
  the file's indent and its final line break. A notebook written by Jupyter and saved
  unchanged by Forge is byte for byte the same file, so Git shows only real changes.
- Language intelligence inside cells is limited to highlighting and editing helpers; the
  Python language servers do not analyse notebook cells yet.

### Command mode and edit mode

Like Jupyter, the editor has two modes. In **edit mode** a cell's editor has the focus (the
cell's frame is orange) and keys type text. `Escape` switches to **command mode**: a cell is
selected and single keys act on cells. Click a cell's gutter to select it, click into its
text to edit it.

| Action | Mode | Windows / Linux | macOS |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Run Cell and Select Below | both | `Shift+Enter` | `Shift+Enter` |
| Run Cell | both | `Ctrl+Enter` | `Cmd+Enter` |
| Run Cell and Insert Below | both | `Alt+Enter` | `Opt+Enter` |
| Run All Cells | both | `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Enter` | `Cmd+Opt+Shift+Enter` |
| Enter Command Mode | edit | `Escape` | `Escape` |
| Enter Edit Mode | command | `Enter` | `Enter` |
| Insert Cell Above / Below | command | `A` / `B` | `A` / `B` |
| Delete Cell | command | `D D` | `D D` |
| Change Cell Type to Code / Markdown / Raw | command | `Y` / `M` / `R` | `Y` / `M` / `R` |
| Select Cell Above / Below | command | `Up` or `K` / `Down` or `J` | same |
| Move Cell Up / Down | command | `Ctrl+Shift+Up` / `Ctrl+Shift+Down` | `Cmd+Shift+Up` / `Cmd+Shift+Down` |
| Interrupt Kernel | command | `I I` | `I I` |
| Restart Kernel | command | `0 0` | `0 0` |

All of them are keymap actions (group **Jupyter**): rebind them in Settings | Keymap, find them
with Find Action (`Ctrl+Shift+A`). The notebook shortcuts win over editor actions with the same
keys only inside notebooks; `Shift+Enter` still starts a new line in every other editor.

## Outputs

![Plot, result and an error with its traceback](docs/screenshots/jupyter-outputs.png)

| Output | How it is shown |
| --- | --- |
| `stdout` / `stderr` streams, `text/plain` results | console text with ANSI colors; `\r` progress bars overwrite their line; file references in tracebacks open the file |
| Errors | the traceback with its colors on an error background |
| Images (`image/png`, `image/jpeg`, `image/gif`, `image/webp`) | the image at its size (the output's `width`/`height` metadata are honoured) |
| `image/svg+xml` | the image after removing scripts, event handlers, `foreignObject` and external references |
| `text/html` | sanitized HTML (no scripts, event handlers, frames, forms or remote resources) in a sandboxed frame that cannot run scripts or load anything |
| `application/json` | a collapsible JSON tree |
| `text/markdown` | rendered Markdown |
| pandas DataFrames (`text/html` of a DataFrame, `application/vnd.dataresource+json`) | a DataFrame table, see below |

Outputs taller than 400 pixels scroll (`jupyter.outputs.limitHeight`). While a cell runs its
outputs stream in; `clear_output(wait=True)` and updated displays (`display_id`) work as in
Jupyter. Interactive widgets (ipywidgets) and JavaScript outputs are not supported; their
plain-text fallback is shown.

## DataFrame tables

DataFrame outputs become the same data grid as the database and CSV editors: the index
columns, the column types when known, sorting by a click on a column header (numbers sort as
numbers; again for descending, a third time for the original order), a **Filter** (rows that
contain the text in any cell; `column: text` filters one column) and pages of
`jupyter.dataframe.pageSize` rows (default 50). The bar shows the frame's size, for example
`1000 rows × 5 columns`, also when pandas printed only part of it.

## Kernels

The first cell you run starts the kernel:

- **In the project's interpreter** (default): Forge starts `ipykernel` with the interpreter
  from the status bar (Settings | Project | Python Interpreter) in the notebook's folder and
  talks to it over ZeroMQ, signing every message with a key of its own (HMAC-SHA256). When the
  interpreter has no `ipykernel`, Forge asks to install it with the environment's package
  manager (pip, uv, Poetry or Pipenv; the output appears in the Run tool window).
  `jupyter.kernel.installWithoutAsking` skips the question.
- **On a Jupyter server**: set Settings | Languages & Frameworks | Jupyter | Jupyter server
  URL (`jupyter.server.url`), for example `http://localhost:8888`, to run kernels on a running
  JupyterLab, Notebook 7 or `jupyter server`. A pasted URL with `?token=…` works; the token
  is moved to the OS keychain and never stored in settings. Enter a token below the URL and
  click **Test Connection** to check it; **Forget Token** removes it. Kernels of Docker, SSH and
  WSL interpreters and of remote projects need a server that runs next to them.

Interrupt Kernel stops the running cell (`KeyboardInterrupt`); cells queued behind a failed
cell are skipped, like in Jupyter. Restart Kernel starts a fresh kernel and forgets every
variable. Closing the notebook shuts its kernel down (`jupyter.kernel.shutdownOnClose`).

## Variables

![Run All with the Variables view](docs/screenshots/jupyter-kernel.png)

**Show Variables** opens the Variables view of the kernel next to the cells, like the Python
Console's: every variable with its type and value, expandable for lists, dicts and objects. It
refreshes after each cell. DataFrames, Series and NumPy arrays have **View**, which opens
**View as DataFrame**: the variable's rows (up to 10,000) in an editor tab with the same table,
sorting, filter and pages.

![View as DataFrame](docs/screenshots/jupyter-dataframe.png)

## Notebook diffs

![A notebook diff, cell by cell](docs/screenshots/jupyter-diff.png)

Diffs of `.ipynb` files (Commit, Show Diff, Git history, Local History, Compare Files) compare
the notebooks **cell by cell** instead of as JSON: added, deleted and modified cells, with the
source and the outputs of a changed cell in separate line diffs, and notes when only the cell
type, the execution count or the metadata changed. Runs of unchanged cells are folded. Cells are
paired by their ids (nbformat 4.5); notebooks without ids are aligned by their sources. Images
are compared by size and a short hash. **Text** in the diff toolbar switches to the JSON diff,
for example to revert single lines; `jupyter.diff.view` chooses what opens first.

## Settings

Settings | Languages & Frameworks | Jupyter:

| Setting | Key | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Jupyter server URL (project) | `jupyter.server.url` | empty: start kernels in the project's interpreter |
| Install ipykernel without asking | `jupyter.kernel.installWithoutAsking` | off |
| Shut down the kernel when the notebook is closed | `jupyter.kernel.shutdownOnClose` | on |
| Scroll long outputs | `jupyter.outputs.limitHeight` | on |
| DataFrame rows per page | `jupyter.dataframe.pageSize` | 50 |
| Show notebook diffs | `jupyter.diff.view` | Cell by cell |

## Files Forge writes

- The kernel's connection file (ports and signing key, readable only by you) in
  `<cache dir>/forge/jupyter/`, deleted when the kernel stops.
- Server tokens in the OS keychain (service `forge-jupyter`).
- Nothing in the project except the notebooks you save.

Source: docs/guide/user/ruby.md

# RubyForge (Ruby)

**RubyForge** brings RubyMine's Ruby support to Forge. Its plugin **Ruby** (`forge.ruby`)
is active in [Ruby projects](docs/guide/getting-started/project-detection.md): a `Gemfile`, a
`Rakefile`, a `.ruby-version`, a `*.gemspec`, a `.rb` file in the root, or two or more
`.rb` / `.rake` files in a folder. [Rails support](docs/guide/user/rails.md) (routes, navigation, generators,
the Rails console and server, data sources, I18n, Stimulus and Turbo) is a separate plugin that
builds on this one.

- Ruby files (`.rb`, `.rake`, `.gemspec`, `.ru`, `.jbuilder`, `Gemfile`, `Rakefile`,
  `Guardfile`, `Capfile`, `.irbrc`, scripts with a `ruby` shebang) get Ruby highlighting;
  `Gemfile.lock` is its own file type.
- Completion, navigation, hover, rename and diagnostics come from **Ruby LSP** (Shopify, MIT),
  which runs like every other [language server](docs/guide/user/language-servers.md) with the project's Ruby.
- Everything else is computed in Rust (`packs/rubyforge/*`): interpreters, the bundle, Rake
  tasks, test discovery and results, command lines and RuboCop's reports.

![inventory_spec.rb with run icons on the example groups and examples](docs/screenshots/ruby-editor.png)

## Ruby SDK

**Settings | Languages & Frameworks | Ruby** lists the interpreters Forge found and the one
the project uses.

![Settings | Languages & Frameworks | Ruby](docs/screenshots/ruby-settings.png)

- Forge finds Rubies of **rbenv** (`$RBENV_ROOT` or `~/.rbenv/versions`), **rvm**
  (`~/.rvm/rubies`, `/usr/local/rvm/rubies`, with the Ruby's gem sets), **chruby**
  (`~/.rubies`, `/opt/rubies`), **asdf** (`~/.asdf/installs/ruby`), **mise**
  (`~/.local/share/mise/installs/ruby`), frum and rv, **Homebrew** (`/opt/homebrew/opt/ruby`),
  **RubyInstaller** (`C:\Ruby*`) and the system Ruby on the `PATH`. Version manager shims are
  skipped: the Ruby behind them is listed by its manager. Forge only reads the folders; Rubies
  outside a manager are asked for their version (`ruby -e 'print RUBY_VERSION'`).
- **Automatic** (the default) uses the version the project asks for in `.ruby-version`,
  `.tool-versions`, `mise.toml` or the Gemfile's `ruby "3.3.6"` / `ruby file:
  ".ruby-version"` line (`3.3` matches the newest installed 3.3.x), else the version
  manager's global version (`~/.rbenv/version`, `~/.tool-versions`), else the newest Ruby.
  The page says which file asked, and a balloon tells you when that version is not installed.
- Choose an interpreter in the list for the project, or **Add Interpreter…** for any other
  `ruby` executable (it is checked before it is added).
- **Tools** shows the gem executables Forge uses (Bundler, Rake, RSpec, RuboCop, rdbg, IRB,
  Ruby LSP); missing RuboCop, the debug gem and Ruby LSP have an **Install** button.
- **Environment** adds variables to every Ruby, Bundler, Rake and test command. Commands run
  with the interpreter's `bin` folder first on the `PATH` (and rvm's `GEM_HOME` /
  `GEM_PATH`), so `gem`, `bundle` and gem executables belong to the chosen Ruby.

The interpreter appears in the status bar (`rbenv: 3.3.6`); clicking it opens the page.

## Bundler and gems

In projects with a `Gemfile`, Ruby scripts, Rake, RSpec, Minitest, RuboCop and IRB run
through `bundle exec` (**Run commands with bundle exec**, on by default; Ruby and Rake
configurations can turn it off for themselves).

- The `Gemfile` and `Gemfile.lock` are read without running Bundler: declared gems with their
  requirements and groups (`group :test do`, `group:` options), platforms, `path:` / `git:`
  sources, and the locked versions with their dependencies. Gems pulled in by others get the
  groups of the gems that need them.
- **External Libraries** in the Project view lists the project's Ruby SDK and the **Bundled
  Gems** with their locked versions; gems of the Gemfile come first, the others are dimmed.
  Opening a Gemfile gem shows its line in the `Gemfile`.
- When gems of the Gemfile are missing from `Gemfile.lock`, a balloon offers **bundle
  install**. **Tools | Bundler: Install / Update** and **Show Outdated Gems** run Bundler in
  the Run tool window. Saving the Gemfile or the lock file reads the bundle again.

![External Libraries with the Ruby SDK and the bundle's gems; an ERB view](docs/screenshots/ruby-erb.png)

## Rake

The **Rake** tool window (right side) lists the project's tasks by namespace with their
arguments and descriptions. Double-click (or **Run**) runs a task as a temporary Rake
configuration, **Debug** runs it under the debugger, **Jump to Source** opens its definition.

![The Rake tool window](docs/screenshots/ruby-rake.png)

- Tasks come from `rake --tasks --all` and their places from `rake --where`. That loads the
  Rakefile, so it runs only in [trusted projects](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md); in Safe Mode (or with
  **Load tasks with rake --tasks** off) Forge reads the `Rakefile`, `rakelib/*.rake` and
  `lib/tasks/**/*.rake` instead: `desc`, `task`, `namespace`, and the tasks of
  `Bundler::GemHelper`, `RSpec::Core::RakeTask`, `Rake::TestTask`, `Minitest::TestTask` and
  `RuboCop::RakeTask`.
- **Run Rake Task…** (Tools) asks for a task, e.g. `release[origin]`.

## Run configurations

- **Ruby** runs a script with interpreter options and arguments (`bundle exec ruby -w
  bin/report.rb --month 2026-10`). A ▶ in the gutter of scripts (a `ruby` shebang or `if
  __FILE__ == $0`) runs or debugs them.
- **Rake** runs a task with arguments (`rake release[origin]`) and Rake options.
- **RSpec** and **Minitest** run tests (below).

## RSpec and Minitest

Spec files (`*_spec.rb`) get ▶ icons on `describe` / `context` / `feature` groups and on
`it` / `specify` / `example` / `scenario`; test files (`*_test.rb`, `test_*.rb`) on test
classes, `def test_*` methods, ActiveSupport `test "…" do` blocks and Minitest::Spec
`describe` / `it` blocks. After a run the icons show the results.

- **RSpec** runs `rspec <file>:<line>` for a group or example, a file, a folder, everything,
  or the examples whose description matches (`--example`), with `--format progress --format
  json --out <report>`. Forge reads the JSON report into the test tree: files, example groups,
  examples, pending examples, the failure message with its backtrace, `expected: … got: …`
  values for **Click to see difference**, and errors outside of examples (a spec that does
  not load).
- **Minitest** runs `ruby -Ilib -Itest <file> -v [-n <filter>]` (a class: `-n
  "/^Shop::CartTest#/"`, a method: `-n Shop::CartTest#test_total`), or loads every test file
  of a folder. Forge reads Minitest's verbose output: one suite per test class, failures,
  errors and skips with their messages, `Expected:` / `Actual:` values, the location and the
  test's own output.
- **Rerun Failed Tests** runs the failed examples (`--example`) or methods (`-n
  "/^(test_a|test_b)$/"`) of the files that failed.

![RSpec results in the test tree](docs/screenshots/ruby-rspec.png)

![Minitest results](docs/screenshots/ruby-minitest.png)

## Debugging

Debug (`Shift+F9`) on a Ruby, Rake, RSpec or Minitest configuration runs it under **rdbg**,
the debugger of the `debug` gem (BSD-2-Clause, Ruby's default debugger): the command starts
in the Run tool window as `rdbg --open --host 127.0.0.1 --port <port> --command -- <command>`,
waits for the debugger, and Forge attaches to it. Breakpoints (also conditional), stepping,
the stack, local and global variables and the debug console work as in the other
[debuggers](docs/guide/user/debugging.md); the program's output stays in the Run console and test runs still
fill the test tree.

![rdbg stopped in Inventory#total_cents](docs/screenshots/ruby-debug.png)

- rdbg comes from `bundle exec rdbg` when the bundle has the `debug` gem, else from the
  interpreter (or **rdbg executable**). Without it, Forge offers to install the gem with the
  interpreter's `gem` (with `--user-install` for system Rubies).
- **Run | Attach to DAP Server…** with the adapter *Ruby (rdbg)* connects to any `rdbg --open
  --port <port>` you started yourself, e.g. in a container.

## RuboCop

RuboCop checks open Ruby files after opening them, after a pause in typing and after saving
(**Check files with RuboCop**). Its offenses appear in the editor and the **Problems** tool
window with the cop name; conventions and refactorings are weak warnings, warnings and errors
keep their level, and the inspection profile can change the severity (inspection
*Ruby | External tools | RuboCop*).

![RuboCop offenses with Alt+Enter autocorrect](docs/screenshots/ruby-rubocop.png)

- `Alt+Enter` on a correctable offense: **RuboCop: autocorrect** (safe corrections, `-a`) or
  **autocorrect all offenses in the file** (also unsafe ones, `-A`).
- **Reformat Code** (`Ctrl+Alt+L`) uses RuboCop's autocorrect (**Reformat Code with**: safe,
  all, Ruby LSP's formatter or nothing). The editor text goes to RuboCop on stdin with the
  file's path, so the project's `.rubocop.yml` and its exclusions apply; nothing is written.
- **Code | Inspect Code with RuboCop** checks the current file and shows the Problems tool
  window. RuboCop runs through `bundle exec` when the bundle has it.
- RuboCop loads the project's configuration and plugins, so it runs only in trusted projects.

## Ruby LSP

Ruby LSP runs with the project's Ruby and its bundle; its formatter follows **Ruby LSP
formatter**. Forge uses `ruby-lsp` of the interpreter's gems, the **ruby-lsp executable**
setting or the `PATH`. When it is missing, Forge offers **Install Ruby LSP**: it runs `gem
install ruby-lsp --install-dir <Forge's data folder>/langservers/ruby/<version>` with the
project interpreter's RubyGems (rubygems.org or your gem sources) — nothing is bundled with
Forge and your Ruby's gems stay untouched — and starts the server with that folder on
`GEM_PATH`. Ruby LSP sets up its own bundle in `.ruby-lsp/` of the project, so it does not
start in Safe Mode.

## ERB

`.erb` files (`*.html.erb`, `*.text.erb`, `*.js.erb`, `.rhtml`) are a template language with
a [template data language](docs/guide/user/file-types.md#template-data-languages): HTML by default, or the language of the inner
extension (`welcome.text.erb` is plain text, `config.js.erb` JavaScript). `<%= %>`, `<%== %>`,
`<% %>` (with `-%>`), and `<%# %>` comments are highlighted over it, with Ruby's keywords and
common view helpers.

## IRB console

**Tools | Run IRB Console** opens a Terminal tab with `bundle exec irb -I lib` (or the
interpreter's `irb`). IRB reads the project's `.irbrc` and Bundler its Gemfile, so the console
is refused in Safe Mode.

## New projects

**File | New Project** has two Ruby generators: **Ruby Gem** runs `bundle gem` (Minitest,
RSpec or test-unit, RuboCop, an executable), with **Ruby Project** — a Gemfile, Rakefile,
`lib/`, `bin/`, Minitest tests and `.rubocop.yml` — as the offline fallback.

## Settings

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ruby interpreter | automatic | the project's Ruby (path or name) |
| Environment | — | `KEY=VALUE` variables of Ruby commands |
| Run commands with bundle exec | on | Bundler projects run gems through `bundle exec` |
| bundle executable | — | another `bundle` |
| Load tasks with rake --tasks | on | ask Rake (trusted projects) or read the Rakefile |
| Reformat Code with | RuboCop (safe) | RuboCop `-a`, RuboCop `-A`, Ruby LSP or nothing |
| Check files with RuboCop | on | on-the-fly and on-save RuboCop checks |
| rubocop executable, Additional options | — | another RuboCop, extra options (`--only Style`) |
| ruby-lsp executable, Ruby LSP formatter | —, automatic | Ruby LSP's executable and formatter |
| rdbg executable | — | another rdbg |

All keys are in the [settings reference](docs/guide/reference/settings.md#languages--frameworks--ruby).

# Ruby on Rails

The plugin **Ruby on Rails** (`forge.rails`) of [RubyForge](docs/guide/user/ruby.md) brings RubyMine's Rails
support to Forge. It is active in Rails applications: a `Gemfile` with `gem "rails"` (or
`railties`) and a `config/application.rb`. The status bar shows the version from
`Gemfile.lock` (`Rails 7`).

Everything is read from the project's files in Rust (`packs/rubyforge/fw-rails`): routes,
controllers, views, models, `db/schema.rb` and the migrations, `config/database.yml`, the locale
files and the Stimulus controllers. Nothing of the application runs, except the few commands
below that need it — and those only in [trusted projects](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md). Code insight for
Ruby itself comes from Ruby LSP, which Rails' features complement.

![ArticlesController with views and routes in the gutter and a folded translation](docs/screenshots/rails-controller.png)

## Routes (Endpoints)

**View | Tool Windows | Endpoints** (or **Show Rails Routes** in Find Action) lists the routes
like `bin/rails routes`: verb, URI pattern, prefix (the route's name: `article` gives
`article_path` and `article_url`) and `controller#action`.

![The Rails routes in the Endpoints tool window](docs/screenshots/rails-endpoints.png)

- Routes are read from `config/routes.rb` without running anything: `resources` and
  `resource` (with `only`, `except`, `controller`, `path`, `as`, `param`, nested resources,
  `member` / `collection` blocks and `on: :member`), `namespace`, `scope` (path, `module`,
  `as`, `controller`), `get` / `post` / `patch` / `put` / `delete` / `match … via:`, `root`,
  `mount`, `concern` / `concerns`, `redirect(…)` and `draw(:admin)` for
  `config/routes/admin.rb`.
- **Read routes with bin/rails routes** (Settings | Languages & Frameworks | Ruby | Rails, off
  by default) asks Rails instead, which also lists the routes of engines and gems (Devise,
  Turbo). It boots the application, so it runs only in trusted projects; Refresh runs it
  again. Each row keeps its place in `routes.rb` when Forge can match it.
- Click a row to open the controller action. The context menu jumps to the route,
  **Generate HTTP Request** opens a new [HTTP request](docs/guide/user/scratches-and-http.md) scratch (`GET
  http://localhost:3000/articles/1`; the host and port come from the first Rails run
  configuration), **Open in Browser**, and copies the URL, path or helper.
- The **Models** tab lists the ActiveRecord models with their table, columns and associations.

## Navigation

- **Navigate | Related Symbol** (`Ctrl+Alt+Home`) in a model, controller, view, helper, test,
  spec, fixture, factory or migration lists the other files of the resource: the model, the
  controllers (also namespaced ones), the views, the helper, tests and specs, fixtures and
  factories, the migrations that create or change the table and the lines of `routes.rb`.
- **Go to Declaration** (`Ctrl+B`, `Ctrl+Click`) on
  - a route helper (`articles_path`, `edit_article_url`) opens its route in `routes.rb`;
  - `render "form"`, `render partial: "comments/comment"`, `render @articles`, `render :edit`
    in a controller and `layout "admin"` open the partial, template or layout (partials are
    looked up in the view's folder, then `application/`);
  - a translation key (`t(".title")`, `I18n.t("articles.index.title")`) opens it in every
    locale file;
  - `data-controller`, `data-action` and `data-*-target` values open the Stimulus
    controller, method or target (also in `data: { controller: "hello" }` hashes);
  - a Turbo frame id (`turbo_frame_tag "comments"`, `<turbo-frame id>`, `data-turbo-frame`,
    `turbo_stream.replace "comments"`) shows the frame and its other uses;
  - a target in `routes.rb` (`"articles#index"`, `resources :articles`) opens the action.
- Gutter icons: an action leads to its views and lists its routes; a view leads to its
  action; a partial lists the places that render it; a model opens its table in
  `db/schema.rb` and the migrations; associations open their model; lines of `routes.rb` open
  the actions; Stimulus controllers list the views that use them and views mark their
  controllers.

## Completion

![Model attributes completed for a form builder](docs/screenshots/rails-view.png)

- Route helpers (`new_ar` → `new_article_path`) with their route.
- Partials and templates in `render "…"`, layouts in `layout "…"`.
- Translation keys in `t("…")`; in a view or action, `t(".` offers the keys of its lazy
  lookup scope (`articles.index.` in `articles/index.html.erb`).
- Model attributes from `db/schema.rb` and the newer migrations: `Article.where(ti` →
  `title:`, `order(:` / `pluck(:` → `:published_at`, `@article.` → columns and associations,
  `Article.` → scopes, `validates :` in a model, `form.text_field :` in a form for the model,
  and `params.require(:article).permit(:`.
- Stimulus identifiers in `data-controller`, `controller#method` in `data-action`, targets in
  `data-<identifier>-target`.
- Turbo helpers (`turbo_frame_tag`, `turbo_stream_from`), `turbo_stream.` actions and the
  frame ids of `turbo_stream.replace "…"` and `data-turbo-frame`.

## Inspections and folding

- **Missing translation** (*Ruby | Rails*): a key that `config/locales/**/*.yml` does not
  define is a warning; a key that some locales miss is a weak warning that names them. Keys of
  Rails itself (`helpers.`, `activerecord.`, `date.`, …) are not reported.
- **Unresolved partial or template**: `render` or `layout` names a file that `app/views` does
  not have.
- **Unknown Stimulus controller, action or target**.
- Translation calls fold to the text of the default locale (`config.i18n.default_locale`, else
  `en`): `t(".created")` reads *Article was successfully created.* until the caret is on it.
  **Fold translation calls** and **Report missing translations** turn this off.

## Run Rails Generator

**Tools | Run Rails Generator…** (`Ctrl+Alt+G`) completes the generators and runs
`bin/rails generate <generator> <arguments>` in the Run tool window: type the generator
(`Tab` completes it), then its arguments (`model Article title:string body:text`); the
generator's usage is shown below. **Pretend**, **Overwrite files** and **Skip existing** add
`--pretend`, `--force` and `--skip`. **Destroy Generated Code…** runs `bin/rails destroy`.

![Run Rails Generator](docs/screenshots/rails-generator.png)

The list comes from `bin/rails generate` (with the generators of the bundle's gems; **List
generators with bin/rails generate**), else from Rails' own generators and
`lib/generators`. Generators load the application, so they run only in trusted projects.

## Console and server

- **Tools | Run Rails Console** opens a Terminal tab with `bin/rails console` (environment and
  `--sandbox` from the settings); **Run Rails Database Console** runs `bin/rails dbconsole`.
  Both are refused in Safe Mode.
- The **Rails** run configuration runs `bin/rails server -b <IP address> -p <port> -e
  <environment>` with the project's Ruby, Ruby arguments and server arguments. Debug runs it
  under [rdbg](docs/guide/user/ruby.md#debugging). Without `bin/rails`, commands run as `bundle exec rails`.
- Database tasks (`db:migrate`, `db:rollback`, `db:seed`) are [Rake](docs/guide/user/ruby.md#rake) tasks: run
  them from the Rake tool window or as Rake configurations.

![The Rails run configuration in the Run tool window](docs/screenshots/rails-server.png)

## Data sources from database.yml

When a Rails project opens, a balloon offers the databases of `config/database.yml` that the
[Database](docs/guide/user/database.md) tool window does not have yet (**Offer data sources from
database.yml**); **Tools | Add Data Sources from database.yml** adds them any time. Each
environment becomes a project data source (`blog_development@localhost (development)`), and the
databases of multi-database setups (`production: primary:`, `cache:`) their own. Production
data sources get the production color, so unfiltered changes ask first.

- Adapters: `postgresql` / `postgis`, `mysql2` / `trilogy`, `sqlite3` (the file relative to
  the project), `sqlserver` and `oracle_enhanced`.
- The ERB in database.yml is read the simple way: `<%= ENV["X"] %>`, `<%= ENV.fetch("X") { 5
  } %>`, `<%= ENV.fetch("X", "d") %>` and `<%= ENV["X"] || "d" %>` take the variable (from the
  environment, the project's `.env` or **Settings | Ruby | Environment**) or the default;
  other Ruby is left out. `url:` is split into host, port, database and user.
- Passwords go to the OS keychain, like every data source password.

![Data sources added from database.yml](docs/screenshots/rails-database.png)

## Settings

**Settings | Languages & Frameworks | Ruby | Rails**:

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Read routes with bin/rails routes | off | ask Rails for the routes (trusted projects) instead of reading `routes.rb` |
| List generators with bin/rails generate | on | the generators of the application and its gems (trusted projects) |
| Console environment | — | the environment of the consoles (empty: development) |
| Run the console in a sandbox | off | `bin/rails console --sandbox` |
| Fold translation calls | on | `t(…)` shows the text of the default locale |
| Report missing translations | on | the Missing translation inspection |
| Offer data sources from database.yml | on | the balloon when a Rails project opens |

![Settings | Languages & Frameworks | Ruby | Rails](docs/screenshots/rails-settings.png)

All keys are in the [settings reference](docs/guide/reference/settings.md#languages--frameworks--ruby--rails).

Source: docs/guide/user/rust.md

# RustForge (Rust)

**RustForge** brings RustRover's Rust support to Forge. Its plugin **Rust** (`forge.rust`)
is active in [Rust projects](docs/guide/getting-started/project-detection.md): a `Cargo.toml`, a
`.rs` file in the root, or two or more `.rs` files in a folder.

- Highlighting of `.rs` files comes from CodeMirror's Rust grammar. Completion, navigation,
  hover, rename and diagnostics come from **rust-analyzer** (MIT OR Apache-2.0), which runs
  like every other [language server](docs/guide/user/language-servers.md).
- Everything else is computed in Rust (`packs/rustforge/*`): toolchains, `cargo metadata`,
  test discovery, command lines, Clippy messages and the debugger setup.

![cart.rs with run icons on the doctest of Cart::total, the test module and its tests](docs/screenshots/rust-editor.png)

## Toolchains

**Settings | Languages & Frameworks | Rust** shows the project's toolchain, the tools Forge
uses and the Rust settings.

![Settings | Languages & Frameworks | Rust](docs/screenshots/rust-settings.png)

- **Toolchain**: *rustup's choice* uses the toolchain rustup picks for the project folder
  (`rustup show active-toolchain`). The page says why: the rustup default, a
  `rust-toolchain.toml` / `rust-toolchain` file, a directory override or `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN`.
  Choosing an installed toolchain runs every cargo, rustc, rustfmt and Clippy command of the
  project with `cargo +<toolchain>`.
- Toolchains are read from `rustup toolchain list -v`. Without rustup, a `rustc` on the
  `PATH` (a distribution package or an official installer) is listed as a standalone
  toolchain.
- The page also shows `rustc -vV`, the project's toolchain file, the **sysroot** and the
  **standard library sources** (`<sysroot>/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library`, the `rust-src`
  component) that rust-analyzer and the debugger use for `std`.
- **Install…** installs a toolchain with `rustup toolchain install <name> --profile minimal
  --component clippy,rustfmt,rust-src`. **Install** next to a missing component (rustfmt,
  Clippy, rust-src, rust-analyzer) runs `rustup component add`. Both run in the Run tool
  window, and only after you agree.
- Forge never changes your toolchains while it only looks: every rustup and cargo command it
  runs on its own gets `RUSTUP_AUTO_INSTALL=0`, so a `rust-toolchain.toml` does not trigger
  an install behind your back.

## Cargo tool window

The **Cargo** tool window (right side) shows the workspace as `cargo metadata` reports it.

![The Cargo tool window with targets, feature checkboxes and dependencies](docs/screenshots/rust-cargo.png)

- **Members** with their **Targets**: lib, bin, test, bench, example, build script and proc
  macro. Double-click runs a binary or example (`cargo run`) or the tests of a target.
- **Features** with checkboxes. They edit **Settings | Rust | Cargo**: the features, *Use all
  features* and *Do not use the default features*. Every build, run and test and
  rust-analyzer use them. In a workspace with several members, features are stored as
  `<package>/<feature>`.
- **Dependencies**: the dependency tree of each member, like `cargo tree`. Packages that
  appeared before are marked `(*)` and not expanded again.
- Toolbar: **Reload Cargo Project**, **Run** and **Debug** the selected target, **Build**,
  **Check**, **Documentation**, **Clean** and **Update** (`cargo update`) for the selected
  package, or for the workspace when nothing is selected.

`cargo metadata` runs only in trusted projects (a project's `.cargo/config.toml` can name
programs). Its result is cached in Forge's cache folder (`<cache>/forge/rust/`) and is read
again when a `Cargo.toml` or `Cargo.lock` changes, or when you click Reload.

## Run configurations

| Type | Options | Command |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Cargo** | Command (`run`, `build --release`, `test --doc`, `clippy -- -W clippy::pedantic` or any other), package, target (`bin:shop`, `example:report`), features, profile, target triple, toolchain | `cargo [+toolchain] <command> -p … --bin … --features … -- <program arguments>` |
| **Cargo Test** | Scope (all, package, target, test, filter), package, target (`lib`, `test:checkout`, `doc` for doctests), test name and *Exact name*, tests or benchmarks, test runner, features, profile, target triple, toolchain, cargo options | `cargo test --no-fail-fast … -- <filter> --exact`, `cargo bench`, `cargo nextest run` or `cargo llvm-cov` |

Both types have the usual environment variables, working directory and
[Run on](docs/guide/user/run-debug.md) targets. Your own options in the command win over the form: a
`--release` in the command is not repeated by the profile.

- **▶ on `fn main`** of binaries and examples offers *Run*, *Debug* and *Modify Run
  Configuration…* with a temporary Cargo configuration (`cargo run -p shop-cli --bin shop`).
- **▶ on tests**: `#[test]`, `#[tokio::test]`, `#[async_std::test]` and other
  `#[<runtime>::test]` attributes, `#[bench]` (nightly), test modules (`mod tests`), and
  **doctests** — fenced code blocks in `///` and `//!` comments whose info string is Rust
  (empty, `rust`, `no_run`, `should_panic`, `compile_fail`, `edition2021`, …; not `ignore`,
  `text` or another language). Doctests run with `cargo test --doc -- "<file> - <item> (line
  N)" --exact`.

## Tests

Test runs fill the shared [test tree](docs/guide/user/testing.md), with a suite per test binary (`src/lib.rs`,
`tests/checkout.rs`, `Doc-tests shop_core`).

![All tests of the shop workspace: a failed assert_eq!, the integration test and the doctests](docs/screenshots/rust-test-tree.png)

- **Output format**: on a nightly toolchain Forge asks libtest for JSON (`-Z unstable-options
  --format json --report-time`). On stable it reads libtest's plain output, so test
  durations are not shown. **Settings | Rust | Tests | Test results** can force either.
- **cargo-nextest** (Settings | Rust | Tests | Test runner, or per configuration) runs tests
  with `cargo nextest run --message-format libtest-json`. Doctests and benchmarks always run
  with cargo test, because nextest does not run them.
- Failures show the panic message and location. `assert_eq!` values open in **Click to see
  difference** (left as expected, right as actual).
- Test locations map back to files through the workspace's modules, so a test opens at its
  function and the gutter icons show the last result.
- **Rerun Failed Tests** runs the failed tests by their exact names
  (`-- --exact a::b c::d`).
- **Run with Coverage** uses **cargo-llvm-cov** (`cargo llvm-cov --lcov --output-path …`) and
  shows the LCOV report in the [Coverage tool window](docs/guide/user/coverage.md). Forge offers to install
  cargo-llvm-cov and cargo-nextest with `cargo install --locked` from Settings | Rust.

## Clippy and rustfmt

- **Run Clippy** (Find Action, or *Run Clippy on save* in Settings | Rust | External Linter)
  runs `cargo clippy --all-targets --message-format=json` for the file's package. Problems
  appear in the editor and the Problems tool window. Clippy's suggestions are quick fixes
  under **Alt+Enter**, so *Try: `cents == 0`* replaces the code it marks. Clippy builds the
  code, so it runs only in trusted projects.

![Clippy problems in money.rs and the Problems tool window, with the quick fix under Alt+Enter](docs/screenshots/rust-clippy.png)

- **Reformat Code** (`Ctrl+Alt+L`) and *Reformat code* on save use **rustfmt** with the
  package's edition and the nearest `rustfmt.toml` / `.rustfmt.toml`, like `cargo fmt`.
  **Settings | Rust | Rustfmt | Reformat Code with** can switch to rust-analyzer's formatting
  or turn formatting off.

## rust-analyzer

Forge starts rust-analyzer from the active toolchain (`rustup component add rust-analyzer`).
Without it, Forge uses its own download, then a rust-analyzer on the `PATH`; you can also
set **rust-analyzer executable**. When rust-analyzer is missing, a balloon offers *Install
with rustup*. Without rustup, it offers *Download…*: Forge downloads a pinned release
from [rust-lang/rust-analyzer's GitHub releases](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-analyzer/releases),
checks it against the SHA-256 digest GitHub publishes for the asset, and keeps it in
`<data dir>/forge/langservers/rust-analyzer`.

Settings | Rust | rust-analyzer configures it:

- **Check on save** with **Clippy** or **cargo check**,
- the Cargo **features** of the tool window,
- a **target triple** (`wasm32-unknown-unknown`),
- **Expand procedural macros** and **Run build scripts**.

rust-analyzer runs the project's build scripts and proc macros, so
[Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md) does not start it.

## Debugging

**Debug** on a Cargo or Cargo Test configuration, or on a ▶ icon, first builds it with
`--message-format=json` (`cargo build`, or `cargo test --no-run` for tests). It then starts
the executable cargo reports under the built-in **LLDB** (`lldb-dap`) or **GDB**
(`gdb -i dap`) adapter of the [debugger](docs/guide/user/debugging.md). *Settings | Rust | Debugger*
chooses the debugger; *auto* uses LLDB when lldb-dap is installed.

![Debugging shop with LLDB: Vec, String, Option and HashMap shown with rustc's pretty printers](docs/screenshots/rust-debug.png)

- **Rust type renderers**: Forge loads rustc's own pretty printers from the toolchain's
  sysroot (`lib/rustlib/etc`), the same ones `rust-lldb` and `rust-gdb` load. For LLDB,
  `lldb_lookup.py` and `lldb_commands` go in as `initCommands`. For GDB, the `rust-gdb`
  adapter adds the folder to the auto-load safe path and sources
  `gdb_load_rust_pretty_printers.py`. `Vec`, `String`, `&str`, `Option`, `Result`,
  `HashMap`, `Rc` and friends then show as values with their elements.
- With `rust-src` installed, `/rustc/<commit>` paths map to the toolchain's sources, so
  stepping into `std` opens real files.
- Tests are debugged one test binary at a time, with `--nocapture --test-threads=1`. Doctests
  are compiled by rustdoc and cannot be debugged.
- The Memory, Disassembly and Registers views, watchpoints and core dumps work as for any
  native program.

## Settings

All keys are listed in the [settings reference](docs/guide/reference/settings.md) under
*Languages & Frameworks | Rust*.

Source: docs/guide/user/go.md

# GoForge (Go)

**GoForge** brings GoLand's Go support to Forge. Its plugin **Go** (`forge.go`) is active in
[Go projects](docs/guide/getting-started/project-detection.md): a `go.mod` or `go.work` in the root
or one folder below, Go files in the root, or two or more `.go` files in a folder.

- Highlighting of `.go` files comes from CodeMirror's Go grammar; completion, navigation,
  hover, rename and diagnostics come from **gopls** (BSD-3-Clause), started like every other
  [language server](docs/guide/user/language-servers.md).
- Everything else — SDK detection and downloads, `go.mod` analysis, test discovery, command
  lines, lint reports, debugging and profiles — is computed in Rust (`packs/goforge/*`).

![A Go test file with run icons on the package, tests, subtests, the benchmark, the fuzz test and the example](docs/screenshots/go-editor.png)

## Go SDK (GOROOT) and GOPATH

**Settings | Languages & Frameworks | Go** shows the project's SDK, the Go tools and the Go
settings in one page.

![Settings | Languages & Frameworks | Go](docs/screenshots/go-settings.png)

- **GOROOT**: *Automatic* uses the newest SDK Forge finds without running anything: the `go`
  on the `PATH`, `GOROOT`, `/usr/local/go`, `/usr/lib/go`, `/usr/lib/golang`, `/opt/go`,
  Snap, Homebrew (`/opt/homebrew/opt/go/libexec`, `/usr/local/opt/go/libexec`, Linuxbrew),
  `C:\Program Files\Go`, `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Go`, SDKs of `golang.org/dl` (`~/sdk/go1.x`),
  `~/go/go1.x` and Forge's own downloads. The version comes from the SDK's `VERSION` file.
  Choose another SDK in the list; the choice (`go.goroot`) is stored with the project.
- **Download…** lists the stable releases of `go.dev/dl` (`?mode=json`, which names the SHA-256
  of every archive) for this platform. After you agree, Forge downloads the archive, checks
  its SHA-256, unpacks it into `<data dir>/forge/go-sdks/go<version>` and makes it the
  project's GOROOT. **SDK download source** (`go.sdk.downloadSource`) points at a mirror.
  When a Go project opens and no SDK is found, a balloon offers the download.
- **Project GOPATH** (`go.gopath`), **GOFLAGS** (`go.goflags`), **Build tags**
  (`go.buildTags`) and **Environment** (`go.environment`, `KEY=VALUE` entries such as
  `GOPRIVATE` or `CGO_ENABLED=0`) apply to every build, run, test, `go generate`, `go vet` and
  debug session of the project.

### Go tools

The page lists the tools GoForge uses, where they were found (the path in the settings,
Forge's tools folder, `GOBIN`, `GOPATH/bin`, the SDK's `bin`, `PATH`) and their licence:

| Tool | Used for | Install |
| --- | --- | --- |
| gopls | the language server | `go install golang.org/x/tools/gopls@v0.23.0` (Go 1.25+) or `@v0.20.0` |
| Delve (`dlv`) | debugging | `go install github.com/go-delve/delve/cmd/dlv@v1.27.2` (Go 1.25+) or `@v1.25.2` |
| goimports | Reformat Code with goimports | `go install golang.org/x/tools/cmd/goimports@v0.30.0` |
| golangci-lint | the golangci-lint annotator | not installed by Forge (GPL-3.0): install it from golangci-lint.run |

**Install** runs the `go install` line with your Go toolchain in the Run tool window
(`GOBIN` = `<data dir>/forge/go-tools/bin`, `GOTOOLCHAIN=auto`), so modules come from your
module proxy and are verified by the Go checksum database. The versions are pinned per SDK
version because Delve only debugs the Go versions it supports.

## go.mod and go.work

`go.mod`, `go.work` and `go.sum` have their own file types (**Go Module**, **Go Workspace**,
**Go Checksums**) with highlighting of directives, module paths, versions and comments.

![Version completion in go.mod](docs/screenshots/go-mod.png)

- Problems are reported while you type: unknown directives, malformed `require`, `replace`
  and `exclude` lines, invalid versions (`v1.2.3`, pseudo-versions and `+incompatible` are
  valid), invalid `go` versions, a missing `module` statement, a missing `)`.
- **Completion** (`Ctrl+Space`): directives at the start of a line; module paths from the
  file's requirements and the module cache (`$GOMODCACHE/cache/download`); versions of a
  module from the module proxy (the first entry of `GOPROXY`, `proxy.golang.org` by default),
  newest first with the latest release marked, cached for 12 hours in
  `<cache dir>/forge/go-proxy` and answered from the cache when the proxy is offline; `go`
  versions of the installed SDKs. **Look up module versions on the module proxy**
  (`go.modules.proxyLookups`) turns the lookups off.
- Actions (Find Action, `Ctrl+Shift+A`): **Sync Dependencies (go mod tidy)**, **Download
  Dependencies (go mod download)** and **Add Dependency…** (`go get module[@version]`). They
  run in the module's folder and show their output in the Run tool window.

## Formatting and annotators

- **Reformat Code** (`Ctrl+Alt+L`) and "Reformat code" on save use **gofmt** by default;
  `go.formatter` switches to **goimports** (also fixes imports), **gopls** or nothing.
- **go vet** runs for the saved file's package after every save (`go.vet.onSave`) and on
  demand (**Run go vet**); its JSON report (`go vet -json`) becomes problems in the editor and
  the Problems tool window.
- **golangci-lint** uses the project's `.golangci.yml` (v1 and v2 are both supported):
  **Run golangci-lint** checks the whole project, `go.golangciLint.onSave` checks the saved
  file's package. Its JSON report becomes problems with the linter as the code.

![golangci-lint problems in the editor and the Problems tool window](docs/screenshots/go-lint.png)

go vet and golangci-lint build the code (and golangci-lint may load plugins), so they run only
in [trusted projects](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md).

## go generate

Every `//go:generate` directive gets a ▶ icon in the gutter: it runs `go generate -run` for
exactly that directive in the file's module. **Run go generate for File** runs all
directives of the open file.

## Go Build

The **Go Build** run configuration builds a package (`./cmd/ledger` or an import path of a
project module), a directory or files:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Run kind | Package, Directory or File |
| Run after build | on: `go run …` with the program arguments; off: `go build -o <output>` |
| Output directory or file | `-o` of `go build` |
| Build tags | added to the project's build tags (`-tags`) |
| Go tool arguments | more flags, e.g. `-race -trimpath` |
| Program arguments | the program's own arguments |

The command runs in the package's module folder unless the configuration sets a working
directory. Debug (`Shift+F9`) starts the same configuration under Delve.

## Go Test

**Go Test** configurations run `go test -json` and show the results in the test tree; a
failing test's `file_test.go:16:` line becomes its message, expected / actual values and a
link.

![The test tree of TestRound with the failing subtest](docs/screenshots/go-test-tree.png)

- **Gutter icons** appear on the `package` clause (all tests of the package), every
  `func TestXxx(t *testing.T)`, `BenchmarkXxx`, `FuzzXxx` and `ExampleXxx`, and on subtests
  and sub-benchmarks started with a literal name (`t.Run("half up", …)`, any depth). After a
  run they show the last result. Subtest names follow `go test`: spaces become `_`.
- **Scopes**: all packages (`./...`), a directory (with or without sub folders), a file (its
  top-level tests), one test or subtest (`-run '^TestRound$/^half_up$'`), or a name pattern.
- **Run**: Tests, **Benchmarks** (`-run '^$' -bench … -benchmem`, optional benchmark time) or
  **Fuzzing** (`-fuzz`, one fuzz test of one package, **Fuzz time** defaulting to
  `go.test.fuzztime`, 10s).
- **Count**, **Build tags**, **Go tool arguments** (`-race -v`) and program arguments (`-args`).
- **Run with Coverage** adds `-coverprofile`; the profile shows in the
  [Coverage tool window](docs/guide/user/coverage.md) and the editor gutter.
- **Rerun Failed Tests** runs the failed top-level tests in their packages
  (`-run '^(TestRound|TestParse)$'`).
- Modules in sub folders run with `go -C <module>`; import paths in the results and coverage
  are mapped to project files.

## Debugging with Delve

Debug (`Shift+F9`) on a Go Build or Go Test configuration starts **Delve** (`dlv dap`, MIT) on
the shared [debugger](docs/guide/user/debugging.md): breakpoints, conditions, logpoints, stepping, goroutines
as threads, variables, watches and evaluation, memory and disassembly views. If Delve is
missing, Forge offers to install it with your Go toolchain.

![A Delve session stopped in report.Total](docs/screenshots/go-debug.png)

- Go Build sessions use Delve's `debug` mode, Go Test sessions its `test` mode for one
  package (fuzz tests run their seed corpus). The program is built into the system temp
  folder, never into the project.
- **Attach to Process…** (`Ctrl+Alt+F5`) lists local processes; choose **Go (Delve)** to
  attach (`mode: local`). **Debug Core Dump…** opens a core file of a Go program.
- **Go Remote** configurations connect to a Delve server started with
  `dlv debug --headless --listen=:2345 --accept-multiclient` (Delve 1.20 or newer), e.g. in a
  container; **Project folder on the remote side** maps breakpoints (`substitutePath`).

Launching programs is refused in Safe Mode; attaching is allowed.

## Profiler

The **Profiler** tool window (shared with [PyForge's cProfile snapshots](docs/guide/user/python.md#profiler);
a project that uses both shows a **cProfile** and a **pprof** tab) shows pprof profiles: a
**Flame Graph** (callers below their
callees; click a frame to zoom, double-click to open its source), the **Call Tree** with total
and self values, and the **Method List** (flat and cumulative values, like `pprof -top`). The
sample type (CPU time, allocations, in-use memory, contentions, …) is chosen on top.

![The CPU profile of BenchmarkReport as a flame graph](docs/screenshots/go-profiler.png)

- Set **Profile** of a Go Test configuration to CPU, Memory, Blocking or Mutex: the run writes
  `-cpuprofile` (…) into `<cache dir>/forge/go-profiles` and the Profiler opens it when the
  run ends. **Profile Test with CPU Profiler** / **Memory Profiler** run the test or
  benchmark at the caret that way.
- **Open Profile (pprof)…** opens any profile file (`go test -cpuprofile`, `runtime/pprof`,
  `net/http/pprof` downloads), gzip compressed or not; the folder icon in the Profiler's
  header does the same.

![The call tree of the profile](docs/screenshots/go-profiler-tree.png)

## Settings

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `go.goroot` | (automatic) | the project's SDK folder |
| `go.sdk.downloadSource` | `https://go.dev/dl` | where Download Go SDK gets releases |
| `go.gopath` | (Go's default) | GOPATH of the project's go commands |
| `go.goflags` |  | GOFLAGS of the project's go commands |
| `go.buildTags` | `[]` | build tags of builds, runs and tests |
| `go.environment` | `[]` | `KEY=VALUE` variables of the project's go commands |
| `go.formatter` | `gofmt` | `gofmt`, `goimports`, `lsp` or `none` |
| `go.goimports.path` |  | goimports executable |
| `go.vet.onSave` | `true` | run go vet for the saved file's package |
| `go.golangciLint.onSave` | `false` | run golangci-lint for the saved file's package |
| `go.golangciLint.path` |  | golangci-lint executable |
| `go.delve.path` |  | dlv executable |
| `go.test.fuzztime` | `10s` | default `-fuzztime` |
| `go.modules.proxyLookups` | `true` | module versions from the module proxy |

gopls has its own settings in Settings | Language Servers (`langservers.servers.gopls.*`).

## Browser mode

`pnpm dev` with `?project=go` opens the `ledger` demo module (a money package with tests,
subtests, a benchmark, a fuzz test and an example; a report package with a `//go:generate`
directive; a store for golangci-lint to find). The mocks run the Rust crates as WebAssembly;
test runs, the Delve session and the profile are simulated.
