Source: docs/guide/user/java.md

# JavaForge

**JavaForge** (plugin `forge.java`) brings Java to Forge in the style of IntelliJ IDEA. It
activates in [Java projects](docs/guide/getting-started/project-detection.md): a `pom.xml`, a Gradle
build (`build.gradle`, `build.gradle.kts`, `settings.gradle`, `settings.gradle.kts`), `*.java`
files in a folder or a `src/main/java` / `src/test/java` tree. Maven and Gradle are reported as
the project's tools.

![The Java editor with completion from Eclipse JDT LS](docs/screenshots/java-editor-completion.png)

## Eclipse JDT Language Server

Code intelligence comes from [Eclipse JDT LS](https://github.com/eclipse-jdtls/eclipse.jdt.ls)
(EPL-2.0) through Forge's shared language server client: completion, Go to Declaration and
Implementation, Find Usages, hover with Javadoc, parameter info, diagnostics in the editor and
the Problems tool window, Rename, quick fixes and code actions (`Alt+Enter`), Optimize Imports
(`Ctrl+Alt+O`) and Reformat Code (`Ctrl+Alt+L`).

JDT LS is never bundled with Forge. When a Java project opens without it, a balloon offers
**Install**, **Not now** and **Don't ask again** (setting **Install Eclipse JDT LS**: Ask,
Always, Never). Install downloads, with your consent:

- the newest JDT LS milestone (or snapshot, see **Release channel**) from
  `download.eclipse.org/jdtls`, checked against the `.sha256` file published next to it, into
  `<data dir>/forge/langservers/jdtls/<version>`;
- Microsoft's [java-debug](https://github.com/microsoft/java-debug) plugin (EPL-1.0) from
  Maven Central, checked against the repository's checksum, into
  `<data dir>/forge/langservers/java-debug`.

Progress shows in the status bar. **Install Eclipse JDT Language Server** in Find Action
(`Ctrl+Shift+A`) installs or updates both at any time.

![The install offer](docs/screenshots/java-jdtls-install.png)

Forge starts JDT LS itself, like the official `jdtls` launcher: with a JDK that it can run on
(Java 21 for 2024–2025 builds; newer builds need Java 25, which Forge reads from the bundles of
the installation), the installation read-only, and its OSGi configuration and the workspace data
in the user cache directory (`<cache dir>/forge/jdtls`), never inside the project. Every
detected JDK is announced to JDT LS as a runtime, the project JDK as the default.

While JDT LS imports a Maven or Gradle build, the status bar shows its progress ("Importing
Gradle project(s) 45%"). After editing a build file, run **Reload All Maven and Gradle Projects**
(Find Action, the main menu's Build menu or the Gradle / Maven tool window) to re-import it.

Settings | Languages & Frameworks | **Java** shows the installed versions and the JDK JDT LS runs
on, and has these options:

| Setting | |
| --- | --- |
| Install Eclipse JDT LS | Ask, Always or Never when a Java project opens without it |
| JDT LS installation | Use your own unpacked JDT LS (a folder with `plugins/` and `config_*`) |
| JDK for the language server | The JDK that runs JDT LS; empty: the project JDK when it is new enough, else the newest that is |
| VM options | `-Xmx1G` by default |
| Release channel | Milestones or snapshots |
| Download site | `https://download.eclipse.org/jdtls` |
| Hot code replace | Automatically, on request or never (see [Debugging](#debugging)) |
| java-debug repository | `https://repo1.maven.org/maven2` |

![Settings | Languages & Frameworks | Java](docs/screenshots/java-settings-jdtls.png)

JDT LS imports and builds projects, which runs code of the project (Gradle build scripts,
annotation processors), so it does not start in [Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md). It runs for local
projects; remote projects do not start it yet.

Minecraft server and proxy plugins (Paper, Spigot, Velocity, …) and Fabric / NeoForge mods have their own project
wizard, descriptor support and Run Paper Server configuration: see
[Minecraft plugins](docs/guide/user/minecraft.md).

## JDKs

Settings | Build, Execution, Deployment | **JDKs** combines IntelliJ's SDK list and Project
settings:

- **Project JDK**: the JDK the project builds and runs with (empty: the newest). Runs of Maven
  and Gradle get it as `JAVA_HOME`.
- **Language level**: the Java release of the sources; empty means the build's (toolchain,
  `maven.compiler.release`) or the project JDK's.
- The JDK list: every JDK Forge detects, with its name (`temurin-21`), home, version, vendor and
  where it was found. Detection reads each JDK's `release` file and looks at `JAVA_HOME`, `java`
  on `PATH`, `/usr/lib/jvm` and `/usr/java` (Linux), `/Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines` and
  `~/Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines` (macOS), `Program Files` and the registry (Windows),
  SDKMAN! (`~/.sdkman/candidates/java`), asdf, jabba, Gradle toolchains (`~/.gradle/jdks`),
  IntelliJ's `~/.jdks` and Forge's own downloads. A JRE without `javac` is not listed.
- **+** adds a JDK from disk, **Detect Again** rescans.

![Settings | Build, Execution, Deployment | JDKs](docs/screenshots/java-jdks-settings.png)

**Download JDK…** (the download button, or Find Action) downloads Eclipse Temurin from the
[Adoptium API](https://api.adoptium.net) (setting **Adoptium API**): pick a version (LTS releases
are marked), and Forge downloads the build for your platform, checks it against the SHA-256 the
API publishes and unpacks it into `<data dir>/forge/jdks/<release>`.

![Download JDK](docs/screenshots/java-jdk-download.png)

## Maven and Gradle

Forge reads the build in the project root: the tool (with both a `pom.xml` and a Gradle build,
setting **Build tool of projects with both**), the wrapper (`mvnw`, `gradlew`) and its Gradle
version, the Kotlin or Groovy DSL, modules (`include` in `settings.gradle(.kts)`, `<modules>` in
`pom.xml`), JaCoCo, the `application` plugin and its main class, Spring Boot, custom tasks and
the Java release.

- **Build Project** (`Ctrl+F9`) compiles main and test sources through the build tool
  (Gradle `classes testClasses`, Maven `test-compile`), or through Eclipse JDT LS with
  **Build and run using: IntelliJ IDEA**.
- **Reload All Maven and Gradle Projects** (the tool windows' ⟳, Build menu) syncs: the build
  tool reports tasks and resolved dependencies, then JDT LS re-imports the build files.
  Gradle and Maven run the project's build scripts and plugins, so
  [Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md) refuses a sync until you trust the project.

### Gradle tool window

The **Gradle** tool window (right stripe) shows the root project and its subprojects with:

- **Tasks** grouped like `gradle tasks --all` (application, build, build setup, documentation,
  help, verification, other). Double-click or ▶ runs one as a temporary Gradle configuration
  (`:app:test` in a subproject).
- **Dependencies** per configuration (`compileClasspath`, `runtimeClasspath`,
  `testCompileClasspath`, `testRuntimeClasspath`, `annotationProcessor`) as resolved trees:
  `1.0 → 1.2` where conflict resolution picked another version, `(*)` for dependencies listed
  above, unresolved ones in red. Before the first sync the tool window lists the dependencies
  the build file declares.
- **Source Sets**: `main`, `test` and other source sets with their `java`, `groovy`, `kotlin`,
  `scala` and `resources` folders (the applied plugins' conventions before a sync, Gradle's
  `sourceSets` after it; see [Groovy and Scala](docs/guide/user/groovy-scala.md#groovy-source-sets)). The Maven
  tool window shows the conventional folders too (GMavenPlus adds `groovy`).
- **Run Configurations**: the project's Gradle configurations.

The toolbar: **Reload All Gradle Projects**, **Execute Gradle Task…** (a command line with
completion of every task, `clean :app:test --info`), **Run**, **Expand All** / **Collapse
All**, **Toggle Offline Mode** (`--offline` for syncs and runs), **Show Dependencies** and
**Gradle Settings**.

A sync runs Gradle with a small init script (`forge-model.gradle`, written to the user cache
directory) whose `forgeModel` task writes the projects, tasks, source sets and dependency trees as JSON
(`--no-configuration-cache`). The result is cached in `<cache>/forge/javaforge/sync`, never in
the project, so the tool window shows it again after a restart.

![The Gradle tool window after a sync](docs/screenshots/java-gradle-tool-window.png)

![Execute Gradle Task](docs/screenshots/java-gradle-execute-task.png)

### Maven tool window

The **Maven** tool window shows **Profiles** with checkboxes (`activeByDefault` profiles start
checked; unchecking one deactivates it with `!id`), then the project and its modules with
**Lifecycle** (clean … deploy), **Plugins** (the default lifecycle plugins and those in
`<build><plugins>`, each with its goals, `jacoco:report`) and **Dependencies** (the tree of
`mvn dependency:tree` with scopes after a sync, the declared ones before).

The toolbar: **Reload All Maven Projects**, **Execute Maven Goal…**, **Run Maven Build**,
**Toggle Offline Mode** (`-o`), **Toggle 'Skip Tests' Mode** (`-DskipTests`; test runs ignore
it), **Expand All** / **Collapse All**, **Show Dependencies** and **Maven Settings**. The
selected profiles (`-Pdev,!prod`) apply to every Maven run.

![The Maven tool window with profiles](docs/screenshots/java-maven-tool-window.png)

### Gradle settings and the wrapper

Settings | Build, Execution, Deployment | Build Tools | Gradle:

| Setting | |
| --- | --- |
| **Use Gradle from** | `'gradle-wrapper.properties' file` (the wrapper, default), **Specified location** (**Gradle home**: a Gradle installation or its `bin/gradle`) or **Local installation** (`gradle` on the `PATH`). |
| **Gradle JVM** | The JDK Gradle syncs, builds and runs with (empty: the project JDK). |
| **Offline work** | `--offline`. |
| **Build and run using** | **Gradle** (default): Build Project runs `classes testClasses`, Application configurations run through Gradle (`forgeRun`, a `JavaExec` task of the init script `forge-run.gradle`, with the main class, arguments, VM options and the source set's runtime class path and toolchain). **IntelliJ IDEA**: JDT LS compiles, Forge runs `java` with the class path java-debug resolves. |
| **Run tests using** | **Gradle** (default) or **IntelliJ IDEA**: JUnit tests run on the JUnit Platform Console Launcher (`junit-platform-console-standalone.jar`: the **JUnit Platform Console Launcher** setting, else the newest in `~/.m2` or Gradle's cache) with JDT LS's class path; TestNG and Run with Coverage always use Gradle. |

The page shows the project's **Gradle wrapper**: the version and distribution from
`gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties` and its `distributionSha256Sum`. **Verify** compares
the checksum with the one Gradle publishes on services.gradle.org (the wrapper refuses a
download whose checksum does not match). **Update Wrapper** (also the action *Update Gradle
Wrapper…*) points `distributionUrl` at the newest release, or the version you enter, and writes
the published SHA-256 sum as `distributionSha256Sum`; it edits the properties file only, so it
runs no project code. The new Gradle is downloaded by the wrapper on its next run.

![Settings | Build Tools | Gradle](docs/screenshots/java-gradle-settings.png)

Maven's page has **Use the Maven wrapper**, **Maven home path**, **Work offline**, **Skip
tests** and **Download sources of dependencies**.

### Editing build scripts

`build.gradle.kts` (Kotlin DSL) and `build.gradle` (Groovy DSL) are highlighted as Kotlin and
Groovy. Completion knows the common blocks and functions of the block the caret is in, with
insert texts in the script's DSL (`implementation("…")` / `implementation '…'`):

- top level: `plugins`, `dependencies`, `repositories`, `java`, `application`, `jacoco`,
  `tasks`, `group`, `version`, `sourceSets`, `configurations`, `buildscript`, `allprojects`,
  `subprojects`, `testing`; settings scripts: `rootProject.name`, `include`, `includeBuild`,
  `pluginManagement`, `dependencyResolutionManagement`;
- `plugins` (core plugins, `id(…) version …`, `kotlin(…)`, plugin ids in `id("…")`),
  `dependencies` (`implementation`, `api`, `compileOnly`, `runtimeOnly`, `annotationProcessor`,
  `testImplementation`, … and `platform`, `project`, `files`, `testFixtures`), `repositories`,
  `java { toolchain { languageVersion, vendor } }`, `application { mainClass }`, `jacoco`,
  `tasks.register<Type>("name")`, `named`, `withType`, `test { useJUnitPlatform() … }`,
  `jacocoTestReport { reports { … } }`, `jar { manifest { … } }`;
- members after `tasks.`, `JavaLanguageVersion.`, `JvmVendorSpec.`, `JavaVersion.`.

In a dependency string (`implementation("guav")`) and in `<groupId>`, `<artifactId>` and
`<version>` of `pom.xml`, completion offers coordinates and versions from **Maven Central**
(newest first; typing `:` after the group or artifact moves on to artifacts and versions).
Answers are cached in `<cache>/forge/maven-central`; offline, the cache and a few well-known
artifacts answer.

**A newer version is available**: declared versions older than the newest release of the same
variant (Guava's `-jre` stays `-jre`; pre-releases only replace pre-releases) get a weak
warning and a gutter icon; **Alt+Enter → Change to …** (or a click on the icon) writes the new
version, in `pom.xml` into the property that holds it (`${guava.version}`).

Settings | Build, Execution, Deployment | Build Tools: **Search Maven Central** turns the lookups
off; **Search API** and **Repository** point them at a mirror.

![Kotlin DSL completion](docs/screenshots/java-gradle-kts-dsl-completion.png)

![Coordinate completion from Maven Central](docs/screenshots/java-gradle-kts-completion.png)

![The newer-version quick fix in pom.xml](docs/screenshots/java-pom-outdated.png)

## Run configurations

| Type | |
| --- | --- |
| **Application** | Runs a main class with the configuration's JDK (empty: the project JDK), VM options, program arguments, environment and working directory. In Gradle projects it runs through Gradle by default (**Build and run using**, see [Gradle settings](#gradle-settings-and-the-wrapper)). Otherwise the class path comes from the build through JDT LS (java-debug resolves it after JDT LS compiled the project); without JDT LS it is the module's build output (`build/classes/java/main`, `target/classes`). **Class path** and **Java module** (`-m module/class`) override it. |
| **Gradle** | Runs tasks (`clean build`), optionally in a module (`:app:build`). |
| **Maven** | Runs goals (`clean install -DskipTests`), optionally in a module (`-pl app -am`). |
| **JUnit**, **TestNG** | Runs all tests, a package, a class, a method or a list of tests through the build tool; see [Tests](#tests). |
| **Remote JVM Debug** | Attaches the debugger to a JVM started with `-agentlib:jdwp=transport=dt_socket,server=y,suspend=n,address=*:5005`. |

Spring Boot applications have their own **Spring Boot** configuration type with profiles and
override properties, see [Spring Boot and Jakarta EE](docs/guide/user/spring.md#spring-boot-run-configuration).

A green ▶ in the gutter next to a `main` method (`public static void main(String[] args)`, and
Java 25's instance `void main()` and compact source files) offers Run, Debug and Modify Run
Configuration; `Ctrl+Shift+F10` runs the class at the caret.

![The Run gutter on main](docs/screenshots/java-run-gutter.png)

## Tests

JUnit 5 (`@Test`, `@ParameterizedTest`, `@RepeatedTest`, `@TestFactory`, `@TestTemplate`,
`@Nested` classes), JUnit 4 (`@Test`), JUnit 3 (`TestCase` subclasses with `test*` methods) and
TestNG (method and class level `@Test`) get gutter icons on their classes and methods, chosen by
the file's imports. They run on the [shared test runner](docs/guide/user/testing.md) through the build tool, as
IntelliJ delegates to Gradle and Maven:

- Gradle: `cleanTest test --tests 'com.acme.CartTest.adds'` (so up-to-date tests run again);
- Maven Surefire: `test -Dtest='com.acme.CartTest#adds' -Dsurefire.failIfNoSpecifiedTests=false`.

The results come from the JUnit XML reports the build writes (`build/test-results/test`,
`target/surefire-reports`), which Forge empties before the run. The tree links tests and stack
traces to their sources; **Rerun Failed Tests** runs the failed ones only.

![A JUnit 5 run through Gradle](docs/screenshots/java-junit-tree.png)

**Run with Coverage** works when the build configures JaCoCo: Gradle runs `jacocoTestReport`
(enable its XML report: `reports { xml.required = true }`), Maven runs
`org.jacoco:jacoco-maven-plugin:report` (with `prepare-agent` bound in the build). Forge reads
`build/reports/jacoco/test/jacocoTestReport.xml` or `target/site/jacoco/jacoco.xml` into the
[Coverage](docs/guide/user/coverage.md) tool window and the editor gutter.

## Debugging

Debug (`Shift+F9`) on an Application, Gradle (`run` and friends), JUnit or TestNG configuration
starts the JVM with a JDWP agent that waits for the debugger (Application: a free port;
Gradle: `--debug-jvm` on port 5005; Maven Surefire: `-Dmaven.surefire.debug`), and attaches
java-debug as soon as the JVM listens. java-debug runs inside JDT LS and serves the Debug
Adapter Protocol, so the [Debug tool window](docs/guide/user/debugging.md) works as for every other language:
threads, frames, variables with expandable objects, watches, Evaluate Expression, breakpoints
with conditions and logpoints, exception breakpoints (caught and uncaught) and inline values.

**Remote JVM Debug** attaches to a JVM on another machine or in a container at `host:port`.

**Hot code replace**: with **Automatically** (the default), java-debug reloads changed classes
into the running JVM after JDT LS rebuilt them on save.

![A java-debug session](docs/screenshots/java-debug-session.png)

## Browser mode

`pnpm dev` with `?project=java` opens the demo Gradle service `inventory-service`
(`?project=java&jdtls=missing` starts without JDT LS to try the install offer;
`?project=java&build=maven` builds it with Maven, with profiles). Syncs, Update Wrapper and
Maven Central answer from recorded data; nothing runs or goes to the network.

Source: docs/guide/user/cpp.md

# CForge (C and C++)

**CForge** brings CLion's C and C++ support to Forge. Its plugin **C/C++** (`forge.cpp`) is
active in [C and C++ projects](docs/guide/getting-started/project-detection.md): a `CMakeLists.txt`,
a `compile_commands.json` (in the root or `build/`), a `meson.build`, a `Makefile` next to
C/C++ sources (or with them in `src/`), C/C++ files in the root, or two or more in a folder.

- Highlighting of C, C++ and CMake files is bundled (CodeMirror's C++ grammar and the CMake
  mode); completion, navigation, hover, rename, code actions and diagnostics (with
  clang-tidy) come from **clangd** (Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception).
- Everything else — toolchain detection, CMake presets and profiles, the CMake code model,
  build problems, test discovery and command lines, coverage and debugger setup — is
  computed in Rust (`packs/cforge/*`).

Two more pages cover the rest of CForge:

- [C/C++ dynamic analysis and packages](docs/guide/user/cpp-tools.md): sanitizers in CMake profiles and the
  Sanitizers tab, Run with Valgrind Memcheck, Profile with perf, vcpkg and Conan.
- [Embedded development](docs/guide/user/embedded.md): PlatformIO, ESP-IDF, Zephyr, OpenOCD Download & Run,
  Embedded GDB Server and the SVD Peripherals view.

![GoogleTest tests with run icons in the gutter](docs/screenshots/cpp-editor.png)

## Toolchains

**Settings | Build, Execution, Deployment | Toolchains** lists the toolchains of the machine,
like CLion: a C and C++ compiler with CMake, a build tool (Ninja or Make) and a debugger.
Forge reads every version itself (`gcc -v`, `clang -v`, MSVC's `cl` banner, `--version` of
the tools) and shows what is missing.

![Settings | Build, Execution, Deployment | Toolchains](docs/screenshots/cpp-toolchains.png)

| Toolchain | Found as |
| --- | --- |
| System GCC / Clang | `gcc` / `g++`, `clang` / `clang++` on the `PATH`, and versioned ones (`gcc-14`, `clang-19`) |
| Cross compilers | `<triple>-gcc` / `<triple>-g++` on the `PATH` (`arm-none-eabi-gcc`, `aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc`), with `<triple>-gdb` or `gdb-multiarch` |
| MinGW-w64 | MSYS2's `ucrt64`, `mingw64` and `clang64`, `C:\mingw64`, `C:\MinGW`, or a GCC on the `PATH` that targets `*-w64-mingw32` |
| Visual Studio | every installation with the C++ tools that `vswhere` reports: the newest `cl.exe`, `vcvarsall.bat` and the CMake and Ninja Visual Studio bundles |

- The debugger of a toolchain is GDB for GCC and LLDB (`lldb-dap`) for Clang, the other one
  when only that is installed. GDB needs version 14 or newer (its DAP server, `gdb -i dap`).
  Microsoft's debugger is not redistributable: MSVC programs are debugged with LLDB.
- **+** adds your own toolchain (`cpp.toolchains`): name, kind, CMake, build tool, C and C++
  compilers, debugger and an environment script (a cross SDK's `environment-setup-*`). Empty
  fields are detected. The page checks the entry while you type. The first toolchain of the
  list is the default; **Copy** turns a detected toolchain into an editable one.
- Remote projects use the compilers of the remote host; the page lists this machine's.

## CMake

### Profiles and presets

**Settings | Build, Execution, Deployment | CMake** holds the project's **profiles**
(`cmake.profiles`, stored with the project): name, build type (Debug, Release,
RelWithDebInfo, MinSizeRel), toolchain, generator, CMake options, build directory (default
`cmake-build-<name>`), build options (`-j 8`) and environment. Without a profile the project
has CLion's **Debug** profile.

![Settings | Build, Execution, Deployment | CMake](docs/screenshots/cmake-profiles.png)

The configure presets of `CMakePresets.json` and `CMakeUserPresets.json` become profiles too
(read-only; **Copy** turns one into a profile). Forge reads them in Rust: schema versions 1
to 10, `include` files, `inherits` chains, `hidden` presets, `condition`s (`equals`,
`inList`, `anyOf`, `not`, …) and the macros `${sourceDir}`, `${presetName}`,
`${hostSystemName}`, `$env{…}` and `$penv{…}`. Preset profiles configure with
`cmake --preset=<name>`.

- **Reload CMake project on editing CMakeLists.txt** (`cmake.reloadOnChange`) reloads after
  saving a CMake file or a presets file.
- **Build the target before running or debugging** (`cmake.buildBeforeRun`).
- **CMake executable** (`cmake.executable`): empty uses the toolchain's CMake.

### The CMake tool window

The **CMake** tool window shows one tab per enabled profile (the active one is selected;
clicking another one switches the active profile, `cmake.activeProfile`), the targets of the
profile's code model and the configure output.

![The CMake tool window with targets and the configure log](docs/screenshots/cmake-tool-window.png)

- **Reload CMake Project** writes a query for CMake's file API
  (`<build>/.cmake/api/v1/query/client-forge/query.json`), runs the configure with the
  toolchain's compilers and `-DCMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS=ON`, and reads the reply:
  configurations, projects, targets (executables, libraries, utilities) with their sources,
  artifacts and the line of `CMakeLists.txt` that defines them. Double-click a target to go
  there; its row has Build, Run and Debug buttons.
- **Reset Cache and Reload Project** deletes `CMakeCache.txt` and `CMakeFiles` first;
  **Stop** ends a configure; **Clean** runs the `clean` target.
- `CMake Error at CMakeLists.txt:6 (find_package):` and warning lines of the log link to the
  file and line; the summary counts errors and warnings.
- Forge loads the CMake project when a trusted project opens. Configuring runs project code,
  so it is refused in [Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md); a model an earlier configure wrote is
  shown anyway.

CMake files get completion of commands (with their signatures), of the keywords of the
command the caret is in (`PRIVATE`, `REQUIRED`, `STATIC`, …) and of `${VARIABLES}` (CMake's
and the ones the file sets).

## Compilation database projects

A folder with a `compile_commands.json` (written by Bear, Meson or another generator) opens
as a C/C++ project without CMake. clangd reads the database in the project root or in
`build/`; **Settings | Languages & Frameworks | C/C++ | Compilation database**
(`cpp.compileCommands`) points at another one. The page shows how many files it lists and
which language standards they use.

## clangd

**Settings | Languages & Frameworks | C/C++** shows the clangd in use, the compilation
database it reads and clang-format.

![Settings | Languages & Frameworks | C/C++](docs/screenshots/cpp-settings.png)

- clangd comes from **clangd executable** (`cpp.clangd.path`), the toolchain's LLVM
  (`clangd` next to `clang++`), the `PATH`, or Forge's download.
- **Download clangd** fetches the pinned release (`19.1.2`) from the official
  [clangd releases](https://github.com/clangd/clangd/releases) after you agree, checks its
  SHA-256 and unpacks it into `<data dir>/forge/langservers/clangd/<version>`. The release
  publishes no checksum files: the SHA-256 is read from the GitHub API's asset digest of the
  pinned release (`api.github.com/repos/clangd/clangd/releases/tags/19.1.2`), and a download
  without one is refused. When a C/C++ project opens without clangd, a balloon offers the
  download.
- clangd starts with `--compile-commands-dir` set to the active profile's build folder (or
  the compilation database), `--background-index`, `--clang-tidy`
  (`cpp.clangd.clangTidy`; the project's `.clang-tidy` files choose the checks),
  `--header-insertion` (`cpp.clangd.headerInsertion`), `--completion-style`
  (`cpp.clangd.completionStyle`) and `--query-driver` with the toolchain's compilers, so
  cross compilers' system headers are found. **Additional clangd arguments**
  (`cpp.clangd.arguments`) adds more. It restarts after a CMake reload, so it reads the new
  database.

### Reformat Code

**Reformat Code** (`Ctrl+Alt+L`) and **Actions on Save | Reformat code** run clang-format
(`cpp.formatter`): it reads the `.clang-format` of the file's folder; **Style without a
.clang-format file** (`cpp.clangFormat.fallbackStyle`) applies otherwise. **clangd** formats
through the language server, **Do not format** leaves C and C++ files alone. `.clang-format`,
`.clang-tidy` and `.clangd` files are highlighted as YAML.

## Build

| Action | Shortcut | What it runs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Build Project | `Ctrl+F9` (macOS `Cmd+F9`) | `cmake --build <build dir>` |
| Rebuild Project | | `cmake --build <build dir> --clean-first` |
| Clean | | `cmake --build <build dir> --target clean` |
| Build Target… | | `cmake --build <build dir> --target <target>` |

The build runs in the Run tool window. When it finishes, Forge parses the compiler and
linker messages in Rust — GCC and Clang (`file:line:col: error: …`, with their notes), MSVC
(`file(line,col): error C2065: …`) and the linkers (`ld`, `lld`, Apple's `ld`, `link.exe`) —
and shows them in the **Build** tab of the Problems tool window and as editor diagnostics.
Notes (candidates, declarations) are nested under their message; a click opens the line.

![Build problems in the Problems tool window](docs/screenshots/cpp-build-problems.png)

Build Project in other projects (JavaForge) keeps its own meaning.

## Run configurations

**CMake Application** runs an executable target of the active profile: **Target**, an
optional **Executable**, **Program arguments**, working directory (default: the folder of
the executable), environment and **Debugger** (the toolchain's, GDB or LLDB). The target is
built first. The CMake tool window's Run and Debug buttons create one.

**OpenOCD Download & Run** and **Embedded GDB Server** flash and debug boards; see
[Embedded development](docs/guide/user/embedded.md). CMake Application, Google Test and Catch2 configurations
also run under [Valgrind Memcheck and perf](docs/guide/user/cpp-tools.md), and their output is searched for
[sanitizer reports](docs/guide/user/cpp-tools.md#sanitizers).

## Tests

| Framework | Run configuration | How it runs | Gutter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| GoogleTest | Google Test | the target's executable with `--gtest_filter` and `--gtest_output=xml:<report>` | `TEST`, `TEST_F`, `TEST_P`, `TYPED_TEST` |
| Catch2 | Catch2 | the target's executable with a test spec, `-c <section>` and `--reporter junit --out <report>` | `TEST_CASE`, `TEST_CASE_METHOD`, `SCENARIO`, `TEMPLATE_TEST_CASE` and their `SECTION`s / `GIVEN` / `WHEN` / `THEN` |
| CTest | CTest | `ctest --test-dir <build dir> --output-junit <report>` with `-R`, `-L` and `-j` | — |

- The test executable is the configuration's **Target**, else the CMake target that compiles
  the test file. It is built first (CTest builds the project).
- Results come from the JUnit XML reports into the test tree, with the file and line of every
  GoogleTest test; disabled tests show as ignored. **Rerun Failed Tests** runs
  `--gtest_filter=*.<test>:…`, the failed Catch2 test cases, or `ctest -R '^(…)$'`.
- Test discovery finds the macros with a small tokenizer that skips comments and keeps string
  literals; a file that includes `gtest/` or `catch2/` belongs to that framework.

![A GoogleTest run](docs/screenshots/cpp-gtest-tree.png)

![A Catch2 run with a failing section](docs/screenshots/cpp-catch2-tree.png)

### Coverage

**Run with Coverage** works for all three: build the profile with coverage instrumentation
(CMake options `-DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS=--coverage` for GCC, or
`-DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS="-fprofile-instr-generate -fcoverage-mapping"` for Clang). Forge clears old
`.gcda` files before the run and turns the data into an LCOV report afterwards: Clang's
`.profraw` files (`LLVM_PROFILE_FILE`) with `llvm-profdata merge` and `llvm-cov export
-format=lcov`, else gcov's `.gcda` files with `gcov --json-format` (the `gcov` that belongs to
the toolchain's GCC). Only project files are kept. The result opens in the
[Coverage](docs/guide/user/coverage.md) tool window. Coverage is collected for local projects.

## Debugging

Debug (`Shift+F9`) on a CMake Application, Google Test or Catch2 configuration builds the
target and starts it under the built-in [LLDB or GDB adapter](docs/guide/user/debugging.md) of the
toolchain (cross toolchains use their own GDB, for example `gdb-multiarch`). Breakpoints,
stepping, watches, the Memory, Disassembly and Registers views, Attach to Process and core
dumps work as for every native program.

![GDB stopped in main with STL containers](docs/screenshots/cpp-debug.png)

**Show STL containers with their elements** (`cpp.debugger.stlRenderers`): GDB registers
libstdc++'s Python pretty printers of the toolchain before the program loads
(`-iex "python …register_libstdcxx_printers…"` from `<prefix>/share/gcc*/python`) and prints
structures on several lines; LLDB uses its built-in C++ formatters (libc++, libstdc++, MSVC
STL). A `std::vector` shows its length and elements, which expand like any other variable.

## Settings

| Key | Page | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `cpp.toolchains` | Toolchains | `[]` | Your own toolchains; the first is the default |
| `cmake.profiles` | CMake | `[]` | The project's CMake profiles (a Debug profile without any) |
| `cmake.activeProfile` | CMake tool window | `""` | The profile builds, runs, tests and clangd use |
| `cmake.executable` | CMake | `""` | CMake to run; empty: the toolchain's |
| `cmake.reloadOnChange` | CMake | `true` | Reload after saving CMake files |
| `cmake.buildBeforeRun` | CMake | `true` | Build the target before running, testing or debugging |
| `cpp.clangd.path` | C/C++ | `""` | clangd executable |
| `cpp.clangd.clangTidy` | C/C++ | `true` | clang-tidy diagnostics |
| `cpp.clangd.headerInsertion` | C/C++ | `iwyu` | `#include` insertion of completion |
| `cpp.clangd.completionStyle` | C/C++ | `detailed` | One item per overload or bundled |
| `cpp.clangd.arguments` | C/C++ | `""` | More clangd arguments |
| `cpp.compileCommands` | C/C++ | `""` | Compilation database of projects without CMake |
| `cpp.formatter` | C/C++ | `clangFormat` | clang-format, clangd or none |
| `cpp.clangFormat.path` | C/C++ | `""` | clang-format executable |
| `cpp.clangFormat.fallbackStyle` | C/C++ | `LLVM` | Style without a `.clang-format` |
| `cpp.debugger.stlRenderers` | C/C++ | `true` | STL pretty printers / formatters |

The settings of Valgrind, perf, vcpkg and Conan are in
[C/C++ dynamic analysis and packages](docs/guide/user/cpp-tools.md); the embedded ones in
[Embedded development](docs/guide/user/embedded.md#settings).

## Browser mode

`?project=cpp` opens the `shapes` demo: a C++20 library with an app, GoogleTest and Catch2
tests, CMake presets and a `.clang-format`. `&build=broken` makes its build fail with
compiler errors. Toolchains, the CMake model and all output are canned; the parsing and the
command lines run the Rust crates through WebAssembly. `?project=pio` opens the PlatformIO
demo `blinky` ([Embedded development](docs/guide/user/embedded.md#browser-mode)).

Source: docs/guide/user/dotnet.md

# DotNetForge (.NET)

**DotNetForge** brings Rider's .NET support to Forge, inside Forge's PHPStorm-style layout.
Its plugin **.NET** (`forge.dotnet`) is active in [.NET projects](docs/guide/getting-started/project-detection.md):
a solution (`.sln`, `.slnx`), a project file (`.csproj`, `.fsproj`, `.vbproj`) in the root or
one level below, `global.json`, a C# or F# file in the root, or two or more in a folder.

- C#, F# and Visual Basic files are highlighted out of the box. MSBuild files (`.csproj`,
  `.fsproj`, `.vbproj`, `.props`, `.targets`, `.slnx`, `.nuspec`, `.runsettings`, `.resx`)
  are XML, Razor (`.razor`, `.cshtml`) is HTML with C# (see [Razor and Blazor](#razor-and-blazor)),
  and `.sln` solutions have their own highlighting (sections, GUIDs, configurations).
- Completion, navigation, hover, rename, code actions and diagnostics for C# come from the
  **Roslyn language server** (see [below](#roslyn-language-server)), F# from FsAutoComplete
  when it is installed (`dotnet tool install --global fsautocomplete`).
- Everything else is computed in Rust (`packs/dotnetforge/*`): solutions and project files,
  launch profiles, SDK selection, build output, test discovery, TRX reports, command lines
  and NuGet answers.

![CartTests.cs with run icons on the xUnit test class and its facts and theories](docs/screenshots/dotnet-editor.png)

## .NET SDK

**Settings | Languages & Frameworks | .NET** shows the `dotnet` host, its SDKs and runtimes,
and the SDK the solution builds with.

![Settings | Languages & Frameworks | .NET](docs/screenshots/dotnet-settings.png)

- The host is the **dotnet executable** of the page, else `DOTNET_ROOT`, the `PATH`, the
  default install folders (`/usr/share/dotnet`, `/usr/lib/dotnet`, `/usr/local/share/dotnet`,
  Homebrew, `C:\Program Files\dotnet`) or `~/.dotnet`.
- SDKs and runtimes come from `dotnet --list-sdks` and `dotnet --list-runtimes`, run outside
  the project, or from the host's `sdk/` and `shared/` folders.
- **SDK in use** follows the dotnet host's rules: `global.json`'s `version`,
  `rollForward` (`patch`, `feature`, `minor`, `major`, `latestPatch`, `latestFeature`,
  `latestMinor`, `latestMajor`, `disable`) and `allowPrerelease`. When `global.json` asks
  for an SDK that is not installed, the page says so.
- Without an SDK, a balloon offers **Install .NET SDK…**: the platform's package manager
  (`apt`, `dnf`, `pacman`, Homebrew, winget) in the Terminal, or the download page. Forge
  never installs an SDK on its own.

## Solutions and projects

Forge reads the solution and its projects from the files, the way Rider shows them before a
design-time build:

- `.sln` (Visual Studio 2005+) and `.slnx` solutions: projects, solution folders and
  configurations (`Debug|Any CPU`). With several solutions, the Build tool window picks the
  active one (stored per project, `dotnet.solution`).
- Project files with the nearest `Directory.Build.props` and `Directory.Packages.props`:
  the SDK (`Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web` makes a web project), `OutputType`, `TargetFramework(s)`,
  `AssemblyName`, `RootNamespace`, project, framework and package references, F# compile
  order, and properties such as `Nullable`, `LangVersion` and `Version`.
- `$(Property)` references are expanded, and simple conditions
  (`'$(Configuration)' == 'Release'`) are evaluated with the active configuration;
  conditions that depend on the target framework keep their references listed.
- **Central package management**: versions from `PackageVersion` items,
  `VersionOverride`, and implicit references (`FSharp.Core`).
- Launch profiles from `Properties/launchSettings.json` (comments and trailing commas are
  fine).
- A test project is one with `IsTestProject`, the `MSTest.Sdk`, or `Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk`
  with xUnit, NUnit or MSTest.

The solution reloads when you save a solution, project, `Directory.*.props`,
`launchSettings.json` or `global.json` file, and with **Reload Solution**.

## Build tool window

The **Build** tool window (bottom) shows the solution on the left and the last build on the
right, like Rider's.

![The Build tool window with the solution and the problems of a failed build](docs/screenshots/dotnet-build.png)

- **Solution tree**: solution folders, projects with their language and target frameworks,
  launch profiles and package references. Double-click runs a project or a launch profile.
- Toolbar: **Build**, **Rebuild**, **Clean** and **Restore NuGet Packages** of the solution
  (or the selected project), **Run** and **Debug** of the selected project or profile,
  **Reload Solution**, **Show Build Output**, the active solution and the build
  configuration (**Debug** / **Release**).
- Builds run `dotnet build` in the Run tool window. Their output is parsed in Rust: the
  compiler (C#, F#, VB), NuGet and MSBuild problems, each once, grouped by file, with the
  summary (errors, warnings, time). Click a problem to open its location; the editor shows
  the same problems (inspection *Build errors and warnings*, source `dotnet-build`).
- **Build | Build Project** (`Ctrl+F9`) builds the solution in .NET projects; the Build menu
  also has **Build Solution**, **Rebuild Solution**, **Clean Solution**, **Restore NuGet
  Packages** and **Reload Solution**.

## Run configurations

The **.NET Project** configuration type runs a project with `dotnet run`:

![Run/Debug Configurations with a .NET Project configuration and its launch profile](docs/screenshots/dotnet-run-config.png)

- **Project**: the runnable projects (`Exe`, `WinExe` and web projects).
- **Launch profile**: a profile of `launchSettings.json` (`--launch-profile`), the default
  (the first one) or **None** (`--no-launch-profile`). Profiles of other kinds (IIS
  Express, Docker) are listed in the Build tool window but `dotnet run` cannot start them.
- **Run with**: `dotnet run`, or `dotnet watch` with [Hot Reload](#hot-reload) (rude edits
  restart the program).
- **Target framework**, **Configuration** (else Settings | .NET), **Do not build** and more
  `dotnet run` options; program arguments go after `--`.
- **Build before running tests and debugging** (Settings | .NET) builds the solution through
  the Build tool window first, so its problems show up there.

## Testing

The **.NET Tests** configuration type runs xUnit, NUnit and MSTest tests with `dotnet test`
on the [shared test runner](docs/guide/user/testing.md):

![A dotnet test run with a failed FluentAssertions comparison](docs/screenshots/dotnet-tests.png)

- Gutter icons on test classes and methods: xUnit `[Fact]` / `[Theory]`, NUnit `[Test]` /
  `[TestCase]` / `[TestCaseSource]`, MSTest `[TestMethod]` / `[DataTestMethod]` in C#, and
  `[<Fact>]` / `[<Test>]` functions and members in F#. Nested classes count (`Outer+Inner`);
  skipped tests (`Skip =`, `[Ignore]`) are marked.
- Scopes: the solution, a test project, a class, a method or a `--filter` expression. Class
  and method runs use `FullyQualifiedName` filters (data rows included).
- Results come from the **TRX report** (`--logger trx`) that `dotnet test` writes into
  Forge's report folder: suites per class, tests per data row, durations, output, failure
  messages with stack traces, and **Click to see difference** for xUnit, NUnit, MSTest and
  FluentAssertions comparisons. The gutter icons show the results.
- **Rerun Failed Tests** runs only the failed methods.
- `global.json` with `"test": { "runner": "Microsoft.Testing.Platform" }` switches to the new
  platform's options (`--report-trx`).
- **Debug** runs the tests with `VSTEST_HOST_DEBUG=1` and attaches netcoredbg to the test
  host when it waits for a debugger.

## Debugging

Debugging uses **netcoredbg** (MIT, Samsung), a Debug Adapter Protocol server for .NET:

- **Debug** on a .NET Project configuration builds the project, finds the built assembly in
  the build output and starts `dotnet <assembly>` under netcoredbg with the launch profile's
  arguments, working folder and environment (including `ASPNETCORE_URLS` from
  `applicationUrl`). **Step through my code only** (Just My Code) is on by default.
- netcoredbg comes from Settings | .NET's path, Forge's download, or the `PATH`. **Download…**
  fetches the pinned release from GitHub after you agree and checks the SHA-256 GitHub
  publishes for it; without one, the download is refused.

## NuGet

The **NuGet** tool window (bottom) searches the feed and manages the solution's packages.

![The NuGet tool window with a search and a package's projects](docs/screenshots/dotnet-nuget.png)

- Without a search term, the list shows the packages installed in the solution, with their
  upgrades. A search asks the feed (nuget.org by default, Settings | .NET | NuGet feed)
  through Forge's Rust client; **Prerelease** includes prerelease versions.
- The details of a package show its versions and every project with the version it uses:
  **Install**, **Upgrade** and **Remove** run `dotnet add <project> package <id> --version
  <v>` / `dotnet remove <project> package <id>` in the Run tool window. With central package
  management, `dotnet` updates `Directory.Packages.props`.
- **Updates** lists the installed packages with a newer version (`Upgrade All`).
- Versions are cached in the user cache folder for six hours and used when the feed cannot
  be reached.

![NuGet upgrades of the solution's packages](docs/screenshots/dotnet-nuget-updates.png)

## Templates

- **File | New Project | .NET Project** creates a solution with a project from a `dotnet
  new` template (console, class library, ASP.NET Core, Blazor, worker, xUnit, NUnit, MSTest,
  or any other template's short name), in C#, F# or Visual Basic, for a chosen framework.
- **Tools | Add Project from Template…** lists the templates `dotnet new list` reports
  (including those added with `dotnet new install`), creates the project in `src/` or
  `tests/` and adds it to the solution (`dotnet sln add`).

![Add Project from Template](docs/screenshots/dotnet-add-project.png)

## Code Cleanup and formatting

- **Code | Code Cleanup…** in a .NET project runs `dotnet format` on the current file, its
  folder or the whole solution. Every rule comes from the project's `.editorconfig` files:
  whitespace, code style (`IDE*`) and analyzers (`CA*`). Settings | .NET chooses what it fixes
  (all, whitespace, style, analyzers) and the minimum severity; a balloon reports how many
  fixes `dotnet format` made.
- **Code | Reformat Code** (`Ctrl+Alt+L`) uses the Roslyn server by default. With *Reformat
  Code with: dotnet format*, Forge formats the editor text with `dotnet format whitespace`
  in a temporary copy that has the same `.editorconfig` files, so the project is not touched.

## Roslyn language server

C# code insight comes from **Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.LanguageServer** (MIT), the server of
VS Code's C# extension. It is never bundled:

- When it is missing, a balloon offers **Download…**. Forge downloads the pinned version for
  your platform from Microsoft's public `vs-impl` NuGet feed, checks it against the SHA-256
  recorded for that version, and keeps it in Forge's data folder. It runs on your .NET
  runtime (9 or newer); **Download the Roslyn Language Server…** is also in Find Action.
- Forge starts it for local projects and opens the active solution (`solution/open`), or the
  project files without one. It replaces csharp-ls while it runs.
- Settings: **Analyze** open files, the whole solution or nothing; parameter and type hints.

## Razor and Blazor

Razor files (`.razor`, `.cshtml`) keep their HTML highlighting, and Razor is a layer on top,
like Rider's template data language: `@expressions`, `@(…)`, `@{ … }` and `@code { … }`
blocks, `@if` / `@foreach` and the other control blocks, directives (`@page`, `@inject`,
`@using`, …), directive attributes (`@onclick`, `@bind-Value`) and `@* comments *@`, with C#
colored inside.

![A Blazor page with C# inside Razor and the parameters of a component in completion](docs/screenshots/dotnet-razor.png)

- **Blazor components**: every `.razor` file is a component named after the file. **Go to
  Declaration** (`Ctrl+B`) on `<Rating>` opens `Rating.razor`.
- **Completion**: after `<` the components; inside a component's tag its `[Parameter]`
  properties (from `@code` blocks and the `.razor.cs` code-behind) with their types,
  `[EditorRequired]` ones first; cascading parameters are left out.
- The components (names, parameters, `@page` routes, `@namespace` from `_Imports.razor`) are
  read in Rust and refreshed when a `.razor` file is saved.

## ASP.NET Core endpoints

In solutions with a web project the **Endpoints** tool window has an **ASP.NET Core** view,
like Rider's Endpoints:

![The Endpoints tool window with minimal API routes, controller actions and Blazor pages](docs/screenshots/dotnet-endpoints.png)

- **Minimal APIs**: `MapGet`, `MapPost`, `MapPut`, `MapDelete`, `MapPatch`, `Map`,
  `MapMethods` and `MapHealthChecks`, with the prefixes of route groups (`var api =
  app.MapGroup("/api")`, chained `MapGroup(…).MapGet(…)`), `WithName` and
  `RequireAuthorization` (a lock).
- **Controllers**: classes with `[ApiController]` or a `Controller` / `ControllerBase` base,
  `[Route]` on the class and the action, `[HttpGet("{id}")]` and the other verbs,
  `[AcceptVerbs]`, `[controller]`, `[action]` and `[area]` tokens and `~/` routes.
- **Blazor** `@page` routes and **Razor Pages** (`Pages/Books/Edit.cshtml` with `@page
  "{id:int}"` is `/Books/Edit/{id:int}`).
- Parameters come from the handler: route values, `[FromQuery]`, `[FromBody]` and the other
  binding attributes, simple types as query parameters and complex ones as the body of `POST`
  / `PUT` / `PATCH`.
- Click a row to open its handler; search by method, route or handler and filter by kind.
- **Generate HTTP Request** (the row's ▶ or its context menu) opens an `.http` request in the
  [HTTP Client](docs/guide/user/scratches-and-http.md#http-client-http-files): against the URL of the project's launch profile
  (`applicationUrl`), route values as `{{variables}}`, query parameters listed, a JSON body
  for body parameters.

![Generate HTTP Request: the request of a controller action in the HTTP Client](docs/screenshots/dotnet-http-request.png)

## Entity Framework Core

The **EF Core** tool window (bottom) appears when a project references EF Core:

![The EF Core tool window with the DbContext, its DbSets and the migrations with their state](docs/screenshots/dotnet-efcore.png)

- **DbContexts** of the sources with their `DbSet`s, the provider of each EF Core project.
- **Migrations** of the sources (`[Migration("…")]` with its `[DbContext]`), with their
  creation time. **Refresh** runs `dotnet ef migrations list --json` and marks each one
  **Applied** or **Pending** (and lists those only the database knows).
- **Add Migration…**, **Remove Last Migration…**, **Update Database…** (to the latest, a
  chosen migration, or `0`), **Scaffold DbContext…** (connection string, provider, tables,
  output folder, data annotations): each opens a dialog with the DbContext project, the
  **startup project** (Settings | .NET | EF Core startup project, else the first application
  that references EF Core) and the DbContext, then runs `dotnet ef` in the Run tool window.
  The same actions are in **Tools | Entity Framework Core** and Find Action; a migration's
  context menu has **Update Database to This Migration**.
- `dotnet ef`'s output is read in Rust: failures get a hint (a missing
  `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Design` package, a DbContext that cannot be created, a build
  error, an unreachable database). When `dotnet-ef` is missing, a balloon offers **Install
  dotnet-ef** (`dotnet tool install --global dotnet-ef`, after you confirm); a local tool in
  `.config/dotnet-tools.json` is used as is.

![Add Migration](docs/screenshots/dotnet-ef-add-migration.png)

## .NET Aspire

AppHost projects (`IsAspireHost`, the `Aspire.AppHost.Sdk` or the `Aspire.Hosting.AppHost`
package) get the **.NET Aspire** run configuration type (`dotnet run` of the AppHost with a
launch profile):

![The AppHost and its resources in the Services tool window with the dashboard link](docs/screenshots/dotnet-aspire.png)

- The **Services** tool window lists each AppHost with the resources its `Program.cs`
  declares: projects (`AddProject<Projects.Bookstore_Api>("api")`, linked to their project),
  containers with their image, Redis, PostgreSQL and other servers with their databases, npm
  apps and executables, with `WithReference` / `WaitFor` references and external endpoints.
  **Start**, **Stop** and **Restart** use the run configuration.
- While the AppHost runs, Forge reads the **dashboard URL** from its output (`Login to the
  dashboard at …`): a balloon offers **Open Dashboard**, the Services details link it, and
  **Open Aspire Dashboard** is in Find Action. Settings | .NET | *Open the Aspire dashboard
  when an AppHost starts* opens it right away.

## Docker

**Tools | Add Docker Support…** writes a Dockerfile for an application project, like Rider's:

![Add Docker Support with the generated Dockerfile](docs/screenshots/dotnet-docker.png)

- A multi-stage build (`sdk` → `build` → `publish` → `aspnet` or `runtime` of the project's
  .NET version) next to the project, built from the **solution folder** so project references,
  `Directory.Build.props`, `Directory.Packages.props` and `NuGet.config` are copied before
  `dotnet restore`; `EXPOSE` of the container port; `ENTRYPOINT` of the assembly.
- A `.dockerignore` in the solution folder (`bin`, `obj`, `.git`, …) unless there is one.
- A **.NET Docker** run configuration: `docker build -f <Dockerfile> -t <image> <context>`
  in its own tab, then `docker run --rm` with the **ports** (`8080:8080`), **environment**
  and options. The container appears in the [Services](docs/guide/user/services.md) tool window.

## Hot Reload

A **.NET Project** configuration with **Run with: dotnet watch** runs with Hot Reload, like
Rider's:

![A dotnet watch run with Hot Reload applied in the status bar](docs/screenshots/dotnet-hot-reload.png)

- The status bar shows the Hot Reload state of the running application, read from `dotnet
  watch`'s output in Rust: watching, applying, **Changes applied** (with the time), no
  changes, a **rude edit** that needs a restart, or a failed build.
- **Run | Apply Changes (Hot Reload)** (`Ctrl+F10`, IntelliJ's *Update Running Application*)
  saves the edited files so `dotnet watch` applies them; after a rude edit it answers `dotnet
  watch`'s restart question. Forge starts `dotnet watch` with
  `DOTNET_WATCH_RESTART_ON_RUDE_EDIT`, so rude edits usually restart on their own.

## User secrets

**Tools | Manage User Secrets** opens the project's `secrets.json` in an editor tab, like
Rider:

![secrets.json of the API in an editor tab](docs/screenshots/dotnet-user-secrets.png)

- The file lives in your user profile, not in the project, so it is never committed:
  `~/.microsoft/usersecrets/<UserSecretsId>/secrets.json` (Linux, macOS) or
  `%APPDATA%\Microsoft\UserSecrets\<UserSecretsId>\secrets.json` (Windows). On Unix it is
  created readable only by you.
- The project is the one of the current file, the only application of the solution, or one
  you choose. A project without a `UserSecretsId` gets one after you confirm (what `dotnet
  user-secrets init` does, without running anything) and an empty `secrets.json`.
- Remote projects keep their secrets on the remote machine; use `dotnet user-secrets` in its
  terminal.

## Unity and Godot

Unity and Godot projects get their own plugins on top of this one: the Unity Hub's editors, the
Forge editor bridge, Unity tests, GDScript with the Godot editor's language server, Godot run
configurations and debugging. See [Unity and Godot](docs/guide/user/unity-godot.md).

## Azure DevOps

Repositories on Azure DevOps (`dev.azure.com`, `*.visualstudio.com`, Azure DevOps Server) get
pull requests, work items and builds in the Pull Requests tool window; see [Code
hosts](docs/guide/user/code-hosts.md#azure-devops).

## Project trust

Building, running, testing, restoring, formatting and debugging run project code (MSBuild
targets, source generators, analyzers), so [Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md) refuses them, and
the Roslyn server and FsAutoComplete do not start. The same goes for `dotnet ef` (it builds
and starts the startup project), the .NET Aspire and .NET Docker configurations (`docker
build`) and `dotnet watch`. Reading the solution, project files and launch profiles, the
endpoints, components, migrations and Aspire resources, generating a Dockerfile, user secrets
and searching NuGet stay available.

## Browser mode

`?project=dotnet` opens the `Bookstore` demo solution (an ASP.NET Core API, a class library
with two target frameworks, xUnit tests and an F# tool, with central package management);
`&build=broken` makes its build fail with compiler errors, `&roslyn=missing` starts without
the Roslyn server. The demo has minimal APIs, a controller, Blazor components, EF Core
migrations, an Aspire AppHost, user secrets (kept in memory) and an Azure DevOps remote;
`dotnet ef`, `docker` and the AppHost print canned output.

# C/C++ dynamic analysis and packages

These features of [CForge](docs/guide/user/cpp.md) find memory errors, data races, undefined behavior and
hot spots while a C or C++ program runs, like CLion's dynamic analysis tools, and connect the
vcpkg and Conan package managers to CMake. Every report is parsed in Rust
(`packs/cforge/analyzers`); Forge never downloads Valgrind, perf, vcpkg or Conan.

All of them start programs of the project, so [Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md) refuses them in
untrusted projects.

## Sanitizers

### Enabling sanitizers in a CMake profile

Settings | Build, Execution, Deployment | CMake has a **Sanitizers** row for every profile:
**ASan** (AddressSanitizer), **UBSan** (UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer), **TSan**
(ThreadSanitizer), **MSan** (MemorySanitizer, Clang only) and **LSan** (LeakSanitizer).
A profile with sanitizers configures with:

- `-fsanitize=<list> -fno-omit-frame-pointer` in `CMAKE_C_FLAGS` and `CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS`
  (appended to flags the profile's CMake options set; MSan adds
  `-fsanitize-memory-track-origins`);
- `-fsanitize=<list>` in `CMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS` and `CMAKE_SHARED_LINKER_FLAGS`.

ThreadSanitizer and MemorySanitizer cannot be combined with AddressSanitizer, LeakSanitizer
or each other; the page shows why under the checkboxes. CMake Application runs of a
sanitized profile get `UBSAN_OPTIONS=print_stacktrace=1` and `ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=1`
unless the environment sets them, so every report has a stack.

> **Note:** Rebuild after changing the sanitizers: CMake reconfigures the profile with the
> new flags (Reload CMake Project or Build).

### The Sanitizers tab

The output of every CMake Application, Google Test, Catch2 and CTest run is searched for
sanitizer reports when the program exits. When there are any, the Run tool window shows a
**Sanitizers** tab next to **Console**, with the number of problems:

- problems grouped by sanitizer, each with its kind (`heap-buffer-overflow`, `data race`,
  `Direct leak`, `signed integer overflow`, `use-of-uninitialized-value`) and where it
  happened in the project;
- its stacks: the access ("READ of size 8 …"), where the memory was allocated and freed,
  the previous access of a race and where the threads were created; LeakSanitizer reports
  each leak on its own;
- frames of project files are highlighted and link to their line; toolchain, C library and
  sanitizer runtime frames are dimmed;
- on the right, the full message, extra lines ("… is located 0 bytes after 24-byte
  region …"), the SUMMARY and a preview of the selected frame's code.

Selecting a problem highlights its line in the editor (red) and the other project frames of
its stacks (yellow), with the message on hover. **Clear Highlights** (the eraser) removes
them; double-click a frame to open it.

![An AddressSanitizer report in the Sanitizers tab](docs/screenshots/cpp-sanitizers.png)

## Valgrind Memcheck

**Run | Run with Valgrind Memcheck** runs the selected CMake Application, Google Test or
Catch2 configuration (building its target first) under

```sh
valgrind --tool=memcheck --xml=yes --xml-file=<temp file> --leak-check=full <options> <program> <args>
```

When the program exits, Forge reads Memcheck's XML (protocol 4) and the Run tool window
shows a **Valgrind** tab:

- the header with the number of errors and the **leak summary** (definitely, indirectly,
  possibly lost and still reachable bytes and blocks);
- **Errors** (`Invalid read of size 8`, `Conditional jump or move depends on uninitialised
  value(s)`, …) with how often they happened, and **Memory Leaks** by size;
- each error's stacks: the error itself and every `auxwhat` stack ("Address … is 0 bytes after
  a block of size 24 alloc'd", "Uninitialised value was created by a heap allocation"),
  with the same navigation, preview and editor highlights as the Sanitizers tab.

![Valgrind Memcheck errors and leaks](docs/screenshots/cpp-valgrind.png)

Settings | Build, Execution, Deployment | **Dynamic Analysis Tools**:

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cpp.valgrind.path` | `""` | The Valgrind executable (empty: `valgrind` on the PATH). |
| `cpp.valgrind.options` | `--leak-check=full --track-origins=yes` | Memcheck options; Forge adds `--tool`, `--xml` and `--xml-file`. |

> **Note:** Valgrind runs local projects on Linux (on Windows, open the project in
> [WSL](docs/guide/user/dev-containers-and-wsl.md)). The XML file is written to the system temp folder and
> deleted after it was read.

## Profile with perf

**Run | Profile with perf** runs the configuration under Linux perf:

```sh
perf record -o <temp file> --call-graph dwarf -F 999 -- <program> <args>
```

When the program exits, Forge runs `perf script` (with source lines), builds the call tree in
Rust and opens it in the shared [Profiler tool window](docs/guide/user/go.md#profiler) as the **perf**
source: **Flame Graph** (click a frame to zoom, double-click to open its source), **Call
Tree** and **Method List** (self and total time). Frames of project files are highlighted.

![A perf flame graph in the Profiler tool window](docs/screenshots/cpp-perf-flame-graph.png)

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cpp.perf.path` | `""` | The perf executable (empty: `perf` on the PATH). |
| `cpp.perf.frequency` | `999` | Samples per second (`-F`). |
| `cpp.perf.callGraph` | `dwarf` | Call stacks: DWARF, frame pointers (needs `-fno-omit-frame-pointer`) or Intel LBR. |
| `cpp.perf.options` | `""` | Extra `perf record` options. |

> **Note:** perf is Linux only, and `/proc/sys/kernel/perf_event_paranoid` must allow
> profiling (2 or lower). On macOS, profile with Instruments or DTrace outside Forge; on
> Windows, use WSL or the Visual Studio profiler. Forge says so instead of starting the run.

## Package managers

### vcpkg

A CMake project with a `vcpkg.json` uses vcpkg in **manifest mode**. Forge finds the vcpkg
root in `cpp.vcpkg.root`, else `VCPKG_ROOT` or `VCPKG_INSTALLATION_ROOT`, and passes
`-DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=<root>/scripts/buildsystems/vcpkg.cmake` to every CMake profile that
does not set its own toolchain file. In `vcpkg.json`, port names of the local vcpkg's `ports/`
folder complete in the `dependencies` array (and in `"name"` of dependency objects).

### Conan 2

A project with a `conanfile.txt` or `conanfile.py` gets **Tools | Conan Install** for the
active CMake profile:

```sh
conan install . -of <profile's build folder> -s build_type=<profile's build type> --build=missing
```

After it finished, the profile configures with the generated `conan_toolchain.cmake` (in the
build folder, its `generators/` folder or `build/<type>/generators` with `cmake_layout`) and
the CMake project reloads. Saving `vcpkg.json` or a Conan recipe reloads the CMake project
too.

Settings | Build, Execution, Deployment | **Package Managers**:

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cpp.vcpkg.root` | `""` | The vcpkg installation. |
| `cpp.vcpkg.useToolchain` | `true` | Pass vcpkg's toolchain file to CMake profiles. |
| `cpp.conan.path` | `""` | Conan 2 (empty: `conan` on the PATH). |
| `cpp.conan.profile` | `""` | Conan profile (`-pr`). |
| `cpp.conan.arguments` | `""` | Extra `conan install` arguments. |
| `cpp.conan.useToolchain` | `true` | Configure with `conan_toolchain.cmake` once it exists. |

## Browser mode

On the `shapes` demo (`?project=cpp`), the configuration **shapes_app (stress)** prints an
AddressSanitizer report, and Run with Valgrind Memcheck and Profile with perf show canned
results of `shapes_app`, parsed by the same Rust code through WebAssembly. The demo has a
`vcpkg.json` and a **Debug-ASan** profile.

Source: docs/guide/user/profiling.md

# Profiling PHP and Node.js

Forge reads the snapshots of the common PHP and JavaScript profilers and shows them in the
**Profiler** tool window, like PHPStorm's Xdebug snapshot view and the V8 CPU and memory
profilers:

| Source | Files | How to get one |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Xdebug** | `cachegrind.out.*`, also gzip-compressed (`.gz`) | Run \| Profile with Xdebug, or Tools \| Analyze Xdebug Profiler Snapshot… |
| **SPX** | php-spx full reports: `spx-full-*.json` and `spx-full-*.txt.gz` | Run \| Profile with SPX, or Tools \| Open Profiler Snapshot… |
| **V8 CPU** | `.cpuprofile` (Node.js `--cpu-prof`, Chrome DevTools) | Run \| Profile with V8 |
| **V8 Heap** | `.heapprofile` (`--heap-prof`) and `.heapsnapshot` (DevTools, `v8.writeHeapSnapshot()`) | Run \| Profile Allocations with V8, or Tools \| Open Profiler Snapshot… |

The Xdebug and SPX sources appear in PHP projects, the V8 sources in JavaScript and
TypeScript projects; any source also appears once it shows a snapshot. Every file is parsed in
Rust (the `forge-profiler` crate); the snapshots of profiling runs are kept in Forge's cache
folder (`<cache>/forge/profiler/`, the newest 20), never in the project. The **Recent
Snapshots** button in the tool window's header reopens them, **Open Profiler Snapshot** opens
a file.

![Xdebug snapshot: Execution Statistics with the callers of a hot function](docs/screenshots/profiler-xdebug-statistics.png)

## The views

The toolbar shows the snapshot's name (hover it for the file, the command and the profiler
version), the **metric** (Xdebug: Time and Memory; SPX: the metrics the report recorded,
such as Wall time and ZE memory usage; V8 CPU: CPU time and Samples; heap profiles: Allocated
bytes and Samples) and the total. The tabs:

- **Execution Statistics**: one row per callable with its **Invocation Count** (samples for
  V8 profiles), **Own Time** (the cost in the callable itself), **Time** (with everything it
  called; recursive calls are counted once) and their share of the total. Click a heading to
  sort, type in the filter to find a callable. Selecting a row shows its **Callees** and
  **Callers** below, with the calls and the time spent through each of them; click one to
  jump to it.
- **Call Tree**: the call paths top down with total and own cost; branches below 0.2% of
  the total are left out.
- **Flame Graph**: the same tree with the root at the bottom; click a frame to zoom into it,
  **Reset zoom** to go back.

Double-click a callable of the project (shown in the accent color) to open its source at the
function's line. Built-in functions (`php::…`), `vendor/` and `node_modules/` code are shown but
not opened.

![The Call Tree of an Xdebug snapshot](docs/screenshots/profiler-xdebug-call-tree.png)

### What the numbers mean

- **Xdebug** writes the cost of each call and the inclusive cost of every call it makes, so
  the statistics, callers and callees are exact. The Call Tree is spread from them: a
  callee's share under a caller is proportional to the cost of the calls between them, like
  in KCachegrind. `Time_(10ns)` (Xdebug 3) and microseconds (Xdebug 2) are shown in
  milliseconds; memory is the change of PHP's memory use, so it can be negative.
- **SPX** records every call start and end with its metrics, so the call tree is exact. SPX
  reports carry no file names, so SPX callables do not open sources.
- **V8 CPU profiles** are sampled: Samples counts how often a function was on top of the
  stack, Own Time is the time of those samples. `(program)`, `(idle)` and
  `(garbage collector)` are V8's own time.

## Profiling PHP with Xdebug

**Run | Profile with Xdebug** runs the selected PHP configuration (PHP Script, PHPUnit, Pest,
Artisan, Codeception, Behat, phpspec, Built-in Web Server) with Xdebug's profiler:

```text
XDEBUG_MODE=profile php -dxdebug.mode=profile -dxdebug.start_with_request=yes -dxdebug.output_dir=<folder> …
```

When the program exits, Forge opens the newest snapshot of the run in the Profiler.
The folder is a temporary folder for local interpreters. For Docker, Docker Compose, SSH and
WSL interpreters and "Run on" targets it is `.forge/test-reports/<run>-profile` in the
project, which the interpreter reaches through its path mappings; the snapshot is read from
there, its container paths are mapped back to the project's files, and the folder is
deleted.

Xdebug 3 has to be installed and loaded by the interpreter (see
[PHP interpreters](docs/guide/user/php.md)). To analyze a snapshot written elsewhere (for example by a web
server with `xdebug.mode=profile`), use **Tools | Analyze Xdebug Profiler Snapshot…** and
pick the `cachegrind.out` file.

## Profiling PHP with SPX

**Run | Profile with SPX** runs the selected PHP configuration with
[php-spx](https://github.com/NoiseByNorthwest/php-spx) full reports:
`SPX_ENABLED=1 SPX_REPORT=full SPX_AUTO_START=1` and `-dspx.data_dir=<folder>`. The SPX
extension has to be installed in the interpreter.

If your `php.ini` sets `spx.data_dir` and you want the reports to stay there, enter the
folder in Settings | Languages & Frameworks | PHP | Debug, section Profiler, **SPX data directory**
(`php.profiler.spxDataDir`): local runs then read the newest report written there during the
run. To open a report of a web request, pick its `spx-full-….json` (or the `.txt.gz` trace) in
**Tools | Open Profiler Snapshot…**; the other file of the report is read from the same
folder.

## Profiling Node.js with V8

**Run | Profile with V8** runs the selected Node.js or npm configuration with
`--cpu-prof --cpu-prof-dir=<folder>` (npm scripts get it through `NODE_OPTIONS`) and opens the
`.cpuprofile` when the program exits. **Run | Profile Allocations with V8** uses
`--heap-prof` and opens the sampling heap profile: the Call Tree and Flame Graph then show
where memory was allocated. The program has to exit normally (not be killed) for Node.js to
write the profile. V8 profiling of npm scripts is for local runs.

Locations of bundled or compiled code are mapped to their sources when the script has a
source map: a `//# sourceMappingURL=` comment (a file or an inline `data:` URL) or a
`<script>.js.map` file next to it.

![A V8 CPU profile as a flame graph](docs/screenshots/profiler-v8-flame-graph.png)

## Heap snapshots (Memory view)

A `.heapsnapshot` (Chrome DevTools | Memory | Heap snapshot | Save, `node
--heapsnapshot-signal=SIGUSR2`, or `require("v8").writeHeapSnapshot()`) opens in the
**Memory** view of the V8 Heap source. The file is read as a stream, so large snapshots work.

- **Summary**: the objects grouped by constructor (`Order`, `Map`) or kind (`(string)`,
  `(array)`, `(closure)`, `(compiled code)`, `(system)`), with their **Count**, **Shallow
  Size** (the objects themselves) and **Retained Size** (what would be freed with them,
  computed from the dominator tree; objects inside an object of the same constructor are
  counted once). Click a row to see its largest objects with their `@id`.
- **Biggest Objects**: the objects that retain the most memory.

Objects that are only reachable through weak references are left out; the toolbar shows how
much memory they take ("unreachable").

![The Summary of a V8 heap snapshot](docs/screenshots/profiler-v8-heap-summary.png)

## Settings and actions

| Action | Where | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Profile with Xdebug | Run menu (PHP projects) | `profiling.profileXdebug` |
| Profile with SPX | Run menu (PHP projects) | `profiling.profileSpx` |
| Profile with V8 | Run menu (JavaScript projects) | `profiling.profileV8` |
| Profile Allocations with V8 | Run menu (JavaScript projects) | `profiling.profileV8Heap` |
| Analyze Xdebug Profiler Snapshot… | Tools menu (PHP projects) | `profiling.analyzeXdebugSnapshot` |
| Open Profiler Snapshot… | Tools menu | `profiling.openSnapshot` |
| Profiler tool window | View \| Tool Windows | `ActivateProfilerToolWindow` |

None of these actions has a default shortcut; assign one in Settings | Keymap. Profiling runs
start programs of the project, so [Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md) refuses them in untrusted
projects; opening snapshot files is always allowed.

Python's cProfile ([Python](docs/guide/user/python.md)), Go's pprof ([Go](docs/guide/user/go.md)) and perf
([C/C++ dynamic analysis](docs/guide/user/cpp-tools.md)) use the same Profiler tool window.

# Embedded development

[CForge](docs/guide/user/cpp.md) supports microcontroller projects like CLion: PlatformIO, ESP-IDF and
Zephyr projects, flashing and debugging boards through OpenOCD or another GDB server, and a
**Peripherals** view of the chip's registers. Forge only builds the command lines (in Rust,
`packs/cforge/embedded`); PlatformIO Core, ESP-IDF, west, OpenOCD and the cross GDB are
installed by you and never downloaded.

Every action starts the project's build tools, so [Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md) refuses them in
untrusted projects.

## Detection

| Framework | Detected by | Project tool |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PlatformIO | `platformio.ini` | `platformio` |
| ESP-IDF | `CMakeLists.txt` with `sdkconfig`, `sdkconfig.defaults`, `idf_component.yml` or `main/idf_component.yml` (or the IDF's `project.cmake` in `CMakeLists.txt`) | `esp-idf` |
| Zephyr | `west.yml`, or `prj.conf` next to a `CMakeLists.txt` | `zephyr` |

These projects are C/C++ projects: clangd, the editor and debugging work as described in
[CForge](docs/guide/user/cpp.md).

## PlatformIO

The **PlatformIO** tool window (right stripe) shows the project's `platformio.ini`:

- **Default** — the tasks for the `default_envs` (or every environment);
- **Environments** — every `[env:…]` with its platform, board and frameworks (default ones in
  bold), resolved like PlatformIO does: `[env]` defaults, `extends`, `${section.key}` and
  `${this.key}` references; problems (an unknown `extends`) are listed on top. Double-click
  an environment to open its section.

Each environment has the tasks **Build**, **Upload**, **Monitor**, **Test**, **Clean** and
**Compilation Database**. Double-click a task (or select it and click ▶) to run it in the
Run tool window:

| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Build | `pio run -e <env>` |
| Upload | `pio run -e <env> -t upload` |
| Monitor | `pio device monitor -e <env>` (type into the console) |
| Test | `pio test -e <env>` |
| Clean | `pio run -e <env> -t clean` |
| Compilation Database | `pio run -e <env> -t compiledb` |

**Compilation Database** writes `compile_commands.json` into the project and restarts clangd,
which then knows the include paths and defines of the environment.

![The PlatformIO tool window](docs/screenshots/platformio-tool-window.png)

`platformio.path` chooses PlatformIO Core; empty uses `pio` on the PATH, then the installer's
`~/.platformio/penv`.

## ESP-IDF

**Tools | ESP-IDF** has **Build**, **Flash**, **Monitor** (in the Run tool window) and
**Menuconfig** (in the [terminal](docs/guide/user/terminal.md), because it is a full-screen program). They run
`idf.py` in the project:

- with `espIdf.path` set: `<python> <IDF_PATH>/tools/idf.py` with `IDF_PATH` in the
  environment (`espIdf.python`, default `python3`);
- else `idf.py` on the PATH (start Forge from a shell that ran ESP-IDF's export script).

Flash and Monitor pass `-p <espIdf.port>`; Flash also `-b <espIdf.baud>`.

## Zephyr

**Tools | Zephyr** has **West Build** (`west build -b <board> -d build -p auto <app>`),
**West Flash** (`west flash -d build`), **West Debug** (`west debug -d build`, in the terminal)
and **Select Board…**. The board comes from `zephyr.board`, else from the last build's
`CMakeCache.txt`; Select Board… suggests the boards the application defines under `boards/`
and stores the choice in the project settings.

## OpenOCD Download & Run

The **OpenOCD Download & Run** run configuration (Run | Edit Configurations…) flashes and
debugs a board through [OpenOCD](https://openocd.org):

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Target / Executable (ELF) | A CMake target (built first) or an ELF file (e.g. `.pio/build/<env>/firmware.elf`). |
| Board config file | OpenOCD configuration: `board/st_nucleo_f4.cfg` (from OpenOCD's scripts) or project `.cfg` files, separated by `;`. Default: `openocd.boardConfig`. |
| GDB port | OpenOCD's GDB server port (3333). |
| Download | **Always**: flash before running or debugging; **Never**: only debug what is on the board. |
| SVD file | The CMSIS-SVD file of the [Peripherals](#peripherals) view (default: `cpp.embedded.svdFile`). |
| GDB | The GDB to use (default: `cpp.embedded.gdb`, the cross toolchain's GDB, `gdb-multiarch` or `arm-none-eabi-gdb`). |

- **Run** flashes and resets the board: `openocd -f <cfg> -c "program {<elf>} verify reset exit"`.
- **Debug** flashes (unless Download is Never), starts `openocd -f <cfg> -c "gdb_port 3333"` in
  the Run tool window, waits until it listens for GDB, and starts a GDB session through the
  [shared debugger](docs/guide/user/debugging.md): GDB's DAP server attaches with `target remote
  localhost:3333`. Breakpoints, stepping, variables, Memory, Disassembly and Registers work
  as for native programs; the OpenOCD tab stops with the debug session.

The **Embedded GDB Server** configuration does the same with any GDB server (J-Link,
ST-LINK's `st-util`, pyOCD, QEMU): **GDB server** and its arguments are started first (leave it
empty when the server already runs), and GDB connects to **'target remote' args**
(`localhost:2331`, `tcp:192.168.1.20:3333`).

> **Note:** GDB 14 or newer is required (its built-in DAP server). The session connects with
> `target remote`; OpenOCD flashes the program before GDB starts.

## Peripherals

A debug session of a configuration with an SVD file gets the **Peripherals** tab in the Debug
tool window: the peripherals of the CMSIS-SVD file (with `derivedFrom`, register arrays and
clusters), filterable by name. Expanding a peripheral reads its registers through the
debugger's `readMemory` (registers that must not be read, such as write-only ones or those
with a read side effect, are skipped) and shows each value with its decoded fields: the bit
range, the value and the name of an enumerated value (`MODER5 [11:10] Output (1)`). Values are
read again whenever the program stops; changed values are highlighted.

![The Peripherals view of an OpenOCD session](docs/screenshots/embedded-peripherals.png)

## Settings

Settings | Build, Execution, Deployment | **Embedded Development**:

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `openocd.path` | `""` | OpenOCD (empty: `openocd` on the PATH). |
| `openocd.boardConfig` | `""` | Default board configuration (project). |
| `cpp.embedded.gdb` | `""` | GDB for embedded targets. |
| `cpp.embedded.svdFile` | `""` | Default SVD file (project). |
| `platformio.path` | `""` | PlatformIO Core. |
| `espIdf.path` / `espIdf.python` | `""` | ESP-IDF folder and its Python. |
| `espIdf.port` / `espIdf.baud` | `""` | Serial port and flash baud rate (project). |
| `zephyr.west` | `""` | west (empty: on the PATH). |
| `zephyr.board` / `zephyr.appDir` / `zephyr.buildDir` | `""` / `""` / `build` | Board, application and build folder (project). |

## Browser mode

`?project=pio` opens `blinky`, a PlatformIO project for an ST Nucleo-F401RE and an ESP32 with a
Unity test, the configuration **blinky (OpenOCD)** and the STM32F401's SVD file. PlatformIO's
environments and the SVD file are read by the Rust code (WebAssembly); the outputs of
PlatformIO and OpenOCD, and the debug session with its register values, are canned.
