# Spring Boot and Jakarta EE

The plugin **Spring Boot and Jakarta EE** (`forge.spring`, JavaForge pack) adds the Spring
support of IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate to [JavaForge](docs/guide/user/java.md) and [KotlinForge](docs/guide/user/kotlin.md). It is
active when the [project detection](docs/guide/getting-started/project-detection.md) finds:

- **Spring Boot**: the `org.springframework.boot` Gradle plugin, the
  `spring-boot-starter-parent` / `spring-boot-dependencies` Maven parent or BOM, or a
  `spring-boot-starter-*` dependency. The status bar shows "Spring Boot 3".
- **Jakarta EE**: the Jakarta EE / Java EE platform APIs (`jakarta.platform`,
  `javaee-api`), JAX-RS, CDI or MicroProfile in the build.

Everything below comes from reading the Java and Kotlin sources and the configuration files.
Forge never starts the application to find beans or endpoints; only the
[run dashboard](#run-dashboard) talks to an application you started.

![The Endpoints tool window](docs/screenshots/spring-endpoints.png)

## Beans and injection points

Forge finds the beans of the project:

- Spring stereotypes: `@Component`, `@Service`, `@Repository`, `@Controller`,
  `@RestController`, `@Configuration`, `@SpringBootApplication`, `@ControllerAdvice` and your
  own annotations that are meta-annotated with one of them;
- `@Bean` methods (in `@Configuration` classes or any bean), with `@Bean("name")`, `@Primary`,
  `@Qualifier`, `@Scope` and `@Profile`;
- Spring Data repository interfaces (`extends JpaRepository<Order, Long>`, also through your
  own base interfaces);
- `@ConfigurationProperties` classes (named `<prefix>-<class>` like Spring does);
- Jakarta EE / CDI: `@ApplicationScoped`, `@RequestScoped`, `@SessionScoped`, `@Dependent`,
  `@Singleton`, `@Named`, EJB `@Stateless` / `@Stateful`, JAX-RS resources and `@Produces`
  producer methods.

Injection points are constructor parameters (the only constructor, the Kotlin primary
constructor, or the `@Autowired` / `@Inject` one; Lombok's `@RequiredArgsConstructor` final
fields), `@Autowired` / `@Inject` / `@Resource` fields and setters, and the parameters of `@Bean`
methods. `Optional<T>`, `ObjectProvider<T>`, `Provider<T>`, `Instance<T>`, `List<T>`, `Set<T>` and
`Map<String, T>` inject `T`. A bean matches when its class or one of its supertypes is the
injected type; `@Qualifier` / `@Named` narrow the candidates, `@Primary` beans come first, and
without a qualifier Spring's fallback to the parameter name applies.

**Gutter icons** (Settings | Languages & Frameworks | Java | Spring Boot, `spring.gutterIcons`):

| Icon | On | Click |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leaf | a bean class or `@Bean` method | the injection points it is a candidate for |
| Link | an injection point | the matching beans (**Autowired Candidates**) |
| Globe | a request handler | Open in HTTP Client, Show in Endpoints |
| Table | a JPA entity | its Spring Data repositories |
| Database | a repository | its entity |
| Sliders | a `@ConfigurationProperties` class | its values in the configuration files |
| ▶ | a `@SpringBootApplication` class | Run, Debug or modify its Spring Boot configuration |

With several targets the **Choose Declaration** popup lists them.

![Autowired candidates of an injection point](docs/screenshots/spring-bean-gutter.png)

The **Spring** tool window (right stripe) lists the beans by Spring and CDI with their kind,
scope, profiles and how often they are injected. While an application runs with the actuator,
its beans are marked live and the beans that only exist at runtime (auto-configuration) are
listed too. **View | Tool Windows | Spring**, or **Tools | Spring | Show Beans**.

![The Spring tool window](docs/screenshots/spring-tool-window.png)

## Endpoints

The **Endpoints** tool window (bottom stripe, **Tools | Spring | Show Endpoints**) lists every
HTTP endpoint with its method, path, handler, produced media types and framework (in a project
that also has Python web frameworks, the window has a tab per language):

- **Spring MVC / WebFlux**: `@RequestMapping`, `@GetMapping`, `@PostMapping`, `@PutMapping`,
  `@DeleteMapping` and `@PatchMapping` on `@RestController` / `@Controller` methods, under the
  class-level `@RequestMapping` prefix. Paths may be constants (`ApiPaths.STOCK`, also
  `API + "/stock"`) and Kotlin templates (`"$BASE/{id}"`).
- **JAX-RS**: `@GET`, `@POST`, `@PUT`, `@DELETE`, `@PATCH`, `@HEAD` and `@OPTIONS` methods of
  `@Path` resources (`jakarta.ws.rs` or `javax.ws.rs`), below the `@ApplicationPath`.

Click a row to open the handler. The row's ✈ button, the toolbar and the context menu **Open in
HTTP Client**: a new `.http` scratch with the request, path variables as `{{variables}}`
declared above it, query parameters, `Accept` and, for request bodies, `Content-Type` and an
empty JSON object. Requests go to the running application, else to `server.port` and
`server.servlet.context-path` of the configuration files. Run them with the ▶ icon like any
[HTTP request](docs/guide/user/scratches-and-http.md). The context menu also copies the URL or the path.

While an application runs, endpoints it serves are marked with a green dot, and mappings that
only the application knows (actuator endpoints, `/error`, library controllers) are listed as
**Runtime**.

![An endpoint opened in the HTTP Client](docs/screenshots/spring-http-client.png)

## application.properties and application.yml

`application.properties`, `application.yml` / `.yaml`, their profile variants
(`application-dev.yml`) and `bootstrap.*` get:

- **completion of keys** with type, default and description. YAML keys are inserted as nested
  mappings with the file's indentation (`servlet.context-path` under `server:` becomes
  `servlet:` / `context-path:`); keys of maps with known keys (`logging.level.root`) are offered
  too;
- **completion of values**: `true` / `false`, the constants of enum types (in Spring's lower
  case form: `banner-mode: off`), the values of the metadata's hints
  (`ddl-auto: create-drop`) and profile names for `spring.profiles.active`,
  `spring.profiles.include` and `spring.config.activate.on-profile`;
- **documentation** on hover and in the completion popup;
- **inspections**: unknown keys ("Cannot resolve configuration property", only reported when
  metadata was found; turn it off with `spring.inspections.unknownProperties`), deprecated keys
  (with **Alt+Enter → Replace with '…'**) and values that are not a boolean or a constant of
  the property's enum;
- **Go to Declaration** (`Ctrl+B`, `Ctrl+Click`) from a key to the field of its
  `@ConfigurationProperties` class, or to the class that declares it.

Relaxed binding applies: `spring.jpa.showSql`, `spring.jpa.show_sql` and `spring.jpa.show-sql`
are the same key, and keys below a `Map` property (`logging.level.com.acme`) are valid.

![application.yml completion with documentation](docs/screenshots/spring-yaml-completion.png)

### Where the metadata comes from

The keys are those of `META-INF/spring-configuration-metadata.json` and
`additional-spring-configuration-metadata.json`:

1. in the dependency jars of the last **Gradle / Maven sync** (Reload All Gradle and Maven
   Projects in the [Gradle or Maven tool window](docs/guide/user/java.md)), looked up in the local Maven
   repository (`~/.m2/repository`) and Gradle's cache
   (`~/.gradle/caches/modules-2/files-2.1`);
2. without a sync, in Spring Boot's own jars (`spring-boot`, `spring-boot-autoconfigure`,
   `spring-boot-actuator-autoconfigure`, …) of the build's Spring Boot version, or the newest
   one in the caches;
3. in the project: `@ConfigurationProperties` classes (fields, record components and Kotlin
   constructor properties, nested classes, Javadoc as description, literal defaults) and
   `src/main/resources/META-INF/additional-spring-configuration-metadata.json`.

The jars are read as zip files; enum constants are read from their class files. Nothing is
downloaded: build the project once (or sync) so the jars are in the caches. The
**Configuration** tab of the Spring tool window shows how many properties were found and from
which jars, the configuration files with their profiles, the `@ConfigurationProperties`
classes, the profiles and the `jakarta.*` / `javax.*` / Spring APIs the sources import.

## Jakarta EE

Besides JAX-RS endpoints and CDI beans (see above), the **Persistence** tab of the Spring tool
window lists the JPA entities (`@Entity`, `@Embeddable`, `@MappedSuperclass` from
`jakarta.persistence` or `javax.persistence`) with their table, id and generated fields,
columns and relations (`@ManyToOne` → `Customer`), and their Spring Data repositories. Click an
entity or field to open it.

## Spring Boot run configuration

**Run | Edit Configurations… | + | Spring Boot** has:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Main class | The `@SpringBootApplication` class; for a Kotlin application with a top-level `main`, the file facade (`ShopApplicationKt`). |
| Active profiles | Comma-separated, passed as `-Dspring.profiles.active`. |
| Override properties | One `key=value` per line, passed as `--key=value` (they win over the configuration files). |
| VM options, Program arguments, JDK, Module | As for [Application](docs/guide/user/java.md) configurations. |
| Run dashboard | Expose the actuator's `health`, `info`, `beans` and `mappings` endpoints (`--management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=…`, unless you override it) so the dashboard can read them, or leave the actuator as configured. |

The configuration runs as an Application configuration: through Gradle's `forgeRun` or with the
class path from Eclipse JDT LS, with the [Java debugger](docs/guide/user/java.md) for **Debug**, and the
console in color (`spring.output.ansi.enabled=always`). The ▶ icon on the
`@SpringBootApplication` class creates a temporary one. Starting an application runs project
code, so it is refused in [Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md).

## Run dashboard

Spring Boot configurations appear in the [Services](docs/guide/user/services.md) tool window (`Alt+8`) under **Spring
Boot**, grouped into **Running** and **Not Started**, with the port and the active profiles. The
toolbar starts, stops and restarts them.

For a running application the details show its status, main class, active profiles, URL (from
the console: "Tomcat started on port 8080 … with context path …"), startup time, PID, web
server and Spring Boot version. With
[Spring Boot Actuator](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/reference/actuator/) in the build,
Forge asks the application on `localhost` (`management.server.port` and
`management.endpoints.web.base-path` are respected) for:

- **Health**: the status and each component (database, disk space, …);
- **Request Mappings**: method, path and handler of every mapping;
- **Beans**: name, type, scope and dependencies.

The tree refreshes the health every few seconds while an application runs
(`spring.dashboard.refreshSeconds`); `spring.dashboard.actuator` turns the requests off.
Without the actuator the details say so.

![A running application in Services](docs/screenshots/spring-run-dashboard.png)

## Settings

Settings | Languages & Frameworks | Java | Spring Boot:

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `spring.metadata.fromJars` | on | Read the configuration metadata from the dependency jars. |
| `spring.inspections.unknownProperties` | on | Report keys the metadata does not know. |
| `spring.metadata.mavenRepository` | empty (`~/.m2/repository`) | The local Maven repository. |
| `spring.metadata.gradleUserHome` | empty (`GRADLE_USER_HOME` or `~/.gradle`) | Gradle's user home. |
| `spring.gutterIcons` | on | The gutter icons above. |
| `spring.dashboard.actuator` | on | Ask running applications' actuators. |
| `spring.dashboard.refreshSeconds` | 5 | How often the dashboard refreshes running applications. |

> **Note:** The analysis is structural (no type checking): beans are matched by their class
> and supertype names, conditional beans (`@ConditionalOn…`) are always listed, and functional
> routes (`RouterFunction`) and Spring's XML configuration are not read. The actuator data of
> the running application fills the gaps.

## Try it in the browser

`pnpm dev` and open `http://localhost:1420/?project=spring`: the Java demo
`inventory-service` as a Spring Boot application with REST controllers, a JAX-RS resource,
Spring Data JPA entities, `@ConfigurationProperties` and two Spring Boot configurations. The
metadata, the console and the actuator answers are canned.

# Groovy and Scala

Groovy and Scala are JavaForge's JVM extras, in the style of IntelliJ IDEA's Groovy and Scala
plugins. They build on [JavaForge](docs/guide/user/java.md): JDKs, Gradle and Maven, the run configurations and
the shared [test runner](docs/guide/user/testing.md). Each is its own plugin in Settings | Plugins
(**Groovy**, `forge.groovy`; **Scala**, `forge.scala`; both in the JavaForge pack) and
activates only in projects that use the language (see
[project detection](docs/guide/getting-started/project-detection.md)).

## Groovy

### Editing

`*.groovy`, `*.gvy` and `*.gy` files (and `Jenkinsfile`) are highlighted as Groovy; Gradle build
scripts (`*.gradle`) are too, but they belong to the Gradle DSL support of
[JavaForge](docs/guide/user/java.md#editing-build-scripts), not to the Groovy plugin. A project is a
Groovy project when it has Groovy sources (`*.groovy` files, a `src/main/groovy` or
`src/test/groovy` tree) or a Gradle build that applies the `groovy` plugin (or a Maven build
with GMavenPlus). There is no Groovy language server: highlighting, the Run gutter and Spock
discovery come from Forge's own scanner.

### Groovy source sets

The [Gradle tool window](docs/guide/user/java.md#gradle-tool-window) shows a **Source Sets** node per
project: `main` and `test` with their `java`, `groovy` (with the `groovy` plugin), `kotlin`,
`scala` and `resources` folders. Before a sync they follow the conventions of the applied
plugins; **Reload All Gradle Projects** replaces them with Gradle's own `sourceSets` (custom
ones such as `integrationTest` included).

![Source sets in the Gradle tool window](docs/screenshots/gradle-source-sets.png)

### Running scripts

A Groovy file with top-level statements is a script and gets a green ▶ on its first line; a
class with a `static void main(String[] args)` (or `static main(args)`) gets one on `main`.
**Run** creates a temporary **Groovy Script** configuration; `Ctrl+Shift+F10` (Run Context
Configuration) does the same from the editor.

Scripts run with **groovy** from a Groovy SDK, or **through Gradle**:

- **groovy**: the launcher of **Groovy SDK** in Settings | Languages & Frameworks | Groovy (a
  Groovy folder, its `bin` folder or the launcher), else `GROOVY_HOME`, SDKMAN!'s current Groovy
  (`~/.sdkman/candidates/groovy/current`, or `SDKMAN_DIR`), else `groovy` on the `PATH`. VM
  options go to `JAVA_OPTS`; `JAVA_HOME` is the configuration's or the project JDK.
- **Gradle**: when the build applies the `groovy` plugin, an init script in Forge's cache folder
  adds a `forgeRunGroovy` task that runs `groovy.ui.GroovyMain` with the main source set's class
  path, so the script sees the project's classes, its Groovy version and its dependencies. No
  Groovy SDK is needed.

**Run Groovy scripts with** (project setting) chooses: *Gradle when the build applies the groovy
plugin, else groovy* (the default), *groovy* or *Gradle*; a configuration's **Run with** field
overrides it. Gradle build scripts are not run as scripts. Both ways run project code, so
[Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md) refuses them.

![A Groovy script run](docs/screenshots/groovy-script-run.png)

### Spock

Spock specifications (classes extending `spock.lang.Specification`, or a project base spec in
a file that imports Spock) get test gutter icons on the class and on every feature method
(`def "adds items"()`, or a method with Spock blocks such as `given:` / `when:` / `then:` /
`expect:`); fixture methods (`setup`, `cleanup`, `setupSpec`, `cleanupSpec`) are not features.
A build that depends on `org.spockframework` reports the Spock framework.

The **Spock** configuration type runs everything, a package, a specification, one feature or a
list of features through Gradle (`cleanTest test --tests 'com.acme.CartSpec.adds items'`) or
Maven Surefire, like [JUnit](docs/guide/user/java.md#tests): Spock 2 runs on the JUnit Platform. Results come
from the JUnit XML reports of the build and point at `src/test/groovy/…`; Rerun Failed Tests
and Run with Coverage (JaCoCo) work as for Java.

## Scala

### Editing and project detection

`*.scala`, `*.sc` and `*.sbt` files are highlighted as Scala. A project is a Scala project when
it has an sbt build (`build.sbt`, or `project/build.properties` with `sbt.version`), Scala
sources (`*.scala`, a `src/main/scala` tree) or a Gradle build with the `scala` plugin. ScalaTest
and MUnit in `build.sbt` report their frameworks.

![The Scala editor with the sbt tool window](docs/screenshots/scala-editor-sbt.png)

### Metals

Code intelligence comes from [Metals](https://scalameta.org/metals/) (Apache-2.0) through
Forge's shared language server client: completion, navigation, hover, diagnostics, rename and
code actions in `.scala`, `.sc` and `.sbt` files. Forge looks for Metals in this order: the
**Metals** setting (Settings | Languages & Frameworks | Scala), the version Forge installed,
`metals` on the `PATH`. It starts it with the project JDK as `JAVA_HOME` and the sbt launcher
in the `metals.sbtScript` setting.

Forge never downloads Metals by itself. When a Scala project opens without it, a balloon offers
**Install**: Forge runs your [Coursier](https://get-coursier.io) (`cs`, or **Coursier (cs)** in
the settings) as

```sh
cs bootstrap --java-opt -Xss4m --java-opt -Xms100m org.scalameta:metals_2.13:1.5.3 \
  -o <data dir>/forge/langservers/metals/1.5.3/metals -f
```

which installs the pinned Metals **1.5.3** from Maven Central (Coursier verifies the
artifacts' checksums) into Forge's data directory, never into the project. **Install Metals
(Scala Language Server)** in Find Action does the same; **Install Metals** (Ask, Never) turns the
offer off. Without Coursier, install it from get-coursier.io or put `metals` on the `PATH`
(`cs install metals`). Metals imports the build with Bloop or sbt, which runs the build
definition: it does not start in [Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md) and runs for local projects.

### The sbt tool window

The **sbt** tool window (right stripe) shows the build like IntelliJ IDEA's: the root project
with the sbt version, every project with its folder and Scala version, and per project
**Tasks** (compile, test, run, console, package, clean, update, doc, publishLocal, reload),
**Dependencies** (`org.typelevel %% cats-core:2.12.0`, with their configuration such as
`(test)`) and **Projects** (`dependsOn` and aggregated projects), plus the build's sbt plugins
from `project/plugins.sbt`. Double-click a task to run it (`core/test`); the toolbar runs the
selected task, opens the **sbt shell**, expands or collapses the tree and opens the settings.

Before an import the tree comes from the files: projects defined with `project`,
`project.in(file("…"))` or `project in file("…")`, `name`, `scalaVersion` (also
`ThisBuild / scalaVersion` and `val`s), `libraryDependencies` (also from setting sequences such
as `commonSettings`), `dependsOn` and `aggregate`. **Reload sbt Project** (the toolbar, or
Find Action) asks sbt itself:

```sh
sbt -batch -no-colors projects "show scalaVersion" "show baseDirectory" "show libraryDependencies"
```

and shows the projects, folders, Scala versions and resolved dependency lists it prints. The
result is cached in Forge's cache directory. sbt runs the build definition, so the import is
refused in [Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md); **Reload the sbt project when it opens** (project
setting, off by default) imports automatically in trusted projects. The sbt launcher is the
**sbt launcher** setting, SDKMAN!'s current sbt or `sbt` on the `PATH`; **VM parameters**
(`-Xmx2g`) are passed as `-J` options.

### sbt Task configurations and the sbt shell

The **sbt Task** configuration type runs sbt tasks: one per line or separated by `;`
(`clean; test`, `~compile`, `runMain com.acme.Main 8080`), scoped to a **Project** when set
(`api/run`). Without tasks it opens the **sbt shell** in the Run tool window, where you type
sbt commands (**Open sbt Shell** in Find Action and the tool window's toolbar). `main`
methods, `App` objects and Scala 3 `@main` methods get a ▶ in the gutter that runs them with
`runMain` in their project.

### ScalaTest and MUnit

ScalaTest suites (FunSuite, FlatSpec with `it should`, WordSpec `when` / `should` clauses,
FunSpec `describe` / `it`, FreeSpec `-` clauses, PropSpec) and MUnit suites (`munit.FunSuite`,
`CatsEffectSuite`, `ScalaCheckSuite`) get test gutter icons on the suite and on every test or
clause. The **ScalaTest** and **MUnit** configuration types run everything, a package, a suite,
one test or a list of suites through sbt `testOnly`:

| Scope | sbt command |
| --- | --- |
| Suite | `core/testOnly com.acme.shop.CartSpec` |
| ScalaTest test | `core/testOnly com.acme.shop.CartSpec -- -z "A Cart should add items"` |
| MUnit test | `core/testOnly com.acme.shop.PriceSuite -- "*formats euros"` |

The project comes from the test file's folder. Results come from the JUnit XML reports sbt
writes to `target/test-reports` (of the project's folder); test names keep their spaces and
locations point at `src/test/scala/…`. Rerun Failed Tests reruns the failed suites.

![ScalaTest results from sbt's reports](docs/screenshots/scala-test-tree.png)

## Settings

| Setting | Key | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Groovy SDK | `groovy.sdk.path` | empty (GROOVY_HOME, SDKMAN!, PATH) |
| Run Groovy scripts with | `groovy.run.runner` (project) | `auto` |
| Metals | `scala.metals.path` | empty (Forge's install, PATH) |
| Install Metals | `scala.metals.autoInstall` | `ask` |
| Coursier (cs) | `scala.coursier.path` | empty (PATH) |
| sbt launcher | `scala.sbt.path` | empty (SDKMAN!, PATH) |
| VM parameters | `scala.sbt.vmOptions` (project) | empty |
| Reload the sbt project when it opens | `scala.sbt.importOnOpen` (project) | off |

## Not yet

Groovy has no language server or debugger yet (scripts run, they do not stop at breakpoints),
and Scala debugging through Metals' debug adapter is not wired up. sbt runs one process per
configuration (no persistent sbt server shared between runs).

Source: docs/guide/user/android.md

# Android

Android support is one of JavaForge's JVM extras, in the style of Android Studio. It is the
**Android** plugin (`forge.android`, JavaForge pack) and builds on [JavaForge](docs/guide/user/java.md)
(Gradle, JDKs) and [KotlinForge](docs/guide/user/kotlin.md) for Kotlin sources.

## Android projects

A project is an Android project when one of its Gradle modules applies the Android Gradle
Plugin (`com.android.application` or `com.android.library`, also as version catalog aliases
such as `alias(libs.plugins.android.application)` and as `apply plugin:`), or has a
`src/main/AndroidManifest.xml` (see [project detection](docs/guide/getting-started/project-detection.md)).
The status bar shows **Android** with the AGP version of `gradle/libs.versions.toml`
(`agp = "8.7.3"`). Gradle itself (the Gradle tool window, tasks, sync) is JavaForge's.

Forge reads each module's `namespace`, `applicationId`, `minSdk`, `targetSdk` and
`compileSdk` from its build file (Kotlin or Groovy DSL); Settings | Languages & Frameworks |
**Android SDK** lists them.

## The Android SDK

Forge uses your own Android SDK and **never downloads it**. It looks in this order:

1. **Android SDK location** in Settings | Languages & Frameworks | Android SDK;
2. `ANDROID_HOME`, then `ANDROID_SDK_ROOT`;
3. `sdk.dir` of the project's `local.properties` (Android Studio writes it);
4. the default folder: `~/Android/Sdk` (Linux), `~/Library/Android/sdk` (macOS),
   `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Android\Sdk` (Windows).

adb is the SDK's `platform-tools/adb` (else `adb` on the `PATH`), the emulator its
`emulator/emulator`. Without an SDK a balloon and the Device Manager show where to get one:
install Android Studio or the command-line tools from developer.android.com/studio, then point
Forge at it.

![The Device Manager without an Android SDK](docs/screenshots/android-sdk-missing.png)

## Device Manager

The **Device Manager** tool window (right stripe) lists the devices adb sees
(`adb devices -l`): emulators with their AVD name (`Pixel 8 API 35`), phones with their model,
the serial and USB port, and the state (**Online**, **Offline**, **Unauthorized** until you
allow USB debugging on the device, **No permissions** without udev rules). Each online device
has **Logcat** and **Run 'app' on this device**.

**Virtual** lists the emulator's AVDs (`emulator -list-avds`); ▶ starts one (it keeps running
after Forge exits, like in Android Studio), and running ones show their serial. Create AVDs
with Android Studio's Device Manager or `avdmanager`. **Refresh** reads the devices again
(**Refresh Android Devices** in Find Action).

![The Device Manager](docs/screenshots/android-devices.png)

adb and the emulator are your SDK's tools and the devices are attached to this machine, so the
Device Manager and Logcat work for local projects.

## Android App run configurations

The **Android App** configuration type builds, installs and starts the app like Android
Studio's:

1. Gradle `:<module>:assemble<Variant>` (`:app:assembleDebug`) with the project's Gradle (the
   wrapper, offline mode and Gradle JDK of the [Gradle settings](docs/guide/user/java.md#gradle-settings-and-the-wrapper)),
   `ANDROID_HOME` set to the SDK;
2. `adb -s <serial> install -r -t <apk>`, by default
   `app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk` (`…/apk/free/debug/app-free-debug.apk` for a
   flavor variant), or the configuration's **APK**;
3. `adb -s <serial> shell am start -n <applicationId>/<activity>` with the launcher activity
   (the `MAIN` / `LAUNCHER` intent filter) of the merged manifest of the last build
   (`build/intermediates/merged_manifests/<variant>/…`), else of `src/main/AndroidManifest.xml`
   (relative names such as `.MainActivity` are qualified with the `namespace`). Without one the
   app's default launcher starts (`monkey -c android.intent.category.LAUNCHER`).

The steps run as one process in the Run tool window (each step is echoed, a failed step stops
the rest). **Deploy to** picks the device; empty means the first running device. **Build
variant**, **Launch activity** and Gradle arguments are optional. The build runs project code
and installing touches the device, so [Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md) refuses the run.

## Logcat

The **Logcat** tool window (bottom stripe) streams `adb logcat -v threadtime` of the selected
device, starting with the last 500 entries (**Recent entries on connect**). Each line shows the
time, process and thread ids, tag, package and level, and is colored by level (Verbose, Debug,
Info, Warn, Error, Assert). The package of each process comes from `adb shell ps` and from
ActivityManager's `Start proc` messages, so processes started later (the app's `:sync`
service) are attributed too.

Stack trace frames (`at com.acme.notes.NoteRepository.save(NoteRepository.kt:17)`) link to the
project's sources: click `NoteRepository.kt:17` to open the file at that line. Exception lines
and frames are marked as stack traces.

![Logcat filtered to the app's warnings and errors](docs/screenshots/android-logcat.png)

### Filters

The filter field takes Android Studio's query language, evaluated in Rust:

| Query | Shows |
| --- | --- |
| `package:mine` | the project's apps (their application ids, also `:` processes) |
| `package:com.acme.notes` | a package |
| `level:warn` (or `level:W`) | that level and above; the level menu sets it |
| `tag:OkHttp` | a tag (`tag:Net*` for a prefix) |
| `tag~:^Note.*` | tags matching a regular expression (also `message~:`, `package~:`) |
| `-tag:Choreographer` | everything except a tag (any key can be negated) |
| `message:timeout` | messages containing the text |
| `process:12034` | a process id |
| `is:crash`, `is:stacktrace` | crashes (errors with a stack trace, `AndroidRuntime`), stack trace lines |
| `timeout okhttp`, `"saving note"` | words (or quoted text) in the tag or message |

Terms with the same key are alternatives (`tag:OkHttp tag:Notes`), different keys must all
match. **Default filter** (`package:mine`) is where a new Logcat starts. The toolbar picks the
device, clears the log (here and on the device, `adb logcat -c`), pauses and resumes the view,
follows new entries and restarts the stream; the counter shows matching and buffered entries.
The buffer keeps the last **Logcat cycle buffer size** entries (20000) in Forge's memory.

## Settings

| Setting | Key | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Android SDK location | `android.sdk.path` | empty (ANDROID_HOME, ANDROID_SDK_ROOT, local.properties, default folder) |
| Logcat cycle buffer size | `android.logcat.bufferSize` | 20000 |
| Default filter | `android.logcat.defaultQuery` | `package:mine` |
| Recent entries on connect | `android.logcat.history` | 500 |

## Browser mode

`?project=android` opens the demo app `notes-app` (Kotlin, version catalog, a Groovy release
script) with recorded adb output: an emulator, a phone and an unauthorized device, three AVDs
and a Logcat stream with a crash. `?project=android&android-sdk=missing` starts without an SDK.

## Not yet

No layout editor, resource tools, APK analyzer, profilers or Android debugger yet; Android
Studio stays the tool for those. Kotlin and Java code intelligence comes from
[KotlinForge](docs/guide/user/kotlin.md) and [JavaForge](docs/guide/user/java.md), which do not know the Android SDK's classes
unless the build provides them.


---

Source: docs/guide/user/unity-godot.md

# Unity and Godot

DotNetForge supports the two game engines that use C#, in the style of Rider's Unity and Godot
support. Two plugins of the [.NET pack](docs/guide/user/dotnet.md) do this:

- **Unity** (`forge.unity`) is active in Unity projects: a folder with
  `ProjectSettings/ProjectVersion.txt` and `Assets/`. It needs the .NET plugin.
- **Godot** (`forge.godot`) is active in Godot projects: a folder with `project.godot`, with
  GDScript, C# or both.

Forge never bundles or downloads Unity or Godot. It uses the editors installed on your machine.
The logic is in Rust (`packs/dotnetforge/gamedev`); see
[dotnetforge-gamedev](docs/guide/developer/crates/dotnetforge-gamedev.md).

## Unity

### The project and its editor

Forge reads the project's editor version from `ProjectSettings/ProjectVersion.txt` (for example
`2022.3.10f1`) and its packages from `Packages/manifest.json`. It looks for installed editors
where the Unity Hub puts them:

| OS | Unity Hub editors | Unity Hub settings |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linux | `~/Unity/Hub/Editor/<version>/Editor/Unity` | `~/.config/UnityHub` |
| macOS | `/Applications/Unity/Hub/Editor/<version>/Unity.app` | `~/Library/Application Support/UnityHub` |
| Windows | `C:\Program Files\Unity\Hub\Editor\<version>\Editor\Unity.exe` | `%APPDATA%\UnityHub` |

It also reads the Hub's custom install folder (`secondaryInstallPath.json`) and the editors
you located manually in the Hub (`editors-v2.json`). The project uses the editor of its exact
version, else the newest one of the same `major.minor` (Unity upgrades the project when it
opens it). **Settings | Languages & Frameworks | .NET | Unity** shows the editors and lets you
choose another one (`unity.editorPath`).

**Tools | Unity | Start Unity** opens the project in its editor.

### Project files

C# code insight uses the `.sln` and `.csproj` files that Unity's IDE packages
(`com.unity.ide.visualstudio`, `com.unity.ide.rider`, `com.unity.ide.vscode`) write into the
project folder. Once they exist, the project is an ordinary [.NET solution](docs/guide/user/dotnet.md): the
Roslyn language server, the Build tool window and NuGet work with it.

**Tools | Unity | Regenerate Project Files** writes them:

- with Unity open and the editor bridge connected, Unity generates them right away;
- with Unity closed, Forge runs the editor in batch mode
  (`-batchmode -quit -executeMethod …`), with the editor bridge's method or the Rider
  package's `SyncSolution`.

### The Forge editor bridge

The editor bridge is a small Unity package (`dev.forge.unity`, MIT, C# source shipped with
Forge) that connects the Unity editor to Forge. **Tools | Unity | Install Editor Bridge…**
copies it into `Packages/dev.forge.unity` after you confirm; Forge never installs it on its
own. Unity compiles it the next time it has focus.

![The Unity tool window without the bridge: Install Editor Bridge asks first](docs/screenshots/unity-bridge-install.png)

With the bridge, choose **Forge** in Unity's **Preferences | External Tools | External Script
Editor**:

- double-clicking a script (or a console message) in Unity opens it in Forge at its line;
- **Regenerate project files** in that preferences page, and new or moved scripts, write the
  project files through the installed IDE package's generator.

While Unity runs, the bridge listens on `127.0.0.1` only (a free port) and writes the port and a
random token into `Library/ForgeBridge.json`. Forge connects to it automatically
(`unity.bridge.autoConnect`) or with **Tools | Unity | Connect to Unity Editor**, and again
after every script reload. The protocol is described in
[Unity editor bridge protocol](docs/guide/developer/unity-bridge-protocol.md).

### The Unity tool window

The **Unity** tool window (bottom) shows the connection and Unity's console:

![The Unity tool window with Unity's console after Play, an exception selected](docs/screenshots/unity-console.png)

- **Play**, **Pause**, **Step** and **Stop** control Play mode in the editor; the status shows
  Playing, Paused and Compiling.
- **Refresh Assets** (`AssetDatabase.Refresh`) and **Regenerate Project Files**.
- The console: errors, warnings and messages with their counts (click to filter), search,
  **Clear**. Select a message for its full text and stack trace; double-click it, or click its
  location, to open the source. Compiler messages (`Assets/Scripts/Enemy.cs(13,22): warning
  CS0618 …`) and stack frames (`(at Assets/Scripts/Enemy.cs:17)`) are read in Rust.
  `unity.console.maxEntries` limits the messages kept.

### Unity tests

The **Unity Tests** configuration type runs the Unity Test Framework in batch mode:
`Unity -batchmode -projectPath <project> -runTests -testPlatform EditMode|PlayMode
-testResults <file>`.

![Unity tests: the NUnit results in the test tree](docs/screenshots/unity-tests.png)

- Gutter icons on NUnit `[Test]` / `[TestCase]` and `[UnityTest]` methods and their classes in
  `Assets/` and `Packages/`.
- Scopes: all tests, a class, a method or a `-testFilter` expression; the test platform
  (Settings: `unity.tests.platform`), categories and assemblies.
- Results come from Unity's NUnit 3 report: suites per test class, data rows, durations,
  output, failure messages with **Click to see difference** and stack traces.
- **Rerun Failed Tests** runs the failed methods.

> **Note:** Unity refuses batch mode while an editor has the project open, so Forge refuses
> the run then and says so. Close Unity to run its tests from Forge. Running tests inside the
> open editor (through the bridge) is not supported yet.

### Debugging Unity

Unity's debugger is **Mono's soft debugger**, not the Debug Adapter Protocol that Forge's
debugger speaks. There is no permissively licensed, maintained debug adapter for Unity:
Microsoft's Unity extension for VS Code (`vstuc`) is under Microsoft's proprietary licence, and
Unity's own MIT adapter (`vscode-unity-debug`) is deprecated. So Forge does not ship one:

- **Run | Attach to Unity Process…** lists the running Unity editors (the project's first) with
  their debugger port, `56000 + pid % 1000`. A player's host and port can be entered too.
- Attaching needs a Mono soft-debugger debug adapter that you set in **Settings | Languages &
  Frameworks | .NET | Unity | Debugger** (`unity.debugger.adapterPath`). Forge starts it on
  stdio and sends `attach` with `address` and `port`. A build of the MIT
  [vscode-mono-debug](https://github.com/mono/vscode-mono-debug) adapter, started by a small
  script (`mono mono-debug.exe`), speaks this protocol.
- Unity must be in Debug mode (the status bar toggle, or **Code Optimization On Startup:
  Debug**).

![Attach to Unity Process](docs/screenshots/unity-attach.png)

> **Warning:** attaching through such an adapter is untested with Unity in Forge; only the
> process discovery, the port and the attach request are. Without an adapter, Forge says why it
> cannot attach.

### Unity file types

- **ShaderLab** (`.shader`): keywords, properties and their types, attributes (`[HDR]`) and
  render states; `HLSLPROGRAM` / `CGPROGRAM` blocks are highlighted as HLSL.
- **HLSL** (`.hlsl`, `.cginc`, `.hlslinc`, `.compute`): types, intrinsics, Unity's macros,
  semantics (`SV_Target`), preprocessor directives.
- **Assembly definitions** (`.asmdef`, `.asmref`) are JSON with a bundled
  [JSON schema](docs/guide/user/json-schema.md): completion, documentation and validation of `name`,
  `references`, `includePlatforms`, `defineConstraints`, `versionDefines` and the rest.
- **UI Toolkit**: `.uss` style sheets are CSS, `.uxml` documents are XML.

![A ShaderLab shader with its HLSL program](docs/screenshots/unity-shader.png)

## Godot

### The project and the Godot executable

Forge reads `project.godot`: the name, the main scene, the engine version of
`config/features` (`4.3`), the `C#` feature or `[dotnet]` section, and the autoloads.
**Settings | Languages & Frameworks | .NET | Godot** shows them.

The Godot executable is the one of Settings (`godot.path`), else `GODOT4` / `GODOT`, else
`godot4`, `godot`, `godot-mono` on the `PATH`, the Flatpak, `/Applications/Godot*.app` on
macOS, or a downloaded `Godot_v4…` executable in `~/Applications`, `~/Downloads`,
`~/.local/bin` or `~/Godot`. C# projects need a .NET build of Godot, so those are preferred for
them.

![Settings | .NET | Godot](docs/screenshots/godot-settings.png)

### GDScript

GDScript (`.gd`) is highlighted: keywords, annotations (`@export`, `@onready`), built-in types,
node paths (`$Sprite2D`, `%Unique`), string names (`&"move_left"`), `class_name`, `func` and
`signal` declarations. Scenes and resources (`.tscn`, `.tres`, `project.godot`, `.import`,
`export_presets.cfg`) and Godot shaders (`.gdshader`) are highlighted too.

![player.gd](docs/screenshots/godot-gdscript.png)

Code insight for GDScript (completion, navigation, hover, diagnostics) comes from **the Godot
editor's language server**, like in Rider and VS Code: Godot has no stand-alone server. While
the Godot editor has the project open, it listens on port 6005 (Editor Settings | Network |
Language Server), and Forge connects to it. When you open a GDScript file and the editor does
not run, a balloon offers **Open in Godot Editor** (**Tools | Godot | Open in Godot Editor**).
Settings: `godot.lsp.enabled`, `godot.lsp.port`, `godot.host`.

C# scripts use the Roslyn server with the project's `.csproj` like any [.NET project](docs/guide/user/dotnet.md).

### Running

The **Godot** configuration type runs the project (its main scene) or a scene, with Godot
options (`--debug-collisions`, **Headless**) and the program's arguments after `--`
(`OS.get_cmdline_user_args()`). **Tools | Godot | Run Current Scene** runs the scene open in
the editor; **Run Godot Project** runs the project.

![The Godot run configuration](docs/screenshots/godot-run-config.png)

### Debugging Godot

**Debug** on a Godot configuration uses (Settings: `godot.debugger`, or the configuration's
**Debug with**):

- **GDScript: the Godot editor's debug adapter.** The Godot editor listens for the Debug Adapter
  Protocol on port 6006 (Editor Settings | Network | Debug Adapter; `godot.dap.port`). Forge
  connects to it and asks the editor to run the project or the scene with its debugger, like
  pressing Play in the editor: breakpoints in `.gd` files, stepping, the call stack and
  variables come from Godot. The editor must have the project open.
- **C#: netcoredbg.** Forge builds the project's `.csproj` with `dotnet build` and starts Godot
  under [netcoredbg](docs/guide/user/dotnet.md#debugging) with the configuration's arguments, so breakpoints in
  C# scripts work.

With **Settings | Godot**, C# projects use netcoredbg and the others the Godot editor.

### GdUnit4 tests

The **GdUnit4** configuration type runs [GdUnit4](https://github.com/MikeSchulze/gdUnit4) test
suites headless with its command line tool (`-s -d
res://addons/gdUnit4/bin/GdUnitCmdTool.gd`): all suites in `test/`, a folder or a suite. Suites
(scripts that extend `GdUnitTestSuite`) get a gutter icon; the results come from GdUnit4's JUnit
report; **Rerun Failed Tests** runs the suites with failures. GdUnit4's command line runs whole
suites, so single test functions run with their suite. C# tests (gdUnit4Net) run with
[.NET Tests](docs/guide/user/dotnet.md#testing).

![GdUnit4 results](docs/screenshots/godot-gdunit.png)

## Project trust

Starting Unity or Godot, generating project files in batch mode, running tests and running or
debugging the game run project code, so [Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md) refuses them. Reading the
project, finding editors, installing the bridge package (after you confirm), the bridge
connection and the Godot editor's language server stay available.

## Browser mode

`?project=unity` opens `Shooter`, a Unity 2022.3 project, with the bridge connected to a
simulated editor; `&bridge=none` starts without the bridge package and `&editor=closed`
without a running editor (tests run then). `?project=godot` opens `Dodge the Creeps`, a Godot
4.3 project with GDScript, C#, scenes, a shader and a GdUnit4 suite; `&editor=closed` starts
without the Godot editor.

Source: docs/guide/user/minecraft.md

# Minecraft plugins and mods

The **Minecraft Development** plugin (`forge.minecraft`, JavaForge pack) helps you write
server and proxy plugins and Fabric and NeoForge mods for Minecraft, in the style of
IntelliJ's Minecraft Development plugin. It builds on [JavaForge](docs/guide/user/java.md) (Gradle, Maven, JDKs, Eclipse JDT LS) and
[KotlinForge](docs/guide/user/kotlin.md) for Kotlin sources.

## New Project: Minecraft Plugin

**File | New Project** (`NewProject`) lists **Minecraft Plugin** in the **Java** group. It
creates the project offline, from Forge's own templates: nothing is downloaded while the
project is created.

![The Minecraft Plugin wizard](docs/screenshots/minecraft-wizard.png)

| Option | |
| --- | --- |
| Platform | Paper, Purpur, Folia, Spigot, Bukkit (servers); Velocity, BungeeCord / Waterfall (proxies) |
| Descriptor | `plugin.yml` or `paper-plugin.yml` (Paper, Purpur and Folia; Minecraft 1.20.6 and newer) |
| Minecraft | The server version the plugin targets (servers only). Each version shows the Java release it needs |
| Build system | Gradle Kotlin DSL (default), Gradle Groovy DSL or Maven |
| Language | Java or Kotlin (Gradle builds) |
| Group ID | The Maven group and the base package, `com.example` |
| Plugin name | Empty: the main class name derived from the project name (`better-chat` → `BetterChat`) |
| Main class | Empty: `<group id>.<project>.<Project>`, e.g. `com.example.betterchat.BetterChat` |
| Authors, Description, Website | Written into the descriptor (authors are comma-separated) |
| API version | `api-version` of the descriptor; empty: the Minecraft version's (`1.21`) |
| Run Paper server (run-paper) | Applies [run-paper](https://github.com/jpenilla/run-gradle) (`runServer`) and adds the **Run Paper Server** configuration (Gradle builds, servers) |
| Shadow jar | Bundles libraries into the plugin jar (Gradle Shadow, Maven Shade); always on for Kotlin, which bundles its standard library |
| Create Git repository | `git init` |

Options that do not apply to the chosen platform or build are hidden (a proxy has no
Minecraft version or run-paper, Maven has no Kotlin). The preview under the form lists the
files that will be written; problems with the group ID, main class, plugin name or versions
show under the form before you create the project.

The project contains:

- the build: `build.gradle.kts` + `settings.gradle.kts`, `build.gradle` + `settings.gradle`, or
  `pom.xml`, with the platform's repository, its API as a `compileOnly` / `provided`
  dependency, the Java release as toolchain and compiler release, and resource filtering that
  writes the project version into the descriptor (`${version}`, Maven `${project.version}`);
  Gradle settings apply the foojay toolchain resolver;
- the descriptor in `src/main/resources`: `plugin.yml` (with the `/hello` command),
  `paper-plugin.yml`, `velocity-plugin.json` or `bungee.yml`; Folia plugins declare
  `folia-supported: true`;
- the main class with `onEnable` / `onDisable` (Velocity: `ProxyInitializeEvent` /
  `ProxyShutdownEvent` with constructor injection), a `/hello` command (Bukkit
  `CommandExecutor`, Paper's Brigadier `BasicCommand` registered through the lifecycle API for
  `paper-plugin.yml`, Velocity `SimpleCommand`, BungeeCord `Command`) and a join listener; Paper
  and proxies use Adventure components, Spigot and Bukkit `ChatColor`;
- `.gitignore` (`build/`, `target/`, `.gradle/`, run-paper's `run/`) and a README;
- with run-paper, `.forge/runConfigurations.toml` with the shared **Run Paper Server**
  configuration.

Gradle projects have no wrapper yet, since the wrapper jar is a binary Forge does not ship: run
`gradle wrapper` once with an installed Gradle (see [Gradle settings and the wrapper](docs/guide/user/java.md#gradle-settings-and-the-wrapper)).

### Platforms and versions

Forge keeps a pinned table of Minecraft versions (1.16.5 to 1.21.11, then 26.1.1, 26.1.2,
26.2 and 26.3; the default is 1.21.11), the Java release each one needs (1.16.5: 8, 1.17: 16,
1.18 to 1.20.4: 17, 1.20.5 to 1.21.11: 21, 26.x: 25) and each platform's dependency:

| Platform | Repository | Dependency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Paper, Folia | `https://repo.papermc.io/repository/maven-public/` | `io.papermc.paper:paper-api:<version>-R0.1-SNAPSHOT` up to 1.21.11 (1.16.5: `com.destroystokyo.paper:paper-api`); from 26.1 `<version>.build.<n>-stable` |
| Purpur (1.18+) | Paper's and `https://repo.purpurmc.org/snapshots` | `org.purpurmc.purpur:purpur-api:<version>-R0.1-SNAPSHOT`; from 26.1 `<version>.build.<n>-stable` |
| Spigot | `https://hub.spigotmc.org/nexus/content/repositories/snapshots/` | `org.spigotmc:spigot-api:<version>-R0.1-SNAPSHOT` |
| Bukkit | the Spigot repository | `org.bukkit:bukkit:<version>-R0.1-SNAPSHOT` up to 1.20.5; newer versions have no Bukkit artifact, so they use `spigot-api` (a superset; the generated code only uses the Bukkit API) |
| Velocity | Paper's | `com.velocitypowered:velocity-api:4.3.1` (Java 25: Velocity 4.x is built for it) |
| BungeeCord / Waterfall | Maven Central | `net.md-5:bungeecord-api:1.21-R0.4` (Java 17) |

From Minecraft 26.1 on, Paper and Purpur publish their API with build numbers
(`26.3.build.240-stable`), so the dependency cannot be derived from the Minecraft version.
The table pins a build for 26.3 (Paper `26.3.build.240-stable`, Purpur
`26.3.build.2655-stable`). For other 26.x versions, Gradle builds use the dynamic version
`<version>.build.+` (the newest build, including pre-release builds when no stable one
exists), and Maven builds need **Refresh** first, which fills in the newest stable build.

Folia plugins compile against the Paper API, which contains Folia's region, entity and global
schedulers; Folia (1.20+) only loads plugins that declare `folia-supported: true`.

The **Refresh** button next to **Minecraft** (the version) reads `maven-metadata.xml` of
paper-api from `repo.papermc.io` and of purpur-api from `repo.purpurmc.org`: it adds the
release versions the table does not have yet and the newest stable Paper and Purpur builds
of each 26.x version. It only runs when you click it, and the result is cached in the user
cache directory (`<cache>/forge/minecraft/versions.json`), never in a project. New versions
get their coordinates and Java release from the same rules.

Pinned values that go out of date over time (refresh to update the Paper / Purpur builds;
the rest changes with Forge releases): the 26.3 builds above, Velocity 4.3.1, BungeeCord
1.21-R0.4, and the build plugins of generated projects: run-paper 3.1.0, Shadow
(`com.gradleup.shadow`) 9.6.1, Kotlin 2.4.21 and the foojay toolchain resolver 1.0.0.

Generated Gradle builds need Gradle 9 or newer (Shadow 9 does not load on Gradle 8). Their
`settings.gradle(.kts)` applies the foojay toolchain resolver, so Gradle downloads the JDK of
the project's Java release (for example 25 for Minecraft 26.x) when it is not installed.
Paper 1.21.11 (Java, run-paper, Shadow), Paper 26.3 (Kotlin), Folia 26.3 with
`paper-plugin.yml`, Purpur 26.2 (Groovy DSL, dynamic build), Velocity 4.3.1, BungeeCord
(Kotlin) with Gradle 9.8.2 and Spigot 26.3 with Maven were built from generated projects.

## New Project: Minecraft Mod

**File | New Project** lists **Minecraft Mod** in the **Java** group, next to Minecraft Plugin.
Like the plugin wizard it works offline: the files come from Forge's own templates and its
pinned version table.

![The Minecraft Mod wizard with Fabric](docs/screenshots/minecraft-mod-wizard-fabric.png)

| Option | |
| --- | --- |
| Loader | **Fabric** (Fabric Loom, Fabric API) or **NeoForge** (ModDevGradle) |
| Minecraft | The game version. Each version shows the Java release it needs; **Refresh** reads newer ones (see below) |
| Loader version | Empty: the newest Fabric Loader or NeoForge version known for the Minecraft version. A NeoForge version must belong to the Minecraft version (`21.1.265` is 1.21.1, `26.3.0.101` is 26.3) |
| Mappings | Fabric: **Mojang mappings** (`loom.officialMojangMappings()`) or **Yarn**; NeoForge: **Parchment** (Mojang's names plus parameter names) or **Official (Mojang)**. Only for Minecraft 1.21.x: from 26.1 on the game ships without obfuscation, so mods use Mojang's names directly and there are no mappings to choose |
| Language | Java or Kotlin (Fabric, with Fabric Language Kotlin) |
| Mod ID | Empty: from the project name (`better-chests` → `better_chests`); 2 to 64 lowercase letters, digits and `_`, starting with a letter |
| Mod name, Version, Group ID, Authors, Description, License | Written into the metadata; the package is `<group id>.<mod id without _>`, the main class the mod id in PascalCase (`com.example.betterchests.BetterChests`) |
| Entrypoints | **Client and server** (the main class and a client initializer), **Client only** or **Server only** (a dedicated server initializer); sets Fabric's `environment` or NeoForge's `displayTest` |
| Mixins | A mixin configuration with an example mixin (and a client mixin) |
| Data generation | A data generator (Fabric API's `fabric-datagen` entrypoint, NeoForge's `GatherDataEvent`) and its run configuration |
| Create Git repository | `git init` |

![The Minecraft Mod wizard with NeoForge](docs/screenshots/minecraft-mod-wizard-neoforge.png)

The project contains:

- `settings.gradle` (the Fabric Maven repository for Loom; the foojay toolchain resolver),
  `build.gradle` and `gradle.properties` with the versions (`minecraft_version`,
  `loader_version`, `loom_version`, `fabric_api_version`, `yarn_mappings` or `neo_version`,
  `parchment_*`). Fabric 26.x builds apply `net.fabricmc.fabric-loom` and depend on the loader
  and Fabric API with `implementation`; 1.21.x builds apply the remapping `fabric-loom` with
  `mappings` and `modImplementation`. Fabric splits client code into `src/client`
  (`splitEnvironmentSourceSets()`). NeoForge builds apply `net.neoforged.moddev` with the
  `client`, `server` (and `data`) runs;
- `gradle/gradle-daemon-jvm.properties`: Loom 1.19 only runs on Java 25, so Gradle's daemon
  runs on a JDK 25, which Gradle downloads when none is installed (also for 1.21.x mods, whose
  code is still compiled for Java 21 through the toolchain);
- `src/main/resources/fabric.mod.json` (entrypoints, mixins, `depends` on Fabric Loader,
  `~<minecraft>`, Java and Fabric API) or `src/main/templates/META-INF/neoforge.mods.toml`
  (Gradle fills in the versions from `gradle.properties`);
- the main class (`ModInitializer`, or `@Mod` with the mod event bus), the client initializer
  (`ClientModInitializer`, or `@Mod(dist = Dist.CLIENT)`), `registry/ModItems` and
  `registry/ModBlocks` with an example item and block (NeoForge: `DeferredRegister`, added to
  the creative tabs), mixins in the `mixin` package, the data generator;
- assets: `lang/en_us.json`, the item and block models, the blockstate, item model
  definitions (`items/`, 1.21.4 and newer), 16×16 placeholder textures and, for Fabric, the
  mod icon (PNGs drawn by Forge, colored by the mod ID);
- `.gitignore`, a README and `.forge/runConfigurations.toml` with the shared **Minecraft
  Client** (`runClient`), **Minecraft Server** (`runServer`) and, with data generation, **Data
  Generation** (`runDatagen` / `runData`) Gradle configurations.

Like every run of project code, the run configurations are refused in
[Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md) until you trust the project. Accept the Minecraft EULA in
`run/eula.txt` before the first `runServer`.

### Mod versions

The pinned table covers Minecraft 1.21.1, 1.21.4, 1.21.8, 1.21.10, 1.21.11, 26.1.2, 26.2 and
26.3 (the default), checked on 2026-11-04:

| Minecraft | Java | Fabric API | Yarn | NeoForge | Parchment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 26.3 | 25 | 0.165.2+26.3 | — | 26.3.0.101 | — |
| 26.2 | 25 | 0.161.0+26.2 | — | 26.2.0.93 | — |
| 26.1.2 | 25 | 0.155.3+26.1.2 | — | 26.1.2.126 | — |
| 1.21.11 | 21 | 0.141.6+1.21.11 | 1.21.11+build.6 | 21.11.48 | 2025.12.20 |
| 1.21.10 | 21 | 0.138.4+1.21.10 | 1.21.10+build.3 | 21.10.64 | 2025.10.12 |
| 1.21.8 | 21 | 0.136.1+1.21.8 | 1.21.8+build.1 | 21.8.57 | 2025.09.14 |

| 1.21.1 | 21 | 0.116.17+1.21.1 | 1.21.1+build.3 | 21.1.265 | 2024.11.17 |

Fabric Loader 0.20.1, Loom 1.19.3, ModDevGradle 2.0.148, Fabric Language Kotlin
1.14.2+kotlin.2.4.21. NeoForge names its versions after the game: `21.1.x` is Minecraft
1.21.1, `21.11.x` is 1.21.11, and from 26.1 on `<year>.<drop>.<hotfix>.<build>`
(`26.3.0.101` is 26.3, `26.1.2.126` is 26.1.2). Fabric API appends the game version
(`0.165.2+26.3`); Yarn stops at 1.21.11.

**Refresh** next to **Minecraft** in the mod wizard reads, only when you click it, Fabric's
meta API (`https://meta.fabricmc.net/v2/versions/loader`, `/game`, `/yarn`), the
`maven-metadata.xml` of Fabric API and Loom on `maven.fabricmc.net`, and of NeoForge
(`https://maven.neoforged.net/releases/net/neoforged/neoforge/maven-metadata.xml`) and
ModDevGradle on `maven.neoforged.net`. It adds the stable Minecraft releases a loader
supports, the newest Fabric API, Yarn and NeoForge version of each (a stable NeoForge version
wins over a newer beta), and newer Fabric Loader, Loom and ModDevGradle versions. The result
is cached with the plugin versions in `<cache>/forge/minecraft/versions.json`.

Generated Fabric (Java with mixins and data generation, and Kotlin, 26.3; Java with Yarn,
1.21.11) and NeoForge (Java with mixins and data generation, 26.3; Parchment, 1.21.1) mods were
built with Gradle 9.8.2.

## Minecraft plugin and mod projects

A project is a Minecraft plugin when its build (`build.gradle(.kts)`, `pom.xml`,
`gradle/libs.versions.toml`) depends on `paper-api`, `purpur-api`, `folia-api`, `spigot-api`,
`org.bukkit:bukkit`, `velocity-api`, `bungeecord-api` or `waterfall-api`, or uses paperweight's
`paperDevBundle`. The status bar shows the platform and the Minecraft version, for example
**Paper Plugin 1.21.8**, and the plugin activates (see
[project detection](docs/guide/getting-started/project-detection.md)). A Gradle build that applies
Fabric Loom (`fabric-loom`, `net.fabricmc.fabric-loom`), Quilt Loom, NeoForge's ModDevGradle
(`net.neoforged.moddev`) or NeoGradle, or ForgeGradle is a mod: **Fabric Mod 26.3**,
**NeoForge Mod 1.21.1**, with the version from `minecraft_version` in `gradle.properties`.

![A generated Paper plugin with the event handler gutter icons](docs/screenshots/minecraft-project.png)

### Plugin descriptors

`plugin.yml`, `paper-plugin.yml`, `velocity-plugin.json` and `bungee.yml` in
`src/main/resources` get completion, documentation on hover and validation from schemas
bundled with Forge (see [JSON Schema](docs/guide/user/json-schema.md)): the keys of each format, `load`,
`api-version`, commands with aliases, usage and permissions, permission defaults and
children, `paper-plugin.yml` dependencies (`load: BEFORE | AFTER | OMIT`, `required`,
`join-classpath`), Velocity's plugin id pattern.

The `main` class is checked against the module's sources (`src/main/java`, `src/main/kotlin`):
an invalid class name or a class that does not exist is an error. **Go to Declaration**
(`Ctrl+B`, `Ctrl+Click`) on the value opens the class.

![plugin.yml with an unresolved main class](docs/screenshots/minecraft-plugin-yml.png)

### Mod metadata

`fabric.mod.json` and mixin configurations (`*.mixins.json`) get completion, documentation on
hover and validation from schemas bundled with Forge: the entrypoint kinds (`main`, `client`,
`server`, `fabric-datagen`, …), `environment`, `depends` and the other dependency maps,
authors and contact, `mixins` entries; in mixin configurations `package`,
`compatibilityLevel`, the `mixins` / `client` / `server` lists, `injectors` and `overwrites`.

The classes they name are checked against the module's sources (`src/main`, `src/client` and
`src/server`, Java or Kotlin): an entrypoint (`pkg.Class` or `pkg.Class::field`, also
`{ "adapter": "kotlin", "value": … }`) or a mixin (`package` + entry) that does not exist is
an error, a mixin configuration listed in `fabric.mod.json` that is missing in the resources a
warning. **Go to Declaration** (`Ctrl+B`, `Ctrl+Click`) opens the class or the configuration.

In `neoforge.mods.toml` (and Forge's `mods.toml`), completion offers the keys of the table the
cursor is in (the root, `[[mods]]`, `[[dependencies.<modid>]]`, `[[mixins]]`,
`[[accessTransformers]]`, `[features.<modid>]`) that it does not have yet, with what each one
means, the values of `type`, `ordering`, `side`, `displayTest` and `modLoader`, and the table
headers after `[`.

### Run Paper Server

Projects that apply run-paper run their plugin on a real server with the **Run Paper Server**
configuration: a Gradle configuration with the `runServer` task, which builds the plugin,
downloads Paper of the configured version into Gradle's cache and starts it in `run/` with the
plugin installed. Start it from the toolbar, **Tools | Minecraft | Run Paper Server**, Find
Action, or the ▶ gutter icon on the plugin's main class. Generated projects have it as a
shared configuration; in other projects Forge creates a temporary one.

Like every run of project code, Run Paper Server is refused in
[Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md) until you trust the project. Accept the Minecraft EULA in
`run/eula.txt` on the first start.

### Gutter icons

Methods annotated with `@EventHandler` (Bukkit, Paper, Spigot, BungeeCord), `@Subscribe`
(Velocity) or `@SubscribeEvent` (NeoForge) show an icon with the event they listen to ("Listens to PlayerJoinEvent"). Turn
the icons off in Settings | Languages & Frameworks | Java | **Minecraft** (**Show gutter
icons**).

## Browser mode

`?project=minecraft` opens `better-chat`, a Paper plugin as the wizard generates it plus a
chat listener. The descriptor check, Go to Declaration, the gutter icons and the wizard's
files run in Rust through WebAssembly; **Refresh** answers with canned versions. The Minecraft
Mod wizard plans its files the same way.

# KotlinForge

**KotlinForge** (plugin `forge.kotlin`) brings Kotlin/JVM to Forge in the style of IntelliJ
IDEA. It builds on [JavaForge](docs/guide/user/java.md) (JDKs, Maven and Gradle, the run and test machinery) and
activates in [Kotlin projects](docs/guide/getting-started/project-detection.md): `*.kt` files in a
folder, a `src/main/kotlin` / `src/test/kotlin` tree, Kotlin scripts (`*.kts` other than Gradle
build scripts), or a build that applies the Kotlin plugin (`kotlin("jvm")`,
`org.jetbrains.kotlin.*`, `kotlin-maven-plugin`). A build that depends on `io.kotest` reports the
Kotest framework.

![The Kotlin editor with completion from kotlin-lsp](docs/screenshots/kotlin-editor-completion.png)

## Editing

`*.kt` and `*.kts` files are highlighted as Kotlin and get Kotlin file icons. **File | New** has
a Kotlin submenu with **Class**, **File**, **Interface**, **Object**, **Enum Class** and
**Script** (`*.main.kts`); the `package` line comes from the folder below its source root
(`src/main/kotlin/com/acme/orders` → `com.acme.orders`). The templates are editable in Settings
| Editor | File and Code Templates.

## Language server

Code intelligence comes from JetBrains' [kotlin-lsp](https://github.com/Kotlin/kotlin-lsp)
through Forge's shared language server client: completion, Go to Declaration, Find Usages,
hover, diagnostics in the editor and the Problems tool window (kotlin-lsp only answers
diagnostic *requests*, LSP 3.17's pull model, which Forge uses for it), Rename, quick fixes and
code actions (`Alt+Enter`), Optimize Imports and Reformat Code (`Ctrl+Alt+L`). The server
imports the Gradle or Maven build itself.

kotlin-lsp is never bundled with Forge: its repository is Apache-2.0, but the server build
contains closed JetBrains components. When a Kotlin project opens without it, a balloon offers
**Install**, **Not now** and **Don't ask again** (setting **Install kotlin-lsp**: Ask, Always,
Never). Install downloads, with your consent, the standalone kotlin-lsp **263.6379.0** for your
platform from `download.jetbrains.com` (about 360 MB, the links of the project's
`RELEASES.md`), checks it against the SHA-256 pinned in Forge (the checksums JetBrains
publishes next to the archives) and unpacks it into
`<data dir>/forge/langservers/kotlin-lsp/<version>`. Progress shows in the status bar;
**Install Kotlin Language Server (kotlin-lsp)** in Find Action (`Ctrl+Shift+A`) does the same.

![The kotlin-lsp download offer](docs/screenshots/kotlin-lsp-install.png)

Forge starts `bin/intellij-server --stdio` with its bundled runtime. The JDK of the build import
is the project JDK (Settings | Build, Execution, Deployment | JDKs), or **JDK for the build
import**, passed as `JAVA_HOME`; **JVM options** go to the server's JVM (`IJ_JAVA_OPTIONS`).

As an alternative, **Language server** can be fwcd's
[kotlin-language-server](https://github.com/fwcd/kotlin-language-server) (MIT), used from the
`PATH` or **Server path**, with the same `JAVA_HOME`.

Gradle build scripts (`*.gradle.kts`) are not sent to the Kotlin server; they belong to the
Gradle DSL support. Both servers import builds, which runs project code, so they do not start
in [Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md); they run for local projects.

Settings | Languages & Frameworks | **Kotlin** shows the server, ktlint, detekt and `kotlinc` as
found, with Install buttons:

| Setting | |
| --- | --- |
| Language server | Kotlin LSP (JetBrains) or Kotlin Language Server (fwcd) |
| Install kotlin-lsp | Ask, Always or Never when a Kotlin project opens without it |
| Server path | An unpacked kotlin-lsp folder (or its `bin/intellij-server`), or the kotlin-language-server launcher |
| JDK for the build import | `JAVA_HOME` of the server; empty: the project JDK |
| JVM options | Options of the server's JVM, e.g. `-Xmx4g` |
| Run Kotlin applications with | The project's build (Gradle, else Maven), else `kotlinc`; or one of them |
| Kotlin compiler | The `kotlinc` of a Kotlin compiler (its `kotlin` runs scripts); empty: the `PATH` |
| Debugger | Kotlin (kotlin-lsp) or Java (java-debug) |
| Check files with ktlint, ktlint, Reformat Code with, Run ktlint format on save | See [ktlint and detekt](#ktlint-and-detekt) |
| Check the project with detekt, detekt, Configuration file | See [ktlint and detekt](#ktlint-and-detekt) |
| Maven repository for ktlint and detekt | `https://repo1.maven.org/maven2` |

![Settings | Languages & Frameworks | Kotlin](docs/screenshots/kotlin-settings.png)

## Run configurations

A green ▶ next to a `main` function offers Run, Debug and Modify Run Configuration;
`Ctrl+Shift+F10` runs the file at the caret. A top-level `fun main()` or
`fun main(args: Array<String>)` (also `suspend`) runs as the file's class (`Main.kt` →
`MainKt`, or the name of `@file:JvmName`); a `@JvmStatic fun main` in an `object` or a companion
object runs as that class.

![The Run gutter on main](docs/screenshots/kotlin-run-gutter.png)

Kotlin applications use JavaForge's **Application** configuration (main class `MainKt`). Kotlin
programs need the Kotlin standard library on the class path, so they run through the build
(setting **Run Kotlin applications with**, or the configuration's `runner` option):

- **Gradle**: Forge adds a `forgeRunKotlin` task (a `JavaExec` over the module's runtime class
  path, for any main class) with an init script kept in Forge's cache directory, and runs
  `gradlew --init-script <cache>/forge/kotlin/run.init.gradle :module:forgeRunKotlin
  -Pforge.mainClass=…`. Program arguments and VM options are passed through.
- **Maven**: `mvn compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=…` (VM options in `MAVEN_OPTS`).
- **kotlinc**, without a build: `kotlinc <file> -include-runtime -d <temp>/app.jar`, then
  `java -cp app.jar MainKt`.

**Kotlin Script** configurations run a `*.kts` / `*.main.kts` file with `kotlin` (or
`kotlinc -script`), with JVM options (`-J…`) and script arguments; scripts get the ▶ on their
first line. Gradle build scripts are never run as scripts.

Every run goes through the Run tool window and is refused in [Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md).

## Tests

Tests in Kotlin files get gutter icons and run on the [shared test runner](docs/guide/user/testing.md) through
Gradle or Maven, with the build's JUnit XML reports:

- **JUnit 5** (and `kotlin.test`), JUnit 4 and TestNG: `@Test`, `@ParameterizedTest`,
  `@RepeatedTest`, `@TestFactory`, `@Nested inner class`, with backtick names
  (``fun `adds items to the cart`()``). They use JavaForge's **JUnit** / **TestNG**
  configurations with Kotlin source roots (`src/test/kotlin`), so results, stack traces and
  coverage link to the `.kt` files.
- **Kotest** ([Apache-2.0](https://github.com/kotest/kotest)): **FunSpec** (`test`, `context`),
  **StringSpec** (`"name" { }`), **DescribeSpec** (`describe`, `context`, `it`) and
  **BehaviorSpec** (`given`, `when`, `and`, `then`), declared in the constructor lambda or in
  `init { }`, also with `.config(…)` and the disabled `x…` variants. Forge reads the specs from
  source; the spec and every test or container get a gutter icon. A spec runs with Gradle's
  `--tests <spec>`; a single test adds Kotest's filter (`kotest_filter_specs`,
  `kotest_filter_tests` with the test path, `totals -- applies the discount`). **Rerun Failed
  Tests** runs the failed specs again.

The **Kotest** configuration type runs all specs, a package, a spec, a test or a list of specs.
**Run with Coverage** reads JaCoCo's report as for Java.

![A Kotest spec run through Gradle](docs/screenshots/kotlin-kotest-tree.png)

## Debugging

Debug (`Shift+F9`) on a Kotlin application, a Kotest or Kotlin JUnit configuration, or Remote
JVM Debug in a Kotlin project uses **kotlin-lsp's debugger**: Forge asks kotlin-lsp to start its
Debug Adapter Protocol server (`start_debug_server`), starts the JVM with a JDWP agent that
waits for the debugger (a free port, or Gradle's `--debug-jvm` port 5005 for tests), and
attaches once the JVM listens. kotlin-lsp maps the bytecode back to Kotlin lines (including the
SMAP of inline functions), so breakpoints in `.kt` files bind, and the [Debug tool
window](docs/guide/user/debugging.md) shows threads, frames, variables, watches and Evaluate Expression as for
every language.

With **Debugger** set to java-debug, Kotlin runs are debugged by JavaForge's java-debug
instead. java-debug resolves line breakpoints with Eclipse's Java parser, so in that mode only
breakpoints in Java files bind.

### Coroutines

While a Kotlin program is suspended, the Debug tool window has a **Coroutines** tab, like
IntelliJ IDEA's Coroutines view: every coroutine with its name and id, state (running,
suspended, created), job and dispatcher, its stack and its creation stack; clicking a frame
opens the source. Forge evaluates the dump of kotlinx-coroutines' debug probes in the selected
frame (`DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines`, or `DebugProbesImpl.dumpCoroutinesInfo()` for evaluators
that only take Java expressions) and parses it in Rust. The probes must be installed in the
program: add `kotlinx-coroutines-debug` to the dependencies and call `DebugProbes.install()` at
startup (or start the JVM with the library as `-javaagent`); otherwise the tab explains this.

![A Kotlin debug session with the Coroutines tab](docs/screenshots/kotlin-debug-coroutines.png)

## ktlint and detekt

[ktlint](https://pinterest.github.io/ktlint/) (MIT) and [detekt](https://detekt.dev)
(Apache-2.0) run as external tools:

- found in the settings (an executable or a `*-all.jar`), on the `PATH`, or downloaded by Forge
  (**Download ktlint and detekt**: ktlint 1.8.0 and detekt 1.23.8 from Maven Central, pinned
  SHA-256, into `<data dir>/forge/langservers/jars`, run with the project JDK's `java -jar`);
- without a detekt CLI, **Run detekt on the Project** uses the project's detekt Gradle plugin
  (`gradlew detekt`, in trusted projects) and reads `build/reports/detekt/detekt.sarif`.

ktlint checks a Kotlin file when it opens and after every save, on the editor text (`--stdin`,
with the project's `.editorconfig`). detekt checks the saved file and, with **Run detekt on the
Project** (Find Action or the Code menu), the whole project, with `config/detekt/detekt.yml` and
its baseline when they exist (setting **Configuration file**). Their findings (ktlint's JSON and
Checkstyle reports, detekt's SARIF and Checkstyle reports, parsed in Rust) show in the editor
and the Problems tool window, with the rule as the problem's code.

**Reformat Code with** ktlint makes `Ctrl+Alt+L` run `ktlint --format`; **Format File with
ktlint** does it once, and **Run ktlint format on save** after every `Ctrl+S`.

![ktlint and detekt problems](docs/screenshots/kotlin-ktlint-detekt-problems.png)

## Browser mode

`pnpm dev` with `?project=kotlin` opens the demo Gradle service `orders-service` (coroutines, a
Kotest spec, JUnit 5 tests, a Kotlin script); `?project=kotlin&kotlin-lsp=missing` starts
without kotlin-lsp to try the download offer.
