# Debugging

Forge has one debugger for every language. The **Debug** tool window (`Alt+5`), breakpoints in
the editor, stepping, variables, watches, Evaluate Expression and the console work the same
for every session; only how a session starts differs:

- **PHP** uses the Xdebug plugin (`forge.xdebug`, PHPForge pack): a DBGp server for **Xdebug 3**
  that accepts any number of connections at once, from the CLI, a web server, Docker
  containers or another machine.
- **Every other language** uses a **debug adapter** that speaks the
  [Debug Adapter Protocol](https://microsoft.github.io/debug-adapter-protocol/) (DAP), through
  the Debugger plugin (`forge.debugger`). **LLDB** (`lldb-dap`) and **GDB** (14 or newer,
  `gdb -i dap`) are built in for C, C++, Rust, Go and other native code; language packs add
  their own adapters, such as debugpy for Python ([PyForge](docs/guide/user/python.md#debugging-with-debugpy)),
  java-debug for Java ([JavaForge](docs/guide/user/java.md#debugging)) and kotlin-lsp's debugger with a
  Coroutines tab for Kotlin ([KotlinForge](docs/guide/user/kotlin.md#debugging)). Adapters are programs
  installed on your machine; Forge does not bundle
  them. See [Debug adapter sessions](#debug-adapter-sessions) below.

The sections up to [Debug adapter sessions](#debug-adapter-sessions) describe Xdebug; the
breakpoints and the Debug tool window are shared.

## Preparing PHP

Install Xdebug 3 and enable step debugging in your `php.ini` (or the container's):

```ini
zend_extension=xdebug
xdebug.mode=debug
xdebug.client_port=9003
; for web requests: start on every request, or use a browser extension / XDEBUG_SESSION cookie
xdebug.start_with_request=trigger
; when PHP runs in Docker or on another machine
; xdebug.client_host=host.docker.internal
```

Forge listens on port **9003** (`php.debug.port`).

## Two ways to start

### Debug a run configuration

Press **Debug** (`Shift+F9`) on a PHP Script, PHPUnit, Artisan or Composer configuration (or a
gutter ▶ menu). Forge starts listening and runs the process with:

```text
XDEBUG_MODE=debug
XDEBUG_SESSION=FORGE
XDEBUG_CONFIG=client_host=127.0.0.1 client_port=9003 idekey=FORGE
PHP_IDE_CONFIG=serverName=<server>   (when a server is chosen)
```

so no `php.ini` change is needed for CLI scripts and tests.

### Listening for connections

For web requests, click the telephone icon **Start Listening for PHP Debug Connections** in
the main toolbar (action `PhpListenDebugAction`). The status bar shows that Forge is listening;
click again to stop. Then open the page with Xdebug triggered (`XDEBUG_SESSION` cookie, query
parameter or browser extension).

![Incoming connection](docs/screenshots/debugger-incoming.png)

### Debugging web pages and HTTP requests

These configurations start listening by themselves when you press **Debug** (`Shift+F9`):

| Configuration | Debug |
| --- | --- |
| **PHP Built-in Web Server** | runs `php -S host:port -t <document root> [router script]` with the Xdebug environment and `-dxdebug.start_with_request=yes`, so every request it serves is debugged; opens the page in the browser |
| **PHP Web Page** | opens the start URL on a server of Settings \| PHP \| Servers with `?XDEBUG_SESSION_START=FORGE` (Xdebug then sets the `XDEBUG_SESSION` cookie for the following requests) |
| **PHP HTTP Request** | sends the request (method, URL, headers, body) with the cookie `XDEBUG_SESSION=FORGE` |
| Requests in `.http` files | click the gutter ▶ and choose **Debug '…' with Xdebug**: the request is sent with the cookie |

![Debug an .http request](docs/screenshots/http-debug-menu.png)

The Run tool window shows the cookie of a debugged request:

![Debugged request](docs/screenshots/http-debug-run.png)

When a connection comes from an unknown server whose script is not a project file, the
**Incoming Connection From Xdebug** dialog asks which project file the server file maps to and
creates a server with that path mapping. Turn on **Ignore external connections through
unregistered server configurations** (`php.debug.ignoreExternalConnections`) to detach such
connections silently.

## Breakpoints

- Click a line number in a PHP file, or in a file of a debug adapter's languages (`.c`, `.cpp`,
  `.rs`, `.go`, …), or press **Toggle Line Breakpoint** (`Ctrl+F8`, macOS `Cmd+F8`).
- Right-click a breakpoint to set a **condition** (an expression of the file's language; the
  program suspends only when it is true) or disable it.
- **View Breakpoints…** (`Ctrl+Shift+F8`) lists all breakpoints: **PHP Line Breakpoints**,
  **Line Breakpoints** of other languages, **Function Breakpoints**, **Watchpoints**, **PHP
  Exception Breakpoints** (an exception class, or `*` for any) and the exception filters of
  debug adapters (for example LLDB's "C++: on throw").
- **Mute Breakpoints** turns all of them off temporarily.

![Breakpoint condition](docs/screenshots/debugger-condition-popup.png)

![Breakpoints dialog](docs/screenshots/debugger-breakpoints.png)

Breakpoints are stored in `<project>/.forge/breakpoints.json`.

### Breakpoint properties, logpoints and temporary breakpoints

The right side of **View Breakpoints…** (and the popup of a right-click on a breakpoint) has
PHPStorm's properties:

| Property | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| **Enabled** | off keeps the breakpoint without stopping |
| **Suspend execution** | off makes a **logpoint**: Forge logs and lets the script run on (yellow dot) |
| **Condition** | an expression; Xdebug or the debug adapter stops only when it is true |
| **Log: "Breakpoint hit" message** | prints `Breakpoint reached at <file>:<line>` to the session's Console |
| **Log: Stack trace** | prints the frames |
| **Evaluate and log** | evaluates an expression in the frame and prints its value (debug adapters: `{expr}` in the text is replaced, e.g. `i={i} sum={sum}`) |
| **Remove once hit** | a **temporary breakpoint**: removed after it suspended once (dot with a ring) |
| **Pass count** | stops only from the n-th hit on (Xdebug's hit condition `>=`, a DAP hit condition) |

- **Shift+click** on a line number adds a logpoint ("Breakpoint hit" message, no suspend) and
  opens its properties.
- **Toggle Temporary Line Breakpoint** (`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F8`, macOS `Cmd+Alt+Shift+F8`) adds a
  breakpoint that is removed once hit.
- **PHP Exception Breakpoints** (**+** in the dialog) stop when an exception of the class (or
  a subclass) is thrown; `*` stops on any exception. They have the same log options.

![Logpoint properties](docs/screenshots/debugger-logpoint.png)

Logged lines appear in the **Console** tab of the debug session:

![Logpoint output](docs/screenshots/debugger-logpoint-output.png)

## The Debug tool window

![Paused](docs/screenshots/debugger-paused.png)

While paused, the execution point is highlighted in the editor and variable values are shown
inline at the end of lines (`php.debug.showInlineValues`). The **Debug** tool window (`Alt+5`)
has a tab per session with:

- **Threads & Variables**: the frames on the left (click to switch), variables on the right.
  Arrays and objects expand lazily.
- **Console**: the script's output, logpoint messages, and a field at the bottom that
  evaluates PHP expressions in the selected frame (see below).
- The evaluate field at the top: type an expression and press `Enter` to evaluate it, or
  `Ctrl+Shift+Enter` to add it as a watch.

| Action | Windows/Linux | macOS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Resume Program | `F9` | `Cmd+Alt+R` |
| Pause Program | toolbar | toolbar |
| Step Over | `F8` | `F8` |
| Step Into | `F7` | `F7` |
| Smart Step Into | `Shift+F7` | `Shift+F7` |
| Force Step Into | `Alt+Shift+F7` | `Alt+Shift+F7` |
| Step Out | `Shift+F8` | `Shift+F8` |
| Run to Cursor | `Alt+F9` | `Alt+F9` |
| Force Run to Cursor | `Ctrl+Alt+F9` | `Cmd+Alt+F9` |
| Evaluate Expression… | `Alt+F8` | `Alt+F8` |
| Quick Evaluate Expression | `Ctrl+Alt+F8` | `Cmd+Alt+F8` |
| Show Execution Point | `Alt+F10` | `Alt+F10` |
| Stop | `Ctrl+F2` | `Cmd+F2` |
| Add to Watches | context menu | context menu |
| Set Value… | `F2` | `F2` |
| Toggle Temporary Line Breakpoint | `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F8` | `Cmd+Alt+Shift+F8` |

![Evaluate Expression](docs/screenshots/debugger-evaluate.png)

### Variables: Set Value and Copy Value

Right-click a variable or watch for **Set Value…** (`F2`), **Copy Value** (arrays and objects
as `print_r` output), **Copy Name**, **Evaluate Expression…** and **Add to Watches**. Set Value
edits the value in place: type a PHP expression (`'paid'`, `42`, `null`, `$other`) and press
`Enter` (Xdebug's `property_set`); `Escape` cancels. The variables and watches reload after the
change.

![Set Value](docs/screenshots/debugger-set-value.png)

![Variable context menu](docs/screenshots/debugger-variable-menu.png)

### Evaluate Expression and the debugger console

The **Evaluate** dialog (`Alt+F8`) and the field at the bottom of the **Console** tab evaluate a
PHP expression in the selected frame (Xdebug's `eval`). Both complete variable names after `$`
and properties after `->` (from the suspended script, `Enter` or `Tab` accepts) and keep a
history of evaluated expressions: `Up` / `Down` in the field, or the history button. Console
results are trees that expand like variables.

![Debugger console](docs/screenshots/debugger-console.png)

Smart Step Into currently behaves like Step Into. Pause depends on the engine and may
report "Pause is not supported by this engine".

## Debug adapter sessions

A debug adapter session drives the same Debug tool window as Xdebug. What the window offers
depends on the adapter (its capabilities): threads, memory, disassembly and registers appear
only when the adapter supports them.

![Debug adapter session](docs/screenshots/dap-session.png)

### Starting a session

| How | Where |
| --- | --- |
| **Debug** a run configuration (`Shift+F9`) | a **Native Application** configuration (executable, program arguments, working directory, debugger, "Stop at the beginning of the program", launch options as JSON), or a configuration type of a language pack that uses an adapter (Node.js, npm, JavaScript Debug and the JavaScript test runners use js-debug, see [JavaScript debugging](docs/guide/user/javascript-debugging.md)) |
| **Attach to Process…** (`Ctrl+Alt+F5`, macOS `Cmd+Alt+F5`) | Run menu: pick a local process (filter by name, command line or PID) and an adapter that can attach |
| **Attach to DAP Server…** | Run menu: connect to an adapter that already listens on a TCP port (`dlv dap --listen 127.0.0.1:4711`, `debugpy --listen 5678`), with optional attach options as JSON |
| **Debug Core Dump…** | Run menu: open a core file with the executable that crashed (LLDB); nothing runs, frames, variables, memory and registers show the state at the crash |

![Attach to Process](docs/screenshots/dap-attach-process.png)

> **Note:** starting a program under the debugger runs project code, so it is refused in
> [Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md). Attaching to a running process or DAP server and opening a
> core dump are allowed.

Program output and the adapter's messages appear in the **Console** tab. Programs that need a
terminal (the adapter's `runInTerminal` request) are started by Forge with their output in the
console; adapters that start child sessions (`startDebugging`, e.g. for subprocesses) get a
session tab per child.

### Threads, variables and the console

- The frames pane has a thread selector; the thread that stopped is marked "(stopped)".
- Variables expand lazily. Scopes other than the locals (globals, statics) are groups at the
  end of the tree.
- Watches belong to the debugger: PHP sessions keep their watches, a C session has its own.
- The console and Evaluate (`Alt+F8`) evaluate in the adapter's language (LLDB also accepts
  its commands) and complete names while you type.
- Values are shown inline in the editor (`debugger.showInlineValues`).
- **Rerun** in the toolbar restarts the session (in place when the adapter supports it).

### Logpoints and watchpoints

Logpoints (**Suspend execution** off, `Shift`+click on a line number) are evaluated by the
adapter when it supports them, so the program does not stop at all; otherwise Forge logs and
resumes. In **Evaluate and log**, `{expression}` is replaced by its value: `i={i} sum={sum}`
prints `i=2 sum=1`; a plain expression `counter` prints `counter = 6`.

![Logpoint output and completion](docs/screenshots/dap-console-logpoint.png)

![Breakpoints dialog with a logpoint](docs/screenshots/dap-breakpoints.png)

**Add Watchpoint** in the context menu of a variable adds a data breakpoint: the program stops
when the value changes. It is listed under **Watchpoints** in View Breakpoints…, where
**Suspend on** chooses write, read or both (as far as the adapter supports it). **Function
Breakpoints** (**+** in the dialog) stop when a function is entered (`main`,
`MyClass::method`).

### Memory, disassembly and registers

| Tab | Shows |
| --- | --- |
| **Memory** | hex and ASCII from an address; type an address or `&variable`, page with the arrows, or choose **View Memory** on a variable. Double-click a byte to change it (when the adapter can write memory). |
| **Disassembly** | the instructions around the selected frame's instruction pointer with symbols and source lines; **Step Over Instruction** and **Step Into Instruction** step one machine instruction |
| **Registers** | the registers of the selected frame |

![Memory view](docs/screenshots/dap-memory.png)

![Disassembly](docs/screenshots/dap-disassembly.png)

![Registers](docs/screenshots/dap-registers.png)

| Action | Default shortcut |
| --- | --- |
| Attach to Process… | `Ctrl+Alt+F5` (macOS `Cmd+Alt+F5`) |
| Attach to DAP Server…, Debug Core Dump… | Run menu |
| Step Over Instruction, Step Into Instruction | Disassembly tab (assign keys in Settings \| Keymap) |
| Add Watchpoint, Set Execution Point to Cursor | context menu / Find Action |
| Rerun Debug Session | Debug toolbar |

### Settings | Build, Execution, Deployment | Debugger

| Option | Setting | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LLDB DAP executable | `debugger.lldb.path` | empty: `lldb-dap` on the PATH |
| GDB executable | `debugger.gdb.path` | empty: `gdb` on the PATH |
| Debug adapter request timeout (ms) | `debugger.dap.requestTimeout` | 10000 |
| Log Debug Adapter Protocol messages | `debugger.dap.trace` | off |
| Show variable values in editor while debugging | `debugger.showInlineValues` | on |
| Memory view: bytes per row | `debugger.memory.bytesPerRow` | 16 |

Language packs add their adapters to the same settings page and dialogs (see
[contribution points](docs/guide/developer/contribution-points.md)).

## Servers and path mappings

When PHP runs in a container or on another machine, its file paths differ from yours. Define a
**server** in Settings | Languages & Frameworks | PHP | **Servers**: **Name**, **Host**,
**Port**, **Debugger** (Xdebug) and **Use path mappings**: the project's folders as a tree,
with the **Absolute path on the server** of each mapped folder (usually just the project root,
e.g. `/var/www/html`; a deeper mapping such as `vendor` wins for its files).

![Servers](docs/screenshots/debugger-servers.png)

A session finds its server from `PHP_IDE_CONFIG=serverName=<name>`, otherwise from
`$_SERVER['SERVER_NAME']` and `SERVER_PORT`. Servers are stored in
`<project>/.forge/php-servers.json`.

## Web Server Debug Validation

**Run | Web Server Debug Validation…** (PHPStorm's "Validate Debugger Configuration on Web
Server") checks whether PHP can connect to Forge:

- **Local Web Server or Shared Folder**: Forge writes a temporary script
  `forge_xdebug_validator_*.php` into the project folder that the web server serves (**Path to
  create validation script**, e.g. `public`), requests it under **URL to validation script**
  and deletes it right after the check. Nothing is written before you press **Validate**.
- **CLI Interpreter**: reads `php -i` of a [CLI interpreter](docs/guide/user/php.md#cli-interpreters) (also
  Docker, Compose, SSH or WSL ones).

Each check shows ✓ (fine), ⚠ (works with conditions) or ✗ (must be fixed) with a hint: the
Xdebug version, `xdebug.mode` (must include `debug`), `xdebug.client_host` (localhost cannot
reach Forge from a container or another machine), `xdebug.client_port` (must be Forge's
`php.debug.port`), `xdebug.start_with_request` (`trigger` needs the cookie or
`XDEBUG_SESSION_START`) and the server name used to find path mappings. For CLI interpreters,
Forge sets mode, host, port and session itself for debug runs, so only the extension matters.
The path and URL are remembered per project (`php.debug.validation.documentRoot`,
`php.debug.validation.url`).

![Web Server Debug Validation](docs/screenshots/debugger-validation.png)

## Settings | Languages & Frameworks | PHP | Debug

![Debug settings](docs/screenshots/debugger-settings.png)

| Option | Setting | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Debug port | `php.debug.port` | 9003 |
| Ignore external connections through unregistered server configurations | `php.debug.ignoreExternalConnections` | off |
| Break at first line in PHP scripts | `php.debug.breakAtFirstLine` | off |
| Step out of files that are not mapped into the project | `php.debug.ignoreUnmappedFiles` | on |
| Show variable values in editor while debugging | `php.debug.showInlineValues` | on |
| Max. children (array elements / properties per page) | `php.debug.maxChildren` | 100 |
| Max. depth (levels fetched at once) | `php.debug.maxDepth` | 1 |
| Max. string length (bytes) | `php.debug.maxData` | 65536 |
| Path to create validation script | `php.debug.validation.documentRoot` | `public` |
| URL to validation script | `php.debug.validation.url` | `http://localhost:8080` |

## Remote projects

In a [remote project](docs/guide/user/remote-development.md), **Start Listening** listens on a free local port
and asks the remote host, over SSH, to listen on `127.0.0.1:<php.debug.port>` (9003) and forward
connections to Forge (a reverse tunnel, re-established after reconnects). Configure Xdebug on
the host with `xdebug.client_host=127.0.0.1`. Xdebug's paths are the host's paths, which are the
project's, so no path mappings are needed. The status bar shows that the listener goes through
the host.

![Listening through the host](docs/screenshots/remote-parity-debug-listening.png)

![Remote debug session](docs/screenshots/remote-parity-debug-session.png)

> **Note:** JavaScript and Node.js debugging are not built in; see
> [WebForge](docs/guide/user/webforge.md#debugging-scripts).

# Terminal

The **Terminal** tool window (`Alt+F12`, bottom stripe) runs your shell on a real pseudo
terminal (xterm.js in the UI, a PTY in Rust), so interactive programs such as `vim`, `htop`,
`git rebase -i`, `php artisan tinker` or Claude Code work.

![Terminal tabs](docs/screenshots/terminal-tabs.png)

## Tabs

| Action | Windows/Linux | macOS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Show/hide the terminal | `Alt+F12` | `Alt+F12` |
| New tab | `Ctrl+Shift+T` | `Cmd+T` |
| Close tab | `Ctrl+Shift+F4` | `Cmd+Shift+F4` |

Tabs are named "Local", "Local (2)", …; while a program runs that sets a title (OSC 0 / OSC 2,
e.g. Claude Code's current task), the tab shows that title instead (**Show application title**).
Double-click a tab or use **Rename Session** to rename it; a renamed tab keeps its name. The arrow next to **+** has **New Tab**, **New Tab in Current Directory**, **SSH Session…**
(see [SSH sessions](#ssh-sessions)), **Rename Session** and **Clear Buffer**. A
tab's context menu has **New Tab**, **New Tab in Current Directory** (the directory the shell
reports, see below), **Rename Session**, **Close Tab** and **Close Other Tabs**. The terminal
area's context menu has **Copy** (`Ctrl+Shift+C`), **Paste** (`Ctrl+Shift+V`), **Select All**
and **Clear Buffer**.

On Windows, the arrow next to **+** also offers `WSL: <distro>` for every WSL distribution: a
shell in that distribution, in the project folder (see
[Dev Containers and WSL](docs/guide/user/dev-containers-and-wsl.md#terminal--wsl)). In projects opened in a dev
container or a WSL distribution, every tab is a shell there.

## Program progress

Programs such as Claude Code, winget or systemd report their progress with the OSC 9;4
sequence. Forge shows it:

- on the **terminal tab**: a ring filled to the percentage, or a spinning arc while the
  program is busy without a percentage;
- in the **status bar** (**Show progress in the status bar**): the ring plus
  "&lt;tab title&gt;: 42%", "Working…", "Error 60%" or "Paused"; click it to show the tab;
- on the **Terminal stripe icon** while the tool window is hidden: the combined progress of
  all tabs (errors first, then paused, then the slowest).

Errors are drawn in the danger color, paused progress in the warning color. The progress
disappears when the program removes it, when the shell shows its next prompt (OSC 133) or
when the shell exits.

![Claude Code with progress](docs/screenshots/terminal-claude-session.png)

![Progress on the stripe icon and in the status bar](docs/screenshots/terminal-progress-hidden.png)

## Notifications and bell

OSC 9 (iTerm2) and OSC 777 (`notify;<title>;<body>`) notifications appear as balloons when
the tab is not visible or Forge is not focused; **Show** opens the tab. The bell flashes the
terminal when the tab is visible and otherwise puts a dot on the tab and on the stripe icon;
with **Audible bell** it also beeps.

## Keyboard

While the terminal has focus, plain `Ctrl`+letter, `Alt`+letter and `Escape` go to the shell
(so `Ctrl+C`, `Ctrl+R`, `Alt+B` behave as in any terminal). Function keys, `Alt`+digit,
`Ctrl+Shift` and `Ctrl+Alt` combinations still reach the IDE, so `Alt+1` or `Shift+Escape`
work from the terminal.

`Shift+Enter` sends ESC CR and `Ctrl+Enter` sends LF, so TUI programs such as Claude Code
insert a newline instead of submitting. On macOS, **Use Option as Meta key** makes `Option`
work as `Alt` in the shell.

## Links

URLs and OSC 8 hyperlinks in the output open with `Ctrl+Click` (`Cmd+Click` on macOS), so a
plain click still selects text; hovering one shows its target at the bottom of the terminal.
Only `http(s)` and `mailto` links open in the browser and `file://` links only open files of
the project; other links are refused. File references such as `app/Models/User.php:42` are
underlined and open in the editor at that line with a click.

## Rendering

The terminal draws with WebGL on the GPU and falls back to the DOM renderer when WebGL is not
available or its context is lost (**Renderer**). Emoji, East Asian characters, braille spinners
and Nerd Font glyphs take the widths modern terminals use (Unicode 15 and grapheme clusters),
and box drawing characters line up without gaps. The font is **Font** (empty: the editor font),
followed by common monospace fonts, Nerd Fonts, color emoji and symbol fonts for missing glyphs.
Settings changes apply to open terminals right away.

## Shell and start directory

The shell is, in this order: Settings | Tools | Terminal | **Shell path**
(`terminal.shellPath`), `$SHELL` on Linux/macOS (then bash, zsh, sh), on Windows PowerShell 7
(`pwsh.exe`), Windows PowerShell or `%ComSpec%`. bash, zsh and fish start as login shells.

New tabs start in the project root unless **Start directory** (`terminal.startDirectory`) is
set; **Environment variables** (`terminal.environment`, one `NAME=value` per entry) are added.

The shell also gets `TERM=xterm-256color`, `COLORTERM=truecolor`, `TERM_PROGRAM=Forge`,
`TERM_PROGRAM_VERSION=<Forge version>` and `FORGE_TERMINAL=1`, and a UTF-8 `LANG` when none is
set. Variables of the terminal Forge itself was started from (kitty, tmux, iTerm2, WezTerm,
Ghostty, …) are removed, so programs do not mistake Forge for that terminal.

Shells that report their directory (OSC 7, or ConEmu's OSC 9;9) let **New Tab in Current
Directory** open the new tab there. Closing a tab ends the shell; a shell that ignores the
hang-up signal is killed after 1.5 seconds.

## Settings | Tools | Terminal

| Option | Setting | Default | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Shell path | `terminal.shellPath` | system default | user |
| Default tab name | `terminal.tabName` | `Local` | user |
| Audible bell (a short tone when a program rings the bell) | `terminal.audibleBell` | off | user |
| Copy to clipboard on selection | `terminal.copyOnSelection` | off | user |
| Shell integration | `terminal.shellIntegration` | on | user |
| Show application title | `terminal.showApplicationTitle` | on | user |
| Show progress in the status bar | `terminal.showProgressInStatusBar` | on | user |
| Use Option as Meta key (macOS) | `terminal.optionAsMeta` | on | user |
| Cursor shape | `terminal.cursorShape` | Block | user |
| Blinking cursor | `terminal.cursorBlink` | on | user |
| Start directory | `terminal.startDirectory` | project root | user, project |
| Environment variables | `terminal.environment` | empty | user, project |
| Font | `terminal.font.family` | editor font | user |
| Size | `terminal.font.size` | 13 | user |
| Line height | `terminal.font.lineHeight` | 1.2 | user |
| Renderer | `terminal.renderer` | Automatic | user |
| Scrollback buffer | `terminal.scrollback` | 10000 lines | user |

![Terminal settings](docs/screenshots/terminal-settings.png)

## Shell integration

With **Shell integration** on, bash and zsh tell the terminal their working directory (shown
in the tab's tooltip) and where each command starts and ends: finished commands get a mark in
the scrollbar, green when they succeeded and red when they failed. Your own startup files
still run: bash starts with an init file that sources `~/.bashrc` (or the profile files for a
login shell), zsh with a `ZDOTDIR` whose files source yours. The scripts live in
`<cache dir>/forge/shell-integration` of the machine the shell runs on (also on remote hosts).
fish, sh and PowerShell start without it; it applies to new sessions.

## SSH sessions

**Tools | Start SSH Session…** and **SSH Session…** in the new-tab dropdown (the arrow next
to **+**) open a terminal tab on another host over SSH: pick one of your SSH configurations, an
SFTP deployment server of the project or **Edit credentials…**. The tab is named after the
host and runs on a pseudo terminal on the SSH channel, so full-screen programs and resizing
work. See [Remote Host and SSH sessions](docs/guide/user/remote-host-and-ssh.md#ssh-sessions); in Safe Mode a
session to a deployment server asks first.

![SSH session](docs/screenshots/ssh-session-terminal.png)

## Other terminals

The Services tool window opens terminals into Docker containers and Kubernetes pods
(`docker exec`, `kubectl exec`), and in a [remote project](docs/guide/user/remote-development.md) the terminal
runs on the remote host, with the same environment as a local one.

![Remote terminal](docs/screenshots/remote-terminal.png)

In browser mode (`pnpm dev`) the terminal is a small fake shell; `claude` replays a recorded
Claude Code session (`claude --thinking` and `claude --error` show the other progress states),
`Ctrl+C` ends it.

Source: docs/guide/user/database.md

# Database tools and SQL console

The plugin **Database Tools and SQL** (`forge.database`) is Forge's DataGrip part. Drivers are
built into Forge — there are no JDBC drivers to download:

| Engine | Driver | Tree | Console |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MySQL, MariaDB | `sqlx` | schemas, tables, views, columns (generated), keys, indexes, checks, triggers, routines with arguments, users | SQL, transactions |
| PostgreSQL | `sqlx` | database, schemas, tables, views, materialized views, sequences, routines with arguments, enum/domain/composite types, columns (identity, generated), keys, indexes, checks, triggers, roles | SQL, transactions |
| SQLite | `sqlx` | tables, views, columns, keys, indexes, checks, triggers | SQL, transactions |
| SQL Server, Azure SQL | `tiberius` (pure-Rust TDS over rustls) | database, schemas, tables, views, sequences, alias types, columns (computed), keys, indexes, checks, triggers, procedures and functions with parameters, logins and server roles | T-SQL (`GO` separates batches), transactions |
| ClickHouse | HTTP interface (port 8123, 8443 with TLS), JSON results | databases, tables, views, materialized views, columns (materialized, alias), primary key, data skipping indexes, users and roles | SQL; every statement on its own |
| Oracle | SQL\*Plus or SQLcl **installed by you** (see [Oracle](#oracle)) | schemas, tables, views, materialized views, sequences, object types, columns, keys, indexes, checks, triggers, procedures, functions (with arguments) and packages | SQL and PL/SQL blocks ending with `/`; every statement on its own |
| Redis | `redis-rs` | databases → keys with type and TTL | Redis commands, one per line |
| MongoDB | official MongoDB driver | databases → collections → fields | shell calls: `db.users.find({...})`, `aggregate`, … |
| DDL data source | SQL files of the project, parsed by Forge (see [DDL data sources](#ddl-data-sources)) | the same tree as the files' dialect | none (no database) |

ODBC is not supported: no permissive Rust crate makes generic ODBC drivers work without a
system driver manager, so Forge supports the engines above natively instead.

## Database tool window

The **Database** tool window (right stripe) is DataGrip's Database Explorer. It shows your data
sources as a tree: data source → database (PostgreSQL, SQL Server) → schemas → tables, views,
materialized views, sequences, routines and types → columns, keys, foreign keys, indexes,
checks and triggers, and the **server objects** (roles and users).

![Database tree](docs/screenshots/database-tree.png)

![Full object tree with routines, triggers and checks](docs/screenshots/database-explorer-tree.png)

- **Routines** show their arguments and result: `close_stale_orders (days int, OUT closed int)
  procedure`, `order_total (o_id bigint): numeric`.
- **Types** list enums with their labels, domains with their base type and composite types.
- Other databases of the server are listed below the connected one (`not introspected`); create
  another data source to browse them.
- **Lazy loading**: schemas are introspected when you open them (the current schema right
  away). Forge caches the model of every data source in its cache folder
  (`<cache dir>/forge/db-models/`, see [File locations](docs/guide/reference/file-locations.md)), so
  after a restart the tree shows at once, without connecting.
- **Refresh** works per node: on a table it re-reads only that table (columns, keys, indexes,
  checks, triggers), on a schema that schema, on the data source the schema list, the server
  objects and every loaded schema. The toolbar's **Refresh** refreshes the selected data source.

Toolbar: **+** (add data source), **Refresh**, **Data Source Properties** (`Shift+Enter`),
**Jump to Query Console…** (`Ctrl+Shift+F10`), **Collapse All**, **Sessions** (see
[Sessions](#sessions)). Context menu of a node: **Quick Documentation**, **Full-Text Search…**,
**New Query Console**, **Edit Data** (tables), **Go to DDL**, **Copy Name**, **Add Virtual
Foreign Key…** (columns), **Add Virtual Column…** (tables), **New › Table…**, **Modify
Table…**, **Rename…**, **Drop…**, **SQL Scripts ›**, **Import/Export ›** (see
[Database objects](#database-objects)), **Schemas…**, **Properties**, **Refresh**,
**Disconnect**, **Delete**. `Ctrl+click` adds nodes to the selection and `Shift+click` selects a
range, for Generate DDL and Drop of several objects.

### Quick Documentation

`Ctrl+Q` (or double-click on a routine, sequence or type) on a node shows its documentation:
the kind and location, the comment, properties (type, nullability, default, auto-increment,
primary key, references and referencing tables, arguments, language, enum labels) and the DDL —
the routine or trigger source when the database keeps it, otherwise generated from the model.
`Escape` closes it.

![Quick Documentation of a procedure](docs/screenshots/database-quick-doc.png)

### Schema filter

The **Schemas** tab of a data source (context menu **Schemas…**) chooses which schemas (MySQL and
ClickHouse: databases; Redis and MongoDB: databases) Forge introspects and shows, like
DataGrip's introspection scope. Hidden schemas are never introspected.

![Schemas tab](docs/screenshots/database-schema-filter.png)

One pattern per line:

| Pattern | Selects |
| --- | --- |
| `shop` | the schema `shop` (names ignore case) |
| `*`, `tenant_*`, `db_?` | wildcards: every schema, schemas starting with `tenant_`, … |
| `:current` | the connection's current schema |
| `/tenant_\d+/`, `/sales/i` | a regular expression (with `i`: ignoring case) |
| `!pattern` | excludes what `pattern` selects, e.g. `*` and `!pg_*` |

No pattern means `:current` (the first schema when there is no current one); only exclusions
start from every schema. **All schemas** and **Current schema** add `*` and `:current`; the
list below shows the result for the server's schemas, and its check boxes add or exclude single
schemas. The tree shows `4 of 6` next to the data source when schemas are hidden.

### Virtual foreign keys and columns

Databases without declared foreign keys (MyISAM tables, legacy schemas, `user_id` columns
without constraints) can get **virtual foreign keys**: right-click a column → **Add Virtual
Foreign Key…**, choose the referenced table and column. **Add Virtual Column…** on a table adds a
computed column (`price * quantity`).

![A virtual foreign key](docs/screenshots/database-virtual-fk.png)

They are stored in the project in `.forge/database/virtual.toml` (share it with your team) and
merged into the model: the tree shows them in italics with the accent colour, Quick
Documentation lists them, the data grid marks their columns, and the console's completion
offers joins over them (see [completion](#query-console)). **Remove Virtual Foreign Key** /
**Remove Virtual Column** delete them. The file looks like this:

```toml
[[foreignKey]]
dataSource = "shop-local-1f3a"
schema = "shop"
table = "orders"
columns = ["customer"]
refTable = "users"
refColumns = ["id"]

[[column]]
dataSource = "shop-local-1f3a"
schema = "shop"
table = "order_items"
name = "line_total"
expression = "quantity * unit_price"
type = "decimal(10,2)"
```

### Full-text search

**Full-Text Search…** (`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F` in the Database tool window, or the context menu)
finds a text in the **data** of tables and views. It opens a tab with the text, the mode
(**Contains**, **Exact match**, **Regular expression**), **Match case**, **All column types**
(also numbers and dates; otherwise text columns only), **Rows per table** (default 100), table
patterns (`users, order_*, !audit_*`) and the scope: data sources and their schemas (none
checked means all shown schemas).

![Full-text search results](docs/screenshots/database-full-text-search.png)

Forge searches table by table with read-only `SELECT`s and shows each table with matches as
soon as it is done, the matching cells highlighted; the progress bar shows how far it is, and
**Cancel** stops it. Double-click a table or row to open the table. The text is always sent as a
quoted literal, with a per-dialect condition: `ILIKE`/`~*` (PostgreSQL), `LIKE`/`REGEXP_LIKE`
(MySQL, Oracle), `LIKE … ESCAPE` (SQLite, SQL Server), `positionCaseInsensitiveUTF8`/`match`
(ClickHouse). SQLite and SQL Server have no regular expressions; Redis, MongoDB and DDL data
sources cannot be searched.

Data sources with a colour tint their rows (see [Colours](#read-only-and-production-data-sources));
`read-only` and the SSH host appear next to the name.

![SQL Server tree](docs/screenshots/database-sqlserver-tree.png)

## ER diagrams

**Diagrams | Show Diagram** (`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+U`, macOS `Cmd+Alt+Shift+U`, or the context
menu of the Database tool window) opens an entity–relationship diagram in an editor tab:

- on a **schema** or a **data source**: every table and view of the schema (of a data source:
  its current schema);
- on a **table** or **view**: that table with the tables it references and the tables that
  reference it;
- in a console or table tab: the schema of its data source (a table tab: that table).

![ER diagram](docs/screenshots/database-er-diagram.png)

Each table lists its columns with their types; primary key columns have a key icon, foreign
key columns a link icon, and nullable columns are dimmed. Foreign keys are drawn from the row of
their column to the row of the referenced column, with an arrow at the referenced table;
nullable and [virtual](#virtual-foreign-keys-and-columns) foreign keys are dashed. Referenced
tables are placed above the tables that reference them, related tables next to each other, and
tables without relations in a grid below. Very long types are shortened (the tooltip shows the
full type).

| Action | How |
| --- | --- |
| Pan | scroll, `Shift`+scroll sideways, or drag the background |
| Zoom | `Ctrl`+scroll (macOS `Cmd`+scroll), or **Zoom In** / **Zoom Out** / **Actual Size** / **Fit Content** |
| Highlight a table's relations | click the table |
| Open the table's data | double-click the table |
| Columns | **All Columns**, **Keys** (primary and foreign key columns only) or **No Columns** |
| Views | show or hide views and materialized views |
| Export | **Export Diagram** → **Export to SVG…** or **Export to PNG…** (twice the size) |
| Refresh | introspect the schema again |

![ER diagram of a table (light theme)](docs/screenshots/database-er-diagram-light.png)

The status bar counts the tables and relations and the foreign keys that point to tables not in
the diagram (other schemas, or not related to the selected table).

## Compare Structure and migrations

**Compare Structure…** (context menu of a data source, schema or table, or `Ctrl+D`, macOS
`Cmd+D`, in the Database tool window) opens DataGrip's structure comparison in an editor tab.

![Compare Structure](docs/screenshots/database-compare-structure.png)

- **Source** is how the schema should be, **Target** the schema to migrate. Each side is a
  schema of any relational data source — including a [DDL data source](#ddl-data-sources),
  so you can compare a database with the `CREATE TABLE` scripts or migrations in the project —
  or **DDL snapshot (paste SQL)** for a script you paste. **Swap** exchanges them.
- **Compare** shows the differences as a tree: tables and views only in the source (**+**,
  created by the migration), only in the target (**−**, dropped) and changed ones, with their
  columns (type, nullability, default, auto increment, comment), primary keys, indexes,
  foreign keys (with their `ON DELETE` / `ON UPDATE` rules), checks, view queries and comments.
  Types are compared normalized (`int4` = `integer`, `character varying` = `varchar`),
  indexes SQLite names itself and the generated names of SQLite's foreign keys are not
  differences. Virtual foreign keys and columns are not part of the database and are ignored.
- **Drop missing objects** (on by default) drops tables, views and columns that exist only in
  the target; off, they are kept and listed as warnings. **Ignore comments** and **Ignore
  defaults** leave those out of the comparison.

The right side is the **migration script** in the target's dialect, ordered so every
statement can run: foreign keys and views that change are dropped first, then indexes, keys
and checks, then tables; new tables, columns, keys, indexes and checks follow, foreign keys and
views come last. Each dialect gets its own syntax (`ALTER COLUMN … TYPE … USING` and
`SET NOT NULL` on PostgreSQL, `MODIFY COLUMN` on MySQL, `ALTER COLUMN … NULL` on SQL Server,
`MODIFY (…)` on Oracle, `DROP FOREIGN KEY` on MySQL, …). SQLite cannot alter most of a table,
so a changed SQLite table is rebuilt: the new table is created, the common columns are copied,
the old table is dropped and the new one renamed, with foreign key enforcement off; its indexes
and triggers are created again. Statements that drop data are marked `-- Destructive`, and what
needs a look (a new `NOT NULL` column without a default, a SQL Server default constraint,
ClickHouse tables without an `ENGINE`) is listed as warnings above the script.

The script never runs on its own:

- **Open in Console** opens it in a new console of the target; nothing runs until you execute
  it there.
- **Run Migration…** asks first, naming how many statements drop data and whether the target is
  a production data source; on a [read-only](#read-only-and-production-data-sources) target it
  is disabled (and the console guard would refuse it). After running, the target is
  introspected again and compared once more.
- **Copy** copies the script.
- With the [Laravel](docs/guide/user/laravel.md) plugin active, **Laravel Migration** writes the migration as
  `database/migrations/<date>_update_<schema>_schema.php` (schema builder calls in `up()`, the
  way back in `down()`) and opens it; with the [Doctrine](docs/guide/user/doctrine.md) plugin active,
  **Doctrine Migration** writes `migrations/Version<date>.php` with the script's statements as
  `addSql()` calls.

## Data sources

**New Data Source…** (the **+** button or Find Action) opens **Data Sources and Drivers**:

![Data source dialog](docs/screenshots/database-data-source-dialog.png)

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| Name, Comment | |
| Driver | MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, SQLite, SQL Server, ClickHouse, Oracle, Redis, MongoDB, [DDL Data Source](#ddl-data-sources) |
| Host, Port, Database / SQLite file | SQLite files are chosen with a file picker. Oracle: **Service** (e.g. `FREEPDB1`); Redis: **Database index** (`0`); MongoDB: also a full `mongodb://` or `mongodb+srv://` URL as the host |
| Authentication | User & Password, or none |
| Password | stored in the OS keychain (service `forge-db`), never in project files |
| SSH/SSL tab | SSH tunnel and SSL/TLS, see below |
| Schemas tab | the [schema filter](#schema-filter): which schemas are introspected and shown |
| Options | read-only, colour, transaction control (Auto / Manual), single session mode, connect timeout, startup script |
| Scope | **Project Data Sources** (`<project>/.forge/dataSources.toml`, shareable) or **Global Data Sources** (`dataSources.toml` in Forge's config folder) |

**Test Connection** shows success with the server version, or the error.

### SSH tunnel and SSL/TLS

The **SSH/SSL** tab reaches databases that are only visible from a bastion host and secures
the connection itself.

![SSH/SSL tab](docs/screenshots/database-ssh-ssl.png)

**Use SSH tunnel**: Forge opens the SSH connection itself (the same SSH client as
[remote development](docs/guide/user/remote-host-and-ssh.md)) and forwards a local port to the database
**host and port as the SSH host sees them** — `localhost:5432` is the database on the bastion.

- **SSH configuration**: one of your saved configurations (Settings | Tools | SSH
  Configurations), which brings its own host, user, authentication and stored secret, or
  **Ad-hoc** with the fields below.
- Ad-hoc: **Host** (also a `~/.ssh/config` alias, with its `HostName`, `Port`, `User`,
  `IdentityFile` and `ProxyJump`), **Port**, **User name** and **Authentication type**:
  **Password**, **Key pair** (private key file and passphrase) or **OpenSSH config and
  authentication agent**.
- The SSH password or key passphrase is stored in the OS keychain (account `<id>#ssh`).
- The first connection to an unknown host shows its key fingerprint: **Trust Host Key and Test
  Again** adds it to `~/.ssh/known_hosts`. A changed key is reported and refused until you trust
  it again.

**SSL** **Mode**:

| Mode | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Disable | no TLS |
| Prefer | TLS when the server offers it, certificate not checked (ClickHouse and Redis: plain) |
| Require | TLS, certificate not checked |
| Verify CA | TLS, certificate signed by the CA file (or the system roots) |
| Verify Full | like Verify CA, and the certificate must name the host |

**CA file**, **Client certificate file** and **Client key file** are PEM files; relative paths
are resolved against the project. An encrypted client key (PKCS#8 `ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY`) is
decrypted in memory with the **Client key password**, which is stored in the keychain (account
`<id>#ssl-key`); legacy OpenSSL-encrypted keys must be converted with
`openssl pkcs8 -topk8`. What each driver does with them:

| Driver | SSL/TLS |
| --- | --- |
| MySQL, MariaDB | `ssl-mode` Disabled / Preferred / Required / Verify CA / Verify Identity, CA and client certificate |
| PostgreSQL | `sslmode` with `sslrootcert`, `sslcert`, `sslkey` |
| SQL Server | Prefer encrypts the login, Require encrypts everything without checking the certificate, Verify uses the CA; client certificate and **unencrypted** key files |
| ClickHouse | HTTPS from Require on (use the HTTPS port, usually 8443); Verify CA also checks the host name |
| Redis | `rediss://` from Require on, CA and client certificate |
| MongoDB | TLS from Require on; the client certificate **and its key in one PEM file** (set as the client certificate) |
| Oracle | configured in the Oracle client (`sqlnet.ora`, wallet) |

Through an SSH tunnel, Verify Full checks the certificate against the configured database host
for SQL Server, Redis and MongoDB; for MySQL and PostgreSQL use Verify CA.

### Oracle

Forge does not bundle Oracle's client and there is no permissive pure-Rust driver for Oracle's
network protocol, so Oracle data sources run through **SQL\*Plus** (from the Oracle Instant
Client "SQL\*Plus" package) or **SQLcl**, which you install yourself; Forge finds `sqlplus` (or
SQLcl's `sql`) on `PATH`. Every statement starts `sqlplus -S -L /nolog`, logs in through the
process's input (the password never appears on a command line), prints CSV and exits, so:

- each statement is committed on its own; there are no manual transactions,
- **Cancel** stops the process,
- PL/SQL blocks (`BEGIN … END;`, `CREATE PROCEDURE …`) end with a line containing only `/`.

### DDL data sources

A **DDL data source** (**+** → **DDL Data Source**) has no database: Forge builds its model from
SQL DDL files of the project — a `schema.sql`, a dump without data, or a folder of SQL migrations
(Flyway `V1__…`, `V2__…`). It needs no server and works offline.

- **Files**: one file or folder per line, relative to the project. Folders are read with their
  subfolders in natural name order (`V2` before `V10`), and the statements are applied in
  order: `CREATE TABLE`/`VIEW`/`MATERIALIZED VIEW`/`INDEX`/`SEQUENCE`/`TYPE`/`DOMAIN`/
  `FUNCTION`/`PROCEDURE`/`TRIGGER`/`SCHEMA`, `ALTER TABLE` (add/drop/rename columns and
  constraints, rename tables), `DROP` and `COMMENT ON`, so migrations give the final schema.
- **Dialect**: PostgreSQL, MySQL / MariaDB, SQLite, SQL Server, Oracle or ClickHouse; MySQL
  scripts may use `DELIMITER`.
- **Default schema**: where unqualified names go (by default `public`, `main` or `dbo`).

![A DDL data source](docs/screenshots/database-ddl-source.png)

The tree, Quick Documentation, **Go to DDL** and SQL completion of consoles use the parsed
model. Statements Forge cannot parse are skipped and listed under **problems** with their
file and line (double-click opens it). Forge parses the files again when they change on disk.
Consoles of a DDL data source complete names but cannot run queries.

### From `.env`

When a project's `.env` has Laravel's `DB_*` variables or Symfony's `DATABASE_URL`, Forge shows
a balloon "Database found in .env" with **Add data source**; the tree also offers **Data
Source from .env**. Turn this off with Settings | Tools | Database | **Suggest data sources
from .env files** (`database.suggestFromEnv`).

## Query console

**New Query Console** on a data source (or **Open Query Console**) opens a console tab:

![Query console](docs/screenshots/database-console.png)

- SQL highlighting for the data source's dialect and completion of keywords, tables and
  columns.
- After `JOIN`, completion offers the tables related to the ones already in the statement by a
  foreign key — real or [virtual](#virtual-foreign-keys-and-columns) — with the whole
  condition: `JOIN ` → `users u ON u.id = o.user_id`.
- **Execute** (`Ctrl+Enter`, macOS `Cmd+Enter`) runs the statement at the caret, or the
  selection. Several statements separated by `;` run one after another.
- SQL in PHP and JavaScript strings runs the same way: `Ctrl+Enter` in an injected SQL string
  opens a console with it (see [Language injections](docs/guide/user/language-injections.md#run-injected-sql)).
- Results appear below in tabs (**Output** plus one tab per result set), paged by
  **Result set page size** (`database.pageSize`, 500).
- **Cancel Running Statements** stops a long query (MySQL `KILL QUERY`, PostgreSQL
  `pg_cancel_backend`, ClickHouse `KILL QUERY`, SQL Server by closing and reopening the
  console's connection).
- **Tx: Auto / Manual** switches the transaction mode; in manual mode use **Commit** and
  **Rollback**. ClickHouse, Oracle, Redis and MongoDB consoles run every statement on its own.
- **New session / Shared session** chooses the console's connection, see [Sessions](#sessions).
- The schema selector at the top right sets the current schema.

SQL [scratch files](docs/guide/user/scratches-and-http.md) attached to a data source open as consoles too.

Consoles are full [SQL editors](docs/guide/user/sql-editor.md): names resolve against the data source with the
SQL inspections and their quick fixes, `Ctrl+B` jumps to a table or column in the tree,
`Shift+F6` renames aliases, user parameters (`:id`, `?`, …) are asked before running, and
**Browse Query History** (`Ctrl+Alt+E`, the clock icon) searches, inserts or re-runs every
statement the data source ran.

### Explain Plan

**Explain Plan** and **Explain Plan (Raw)** (the plan icon in the console toolbar, or Find
Action) show how the database would run the statement at the caret (or the selection),
without running it:

| Dialect | Explain Plan runs | Explain Plan (Raw) runs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PostgreSQL | `EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON) …` | `EXPLAIN …` |
| MySQL | `EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE …` (MariaDB: `EXPLAIN …`) | `EXPLAIN …` |
| SQLite | `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN …` | the same |
| SQL Server | `SET SHOWPLAN_ALL ON`, the statement, `SET SHOWPLAN_ALL OFF` | the same |
| ClickHouse | `EXPLAIN json = 1, description = 1 …` | `EXPLAIN …` |

**Explain Plan** opens a **Plan** result tab with the plan as a tree — operation, object
(table or index), estimated cost, the operation's own cost (its cost minus its children's),
estimated rows and details such as filters and join conditions — and, with **Flame Graph**,
as bars whose width is the share of the estimated cost (or of the rows, or equal shares when
the database gives no estimates, as SQLite). **Explain Plan (Raw)** shows the rows of the
`EXPLAIN` as they are.

![Explain Plan](docs/screenshots/database-explain-plan.png)

![Explain Plan as a flame graph](docs/screenshots/database-explain-flame.png)

A statement that already starts with `EXPLAIN` runs as it is; since that may be
`EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, which executes the statement, it goes through the read-only and production
checks like **Execute**.

> **Note:** Explain Plan is not available for Oracle (Forge runs every Oracle statement in its
> own SQL\*Plus session, so the plan table is empty afterwards), Redis and MongoDB.

### Sessions

Every console runs in a **session** (an open connection). By default each console has its own
session, so transactions in one console are invisible to the others. **Shared session** in the
console toolbar (or **Single session mode** in the data source's Options) makes all consoles of
the data source share one connection and its transaction.

**Sessions** (the pulse icon in the Database tool window toolbar) lists the open sessions with
their data source, transaction mode, open transaction (statements and age), the running or
last statement, and **Commit**, **Rollback**, **Cancel** and **Close Session**.

![Sessions](docs/screenshots/database-sessions.png)

### Redis

A Redis data source shows its databases (`db0`, … from `INFO keyspace`). Expanding one lists the
keys matching the **key pattern** at the top (`*`, `user:*`, …; `Enter` reloads) with their type
and TTL; at most 1000 keys are listed. Double-click a key to open its **value viewer**: strings
as text (JSON pretty-printed), lists and sets as numbered rows, hashes as field/value rows,
sorted sets with scores and streams as JSON.

![Redis keys and value viewer](docs/screenshots/database-redis.png)

The console runs one command per line (`GET user:1`, `HGETALL user:1`, `SCAN 0 MATCH s*`,
quotes for spaces: `SET motd "hello world"`).

### MongoDB

A MongoDB data source shows databases → collections → fields (sampled from the first documents,
with their BSON types). Double-click a collection to open a console that finds its documents;
**JSON** in the result toolbar shows them as documents instead of a grid.

![MongoDB documents](docs/screenshots/database-mongodb.png)

The console understands the shell calls you would type in `mongosh`:

```text
db.users.find({ age: { $gt: 30 } }, { name: 1, email: 1 }).sort({ age: -1 }).limit(5)
db.orders.aggregate([{ $group: { _id: "$status", n: { $sum: 1 } } }])
db.orders.countDocuments({ status: "paid" })
db.users.distinct("address.country")
db.users.insertOne({ name: "Ada" })   db.users.updateMany({...}, { $set: {...} })   db.users.deleteMany({...})
db.users.getIndexes()   db.getCollectionNames()   show dbs   show collections   use shop
```

Arguments are relaxed JSON: unquoted keys, single quotes, `ObjectId("…")`, `ISODate("…")`,
`NumberLong(…)`, `NumberDecimal("…")` and `/regex/i`.

## Read-only and production data sources

**Read-only** (Options tab) protects a data source: the console refuses statements that change
data or schema (DML and DDL, Redis write commands, MongoDB writes) with a clear message, and the
driver refuses them too — MySQL and PostgreSQL sessions are `READ ONLY`, SQLite opens the file
read-only, ClickHouse gets `readonly=2`, Oracle `SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY`, SQL Server declares
`ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly`, Redis and MongoDB connections only accept reads.

**Colour** marks a data source as development (**green**), staging (**yellow**) or production
(**red**); the tree, its console and table tabs and the console editor are tinted, and the
console shows a badge. Before running `UPDATE` or `DELETE` without `WHERE`, `TRUNCATE`,
`FLUSHDB`/`FLUSHALL`, `deleteMany({})`/`updateMany({}, …)` or `drop()` on a **production**
data source, Forge asks for confirmation:

![Production warning](docs/screenshots/database-production-warning.png)

## Data grid and table editor

**Edit Data** (or double-click a table) opens the table in an editor tab with paging (**First,
Previous, Next, Last Page**), a **WHERE** filter and an **ORDER BY** field.

![Editing data](docs/screenshots/database-grid-edit.png)

| Action | Windows/Linux | macOS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Edit a cell | double-click or `Enter` | same |
| Value Editor | `Shift+Enter` | `Shift+Enter` |
| Go to Referenced Data | `Ctrl+B` | `Cmd+B` |
| Find Referencing Rows | `Alt+F7` | `Alt+F7` |
| Add Row | `Alt+Insert` | `Cmd+N` |
| Delete Rows | `Ctrl+Y` | `Cmd+Backspace` |
| Revert Selected | `Ctrl+Alt+Z` | `Cmd+Alt+Z` |
| Submit | `Ctrl+Enter` | `Cmd+Enter` |
| Reload Page | toolbar | toolbar |

Cell context menu: **Copy**, **Copy with Header**, **Edit**, **Set NULL**, **Edit Value…**,
**Set DEFAULT**, **Filter by** the cell's value, **Go to** the referenced table and **Find
Referencing Rows…**. Changes are applied in one transaction on **Submit**.

NULL is displayed as `<null>` (**Show NULL as**, `database.showNullAs`). Binary values are shown
as hex.

## Data editor

The table editor and console results work like DataGrip's data editor. Everything that needs
the database runs there (sort, filter, the DML), and everything else is computed by Forge's Rust
core (crate [`forge-dataedit`](docs/guide/developer/crates/forge-dataedit.md)).

### Sort and filter

- **Click a column header** to sort by it: ascending, descending, then off. **Ctrl+Click**
  (`Cmd+Click`) adds the column to the sort, so several columns sort in order (the header shows
  the position). The header context menu has **Sort Ascending**, **Sort Descending**, **Add to
  Sort**, **Clear Sort** and `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL` filters.
- **WHERE** takes any condition of the database's SQL. Column names are completed while you
  type (`↑`/`↓`, `Enter` or `Tab`); `Enter` applies the filter.
- **Filter by value** in a cell's context menu adds a condition such as `status <> 'cancelled'`
  or `shipped_at IS NULL`. The conditions show as chips under the filter row; `×` removes one.

![Filter and sort](docs/screenshots/data-editor-filter-sort.png)

Table editors sort and filter **on the server**: Forge builds the `SELECT … WHERE … ORDER BY`
for the data source's dialect (quoting, `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` or `OFFSET … FETCH`) and shows it in the
status. The typed condition must stay one read-only condition: Forge refuses it when it holds a
`;`, unbalanced brackets, an unclosed quote or comment, or writes (`DELETE`, `UPDATE`,
`INSERT`, `DROP`, `SELECT … INTO`, …, also in subqueries).

Console results come from arbitrary queries, so header sort and **Filter by value** run
**locally** on the fetched rows (NULLs first, numbers and decimals numerically).

### Value editor

**Shift+Enter** (or the panel icon, or **Edit Value…**) opens the value editor of the current
cell at the right. It picks the editor from the column type and the value:

| Value | Editor |
| --- | --- |
| Text | multi-line text |
| JSON (`json`, `jsonb`, or text that holds JSON) | formatted, validated while you type (line and column of the error), **Reformat** and **Minify**; the key order is kept |
| XML | indented and checked for well-nested tags |
| Binary | size, hex dump and an image preview for PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP and BMP |
| `date`, `datetime`, `timestamp`, `time` | a date/time picker plus the text, normalized on **Apply** (`2025-1-6 9:05` → `2025-01-06 09:05:00`) |
| `enum(…)`, `set(…)` | a list of the allowed values (check boxes for `set`) |
| Boolean, number | a selector or a number field |

**Apply** writes the value into the grid as a pending change. **Set NULL** and **Set DEFAULT**
(for columns with a default or auto increment) are there too. In console results the value
editor is a read-only viewer.

![Value editor with JSON](docs/screenshots/data-editor-value-json.png)

### Pending changes and the DML preview

Edits, new rows, deleted rows, `NULL` and `DEFAULT` stay **pending** until you **Submit** them;
**Revert** drops them. **Preview Pending Changes** (the list icon next to Submit) shows the
statements Forge will run, generated for the dialect:

![Pending changes with the DML preview](docs/screenshots/data-editor-pending-dml.png)

Rows are identified by the **primary key**; a table without one uses a **unique key whose columns
are all NOT NULL**. A table with neither refuses updates and deletes (new rows still work):
edit it with an `UPDATE` in a console instead. A statement that would change more than one row
rolls the whole batch back.

Writes honour the data source: **read-only** data sources refuse them, and on **production** (red)
data sources Submit shows the statements and asks for confirmation first.

### Foreign-key navigation

**Ctrl+B** on a cell of a foreign-key column opens the referenced table filtered to the
referenced row (`id = 23`); with several keys on the column, a popup lets you choose.
**Alt+F7** (**Find Referencing Rows…**) goes the other way: it lists the tables whose foreign
keys reference this table and opens the rows that reference the current one. Both work with real
and [virtual foreign keys](#virtual-foreign-keys-and-columns).

![Jump to the referenced row](docs/screenshots/data-editor-fk-jump.png)

### Transpose

**Transpose** shows each row as a column, with one line per column of the table — handy for wide
tables. Click a cell to select it; double-click opens it in the value editor.

![Transposed view](docs/screenshots/data-editor-transposed.png)

### Aggregates

When several cells are selected, the line under the grid shows their **Count**, **Sum**, **Avg**,
**Min**, **Max**, **Distinct** count and NULLs. Decimals are summed exactly. **Aggregate View**
(the Σ icon, or a click on the line) lists the aggregates per selected column.

![Aggregates](docs/screenshots/data-editor-aggregates.png)

### Compare data

**Compare With…** (toolbar or context menu, in table editors and console results) compares the
rows with another open result, an open table or any table of a connected data source. Pick the
**key** columns (the primary key is preselected); Forge matches rows by key and opens a
comparison tab with **changed** rows (old → new in each changed cell), **added** and **removed**
rows. The counters filter the rows; **unchanged** rows are hidden at first. Without a key, whole
rows are matched. Tables are compared on their first 5,000 rows.

![Compare data](docs/screenshots/data-editor-compare.png)

### Charts

**Show Chart** turns the result into a chart: **bar**, **line**, **area**, **pie** or
**scatter**. Pick the **X** column, one or more **Y** columns, an optional **Group by** column
(one series per value) and how values of the same X are combined (**SUM**, **AVG**, **MIN**,
**MAX** or **COUNT**). Numbers and dates on the X axis are sorted.

![Chart](docs/screenshots/data-editor-chart.png)

## Database objects

DataGrip's object dialogs work on every SQL data source (MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, SQLite,
SQL Server, Oracle and ClickHouse). The SQL they show is generated by Forge for the data
source's dialect; it runs only when you confirm.

![Context menu with SQL Scripts](docs/screenshots/database-objects-menu.png)

### Create Table and Modify Table

**New › Table…** (context menu of a data source, schema or table) and **Modify Table…**
(`Ctrl+F6` on a table) open the table dialog:

- the **structure tree** on the left: the table, its **columns**, **keys** (primary and unique),
  **foreign keys**, **indexes** and **checks**; **+** adds a column, key, foreign key, index or
  check, **−** removes the selected one, the arrows reorder columns;
- the **properties** of the selected node on the right: a column's name, **type** (with the
  dialect's types as completion), **default**, **comment**, **Not null**, **Auto increment**
  (`AUTO_INCREMENT`, `IDENTITY(1,1)`, `GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY`) and **Primary key**; a
  foreign key's columns, **target table** and **target columns** (from the loaded schemas),
  **On update** and **On delete**; an index's columns, **Unique** and **method** (PostgreSQL,
  MySQL); a check's expression;
- the table node holds the name, comment and the dialect's **table options**: MySQL engine,
  charset and collation; PostgreSQL tablespace and `UNLOGGED`; SQLite `WITHOUT ROWID` and
  `STRICT`; ClickHouse engine, `ORDER BY` and `PARTITION BY`; Oracle tablespace; temporary
  tables;
- a live **SQL preview** below.

![Create Table](docs/screenshots/database-create-table.png)

**Modify Table** compares the table as loaded with your edits and shows the `ALTER` script.
Columns keep their original names, so changing a name is a **rename** (`RENAME COLUMN`,
`sp_rename`, MySQL `CHANGE COLUMN` when the definition changes too), not a drop and an add. Keys,
foreign keys and indexes follow renamed columns. Changes that may lose data — a dropped column,
a type change, SQLite tables that must be rebuilt — are listed as **warnings** in red above the
script, and **OK** asks again before running it; a column that becomes `NOT NULL` is a warning
too.

![Modify Table](docs/screenshots/database-modify-table.png)

Per dialect: PostgreSQL uses `ALTER COLUMN … TYPE … USING`, `SET/DROP NOT NULL`, `SET/DROP
DEFAULT` and `COMMENT ON`; SQL Server looks up the generated name of a default constraint before
it drops it and keeps comments as `MS_Description` extended properties; Oracle uses `MODIFY (…)`;
ClickHouse `MODIFY COLUMN` and `COMMENT COLUMN`. SQLite can only rename and add columns in
place: for other changes Forge rebuilds the table (create `<table>_new`, copy the rows, drop the
old table, rename, recreate the indexes) and says so.

At the bottom choose **Execute in database** or **Open in console** (to review or edit the
script first). Executing runs the statements one by one on their own connection and stops at the
first error, naming the failed statement. A **read-only** data source refuses the script; a
**production** (red) data source asks before *any* change, not only unfiltered ones. The schema
is refreshed afterwards.

### Rename and Drop

**Rename…** (tables, views) and **Rename Column…** (columns) show the `RENAME` statement for the
dialect. **Drop…** drops tables, views, materialized views, sequences, routines, types, indexes
and triggers — one or several selected nodes — with a preview and a **Cascade** option:
`CASCADE` (PostgreSQL), `CASCADE CONSTRAINTS` (Oracle), or, where the database has no cascade
(MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server), the foreign keys of other tables that reference the dropped table
are dropped first.

### Generate DDL

**SQL Scripts ›** on one or several selected objects (tables, views, routines, sequences, types,
indexes, triggers, or a whole schema):

- **Generate DDL to Clipboard**, **to Query Console** or **to File…**;
- **SQL Generator…**: pick the objects in a list and set the options **Include DROP
  statements**, **IF NOT EXISTS / OR REPLACE** and **Qualify names with schema**; the script
  updates as you change them; **Copy**, **File…** or **Open in Console**.

![SQL Generator](docs/screenshots/database-generate-ddl.png)

The script is in **dependency order**: types, sequences, tables ordered by their foreign keys
(referenced tables first), views ordered by the views they read, routines, indexes, triggers.
Foreign keys between tables that reference each other are added with `ALTER TABLE` after both
tables exist. `DROP … IF EXISTS` statements come first, in reverse order. The script is formatted
with your SQL code style (Settings | Editor | Code Style | SQL) and works for DDL data sources
too.

## Import data

**Import/Export › Import Data from File…** (on a data source, schema or table) imports a file
into an existing table or a new one:

- **Source**: **CSV**, **TSV**, **Excel** (`.xlsx`, `.xls`, `.ods`; choose the **sheet**) or
  **JSON** (an array of objects, an array of arrays with a header row, or one object per line —
  NDJSON). For CSV: **delimiter** (detected from the first lines: comma, semicolon, tab or pipe),
  **quote**, **encoding** (detected from a byte order mark, else UTF-8, else Windows-1252; or
  choose one), **First row is header**, **Trim whitespace** and **Skip rows**. Quoted fields may
  contain delimiters, line breaks and doubled quotes; rows with missing fields are padded and
  reported. An empty unquoted field is `NULL`, `""` an empty string.
- **Columns**: every source column with its **detected type** (integer, decimal, boolean, date,
  date-time or text; values with leading zeros stay text), the **target column** (a column of the
  existing table, matched by name; or a name for the new table) and, for a new table, its SQL
  **type** in the target dialect. Untick a column to leave it out.
- **Preview**: the first 10 to 100 rows; a new table shows its `CREATE TABLE`.
- **Target**: schema and an existing table, or **New** with a name (the file's name by
  default).
- **Options**: **On error** — *Skip the row and continue* (a failing batch is retried row by row
  and the failing rows are reported) or *Abort* (stops at the first error and, where the driver
  has transactions, keeps nothing); **Batch size**; **Empty values as NULL**.

![Import mapping dialog](docs/screenshots/database-import.png)

Rows are inserted with multi-row `INSERT` statements per batch (at most 1000 rows per statement
on SQL Server, `INSERT ALL … SELECT 1 FROM dual` on Oracle; booleans, dates and numbers as
literals of the dialect). A progress bar shows the rows done; **Cancel** stops after the current
batch. Read-only data sources refuse imports; production data sources ask first.

## Export

**Export Data** (the download icon in a result or table) writes the rows as **CSV**, **JSON**,
SQL **INSERT** statements for the dialect, a **Markdown** table, or an **Excel** workbook
(`.xlsx`, with a bold, frozen header row; numbers and booleans stay numbers and booleans).
**Copy as** puts CSV, JSON, SQL or Markdown on the clipboard.

## Dump and restore with native tools

**Import/Export ›** on a data source, schema or table also offers the database's own dump and
restore tools, **installed by you** (Forge does not ship them):

| Data source | Dump | Restore |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MySQL, MariaDB | `mysqldump` | `mysql` (`source <file>`) |
| PostgreSQL | `pg_dump` (plain, custom, directory or tar) | `pg_restore` (custom, directory, tar) or `psql` (plain SQL) |
| SQLite | `sqlite3 .dump` / `.schema` | `sqlite3 .read` |
| SQL Server | `sqlcmd` `BACKUP DATABASE … TO DISK` | `sqlcmd -i script.sql`, or `RESTORE DATABASE` for a `.bak` |

The dialog has the **path** to the tool (empty: found on the `PATH`), the **output** or **input
file**, the **schemas** (MySQL: databases) and **tables** to include (selected tables are
preselected) and the options: **Structure**, **Data**, **Drop objects first** (`--add-drop-table`,
`--clean --if-exists`), **Create database**, **Single transaction**, **No owner**, the pg_dump
**format** and parallel **jobs**, and **More arguments**. The **command line** is shown as it
will run.

![pg_dump dialog](docs/screenshots/database-dump.png)

**Run** starts the tool in the **Run** tool window with the data source's connection: host,
port, user and database come from the data source, the password is passed in the tool's
environment variable (`MYSQL_PWD`, `PGPASSWORD`, `SQLCMDPASSWORD`) and **never on the command
line**, and a data source with an SSH tunnel is reached through the tunnel (open while the tool
runs). A restore asks for confirmation, is **refused on read-only** data sources and asks again
on **production** ones. Running tools is refused in Safe Mode (an untrusted project). In a remote
project the tools run on the host, so the file paths are paths on the host.

## Settings | Tools | Database

| Option | Setting | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Result set page size | `database.pageSize` | 500 |
| Show NULL as | `database.showNullAs` | `<null>` |
| Suggest data sources from .env files | `database.suggestFromEnv` | on |
| User parameters `?`, `:name`, `$1`, `${name}`, `#{name}` | `database.parameters.*` | on |
| Query history entries per data source | `database.history.limit` | 1000 |
| Run SQL Script: stop at the first error | `database.runFile.stopOnError` | on |

## Remote projects

In a [remote project](docs/guide/user/remote-development.md), project data sources (and the `.env`
suggestions) are read from the host, and Forge connects to them through an SSH tunnel to their
host and port **as the remote host sees them** — `localhost:3306` means the database on the
server. The data source shows which host it goes through. Global data sources connect directly
from your machine.

![Remote data source](docs/screenshots/remote-parity-data-source-dialog.png)

![Remote database](docs/screenshots/remote-parity-database.png)

A data source with its own SSH tunnel uses that tunnel instead.

> **Note:** SQLite files on the remote host cannot be opened.

Source: docs/guide/user/sql-editor.md

# SQL editor

`.sql` files and [query consoles](docs/guide/user/database.md#query-console) share one SQL editor, DataGrip's.
The work is done in Rust (`forge-sqlcode`); it never connects to a database while you type:
names resolve against the data source's **cached model** (the schemas the Database tool window
has loaded) or a [DDL data source](docs/guide/user/database.md#ddl-data-sources)'s files.

![Unresolved column, type mismatch, unused alias and the Add WHERE clause quick fix](docs/screenshots/sql-editor-unresolved-quick-fix.png)

## Dialects

Every SQL file has a dialect: **Generic SQL**, **MySQL**, **PostgreSQL**, **SQLite**, **SQL
Server**, **Oracle** or **ClickHouse**. The dialect decides the highlighting and keywords, how
names are quoted (`` `name` ``, `"name"`, `[name]`), comments (`#` in MySQL), strings (`$$`
bodies in PostgreSQL, backslash escapes in MySQL), the statement separators (`GO`, `/`) and the
formatter's quirks.

- **Settings | Languages & Frameworks | SQL Dialects**: the **Global SQL Dialect**, the
  **Project SQL Dialect** and a table of mappings — a file or folder, its dialect and the
  **data source** its names resolve against. The most specific path wins, so a folder of
  migrations can be PostgreSQL while one file in it is SQLite.
- The **status bar widget** of the active SQL editor shows the dialect and the data source
  (`MySQL · shop@localhost`). Its popup switches both for the file (it writes a mapping) and
  opens the settings page.
- **Consoles** use their data source's dialect and resolve against their data source.

![The SQL dialect widget](docs/screenshots/sql-editor-dialect-widget.png)

![Settings | Languages & Frameworks | SQL Dialects](docs/screenshots/sql-dialects-settings.png)

## Resolve and navigation

Names are mapped to the model: tables and views (with aliases, `schema.table`), columns
(qualified or not; an unqualified column is looked up in the query's tables, then in the
enclosing queries, so correlated subqueries work), CTEs and their columns (`WITH … AS`, also
`RECURSIVE` and explicit column lists), subqueries in `FROM` with their aliases, select-list
aliases in `ORDER BY`, `GROUP BY` and `HAVING`, schemas, and routines of the model. `INSERT`
column lists, `UPDATE … SET`, `DELETE … USING`, `ON CONFLICT` / `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`,
`RETURNING`, `CREATE VIEW … AS`, `ALTER TABLE`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE` and `CREATE INDEX` resolve
too. Schemas that were not introspected and table functions resolve to "unknown" and are never
reported.

| Action | Shortcut | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Go to Declaration | `Ctrl+B`, `Ctrl+Click` | an alias or CTE: its definition; a table, view or column: the node in the Database tool window; with a DDL data source: the `CREATE TABLE` (or `ALTER TABLE … ADD`) in its files. On a definition it shows the usages |
| Find Usages | `Alt+F7` | the usages of the column, table, alias or CTE in the file |
| Rename | `Shift+F6` | renames an alias, CTE or select-list alias with all its usages in place |
| Show Context Actions | `Alt+Enter` | the quick fixes of the problem at the caret |

## SQL inspections

The inspections are part of the inspection profile (**Settings | Editor | Inspections**,
group **SQL**), so they can be turned off, get another severity or be suppressed like any other.

| Inspection | Id | Reports | Quick fix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unresolved reference | `SqlResolve` | tables, columns, schemas and aliases that do not exist (red) | — |
| Ambiguous column reference | `SqlAmbiguousColumn` | an unqualified column that several tables of the query have | Qualify with `u.` (one per table) |
| Delete or update statement without where clauses | `SqlWithoutWhere` | `DELETE` / `UPDATE` without `WHERE` | Add WHERE clause (`WHERE FALSE`, selected to type over) |
| Unused table alias | `SqlUnusedAlias` | an alias no column uses (greyed out) | Remove alias |
| Unused common table expression | `SqlUnusedCte` | a CTE the statement never reads | Remove unused CTE |
| Types compatibility | `SqlType` | a column compared with a value of another type family (`id = 'abc'`, `name = 5`) when the model knows the column's type | Quote the value |
| Redundant ordering direction | `SqlRedundantOrderingDirection` | `ASC` | Remove redundant ASC |
| Redundant ELSE NULL clause | `SqlRedundantElseNull` | `ELSE NULL` in `CASE` | Remove ELSE NULL |
| Redundant alias expressions | `SqlRedundantAlias` | `users users`, `name AS name` | Remove redundant alias |

Without a data source, only the script's own names are checked (aliases, CTEs and their
columns). SQLite skips the type check (it compares values of any type).

## Formatter

**Code | Reformat Code** (`Ctrl+Alt+L`) and the **Reformat code** action of
[Actions on Save](docs/guide/user/actions-on-save.md) format SQL with **Settings | Editor | Code Style | SQL**:

| Tab | Options |
| --- | --- |
| Tabs and Indents | tab size, indent, tabs or spaces |
| Spaces | after comma, around operators, within parentheses |
| Wrapping and Braces | clauses on a new line, clause keywords aligned left or right ("river"), AND / OR on a new line, select / SET / ORDER BY items on separate lines, comma at the end or the start of the line |
| Blank Lines | blank lines kept between statements |
| Case | keywords and identifiers: as is, upper or lower case |

Subqueries and `CREATE TABLE` column lists are indented blocks. Comments and string contents
never change; routines and procedural blocks (`CREATE FUNCTION`, `BEGIN … END`) keep their
layout and only get the keyword case; `GO` batches and Oracle's `/` stay on their own lines.

![Code Style | SQL with the preview](docs/screenshots/sql-editor-formatter-settings.png)

## User parameters

Before a console runs a statement with placeholders, the **Parameters** dialog asks for their
values: `?` (positional), `:name`, `$1`, `${name}` and `#{name}`. Values are inserted as
written, so strings need quotes (`'admin'`). The console remembers the last values. Each
pattern can be turned off in **Settings | Tools | Database | User Parameters**; placeholders in
strings and comments are ignored, and PostgreSQL casts (`x::int`) are not parameters.

![The Parameters dialog](docs/screenshots/sql-editor-parameters.png)

## Query history

Every statement a console or Run SQL Script executes is recorded per data source with its
time, duration and row count (`<data dir>/forge/sql-history/<data source>.json`, at most
**Query history entries per data source**, 1000). **Browse Query History** (`Ctrl+Alt+E`, or
the clock icon of the console toolbar) searches it by words, optionally only the current
console; **Insert** adds the statement to the console, **Run** adds and executes it.

![Query history](docs/screenshots/sql-editor-history.png)

## Run SQL Script

**Run 'file.sql'…** in the Project view's context menu, the editor's context menu or Find
Action (**Run SQL Script…**) runs a `.sql` file against a data source (the file's mapped data
source comes first). Statements run in order on a new session, with a progress bar and one row
per statement (rows, time or the error). **Stop at the first error** (on by default) or
continue; **Stop** cancels the running statement. Read-only data sources refuse the script and
production data sources ask first, like consoles.

![Run SQL Script](docs/screenshots/sql-editor-run-file.png)

## Live templates

The **SQL** live template group works in SQL files and consoles: `sel`, `selc`, `selw`, `ins`,
`upd`, `del`, `join`, `lj`, `rj`, `tab` (create table) and `col`. See
[Live templates](docs/guide/user/live-templates.md).

## For developers

See [forge-sqlcode](docs/guide/developer/crates/forge-sqlcode.md) and
[Architecture](docs/guide/developer/architecture.md).
