Source: docs/guide/user/scratches-and-http.md

# Scratches, consoles and HTTP client

**Scratch files** are throw-away files for experiments, like PHPStorm's "Scratches and
Consoles". They are **global**: they do not belong to a project and are kept in Forge's config
folder (`<config dir>/forge/scratches/`), so they are available in every project.

## Creating scratches

| Action | Windows/Linux | macOS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| New Scratch File… | `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Insert` | `Cmd+Shift+N` |
| New Scratch Buffer | Find Action | Find Action |

**New Scratch File** asks for the language: type to filter (fuzzy), recently used languages
come first. Every file type with an extension is available.

![New Scratch File](docs/screenshots/scratches-new-popup.png)

New scratches are numbered `scratch.php`, `scratch_1.php`, …; HTTP scratches start as
`rest-api.http`. **Scratch buffers** are plain text files `buffer1.txt` … `buffer5.txt`; after
five, the oldest is reused.

## Scratches and Consoles in the Project view

The bottom of the Project tool window has a **Scratches and Consoles** node with **Scratches**
and **Database Consoles**. A scratch's context menu has **Rename…**, **Delete** and, for SQL
scratches, **Attach Data Source…**.

![Scratches in the Project view](docs/screenshots/scratches-project-view.png)

## Running scratches

Scratches with a runner get a ▶ icon in the gutter; `Ctrl+Shift+F10` runs the current one.
The output appears in the Run tool window.

| Language | Runs with |
| --- | --- |
| PHP | `php.interpreter`, with `-d auto_prepend_file=<project>/vendor/autoload.php` when the open project has an autoloader, so your classes are available |
| JavaScript | `node` |
| TypeScript | `node --experimental-strip-types` (Node 22.6+) |
| Python | `python3` (`python` on Windows) |
| Shell (`.sh`, `.bash`) | `sh` |
| Lua | `lua` |

![PHP scratch run](docs/screenshots/scratches-php-run.png)

Other languages show "Scratches of this language have no runner."

## SQL scratches

A `.sql` scratch can be attached to a data source (**Attach Data Source…**); it then opens as a
query console of that data source with execution, results and transactions. See
[Database tools](docs/guide/user/database.md).

![SQL scratch](docs/screenshots/scratches-sql-console.png)

## HTTP client (`.http` files)

`.http` files hold one or more requests in PHPStorm's HTTP Client format. They work as
scratches (New Scratch File → HTTP Request) and as files in your project. Each request gets a ▶
icon in the gutter; click it and choose **Run** to send the request (`Ctrl+Shift+F10` sends
the request at the caret). The response (status, headers, body) appears
in the Run tool window, followed by the report of its response handler. Project `.http` files
run as an `http-request` run configuration.

The ▶ menu also offers **Debug '…' with Xdebug**: it starts
listening for Xdebug and sends the request with the cookie `XDEBUG_SESSION=FORGE`, so the PHP
application stops at your breakpoints (see
[Debugging](docs/guide/user/debugging.md#debugging-web-pages-and-http-requests)).

![HTTP request](docs/screenshots/scratches-http-request.png)

### Syntax

```http
@host = localhost:8000

### List users
GET http://{{host}}/api/users?page=1
Accept: application/json

###
# @name createUser
POST http://{{host}}/api/users
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer {{token}}
X-Request-Id: {{$uuid}}

{ "name": "Ada", "age": {{$random.integer(18, 99)}} }

> {%
  client.global.set("userId", response.body.id);
  client.test("User was created", function () {
    client.assert(response.status === 201, "Expected 201 but got " + response.status);
  });
%}

### Body from a file
POST http://{{host}}/api/import
Content-Type: application/json

< ./import.json

### Long query strings can continue on indented lines
GET https://{{host}}/search
    ?q=forge
    &limit=10
```

- `###` separates requests; text after it names the request. `# @name x` also names one.
- A request is a request line `METHOD URL [HTTP/version]` (the method defaults to `GET`;
  `http://` is added when the URL has no scheme), optional indented `?`/`&` lines continuing the
  query string, headers, a blank line and the body.
- `@name = value` defines a file variable; `{{name}}` uses it in the URL, headers and body.
  Variables may refer to other variables. Unknown variables are left as they are.
- **Body files**: a body line `< ./file.json` inserts the file as it is, `<@ ./file.json` also
  substitutes variables in it. Paths are relative to the `.http` file.
- Comments start with `#` or `//`.

![Body from a file](docs/screenshots/editor-polish-http-body-file.png)

### Dynamic variables

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `{{$uuid}}`, `{{$random.uuid}}` | a random UUID |
| `{{$timestamp}}` | Unix time in seconds |
| `{{$isoTimestamp}}` | the current time in ISO 8601 |
| `{{$randomInt}}` | a random integer 0–1000 |
| `{{$random.integer(from, to)}}` | a random integer in the range |

### Environments

Put environment files in the project root, as in PHPStorm:

```json
// http-client.env.json (commit it)
{
  "dev":  { "host": "localhost:8000" },
  "prod": { "host": "shop.example.com" }
}
```

```json
// http-client.private.env.json (keep it out of Git)
{
  "dev": { "token": "s3cret" }
}
```

Every `.http` editor has a toolbar with an **environment selector** listing the environments of
these files. The choice is stored per project in `httpClient.environment` (Settings | Tools |
**HTTP Client**): empty means `dev`, else the first environment; `$none` runs without an
environment. Private values win over public ones.

![Environment selector](docs/screenshots/editor-polish-http-environments.png)

Variable precedence, lowest first: environment < `client.global` (set by handlers) < in-file
`@name = value`.

### Response handlers

A handler after a request, inline `> {% … %}` or in a file `> ./handler.js`, runs when the
response arrives. Forge implements a safe subset of PHPStorm's HTTP Client API without a
JavaScript engine:

- `client.global.set(name, value)`, `get`, `clear`, `clearAll`, `isEmpty` — globals live for
  the IDE session and can be used as `{{name}}` in later requests;
- `client.test(name, function () { … })`, `client.assert(condition, message?)`,
  `client.log(…)`;
- `response.status`, `response.body` (parsed JSON, else text) with `.a.b`, `["a"]`, `[0]`,
  `response.headers.valueOf(name)` / `valuesOf(name)`, `response.contentType.mimeType` /
  `charset`;
- `JSON.stringify` / `JSON.parse`, string and array helpers (`length`, `includes`,
  `startsWith`, `endsWith`, `indexOf`, `toLowerCase`, `toUpperCase`, `trim`);
- `var`/`let`/`const`, `if`/`else`, `return`, functions and arrow functions, literals,
  arithmetic, comparisons, `&&`, `||`, `??` and `?:`.

Loops and anything else stop the script with an error that names the unsupported construct.
Test results and log lines are printed after the response.

![Handler report](docs/screenshots/editor-polish-http-handler.png)

> **Note:** response references (`<> file`) are skipped.

### Remote projects

In a [remote project](docs/guide/user/remote-development.md) environment files and `< file` bodies are read on
the host, and requests are sent **from the host**: Forge forwards a local port through the
project's SSH connection (`direct-tcpip`) to the URL's host and port as the remote host sees
them, so `http://localhost:8000` reaches the server running there. The URL's host stays the
`Host` header and the TLS server name; redirects are not followed. The console says
"Sent from user@host through an SSH tunnel".

Settings | Tools | HTTP Client | **Send requests from** (`httpClient.sendFrom`, per project):
**Remote host** (default) or **This machine**.

![HTTP request sent from the remote host](docs/screenshots/remote-finish-http.png)

## OAuth 2.0, cURL, GraphQL, WebSocket and gRPC

The HTTP client also acquires OAuth 2.0 tokens (`{{$auth.token("id")}}` with `Security.Auth`
in the environment file), imports and copies cURL commands, and runs `GRAPHQL`, `WEBSOCKET`
(with a live message log) and `GRPC` requests. See
[Web tooling](docs/guide/user/web-tooling.md#http-client-extras).

Source: docs/guide/user/services.md

# Services

The plugin **Docker and Kubernetes** (`forge.services`) fills the **Services** tool window
(`Alt+8`, macOS `Cmd+8`). It talks to the Docker Engine API directly (Unix socket, Windows
named pipe or TCP with TLS) and to the Kubernetes API with your kubeconfig. The docker CLI is
only used for `docker compose`, image builds and interactive terminals; `kubectl` only for pod
terminals.

![Services](docs/screenshots/services-docker-dashboard.png)

The tree has three roots:

| Root | Children |
| --- | --- |
| **Docker** | Containers, Images, Networks, Volumes |
| **Docker Compose** | compose projects found in the project root and one folder below, with their services and containers |
| **Kubernetes** | contexts → namespaces → Pods, Deployments, Services; the node says where the contexts come from (`~/.kube/config`, or `from host deploy@shop.example.com` in a remote project) |

Spring Boot run configurations add a **Spring Boot** root with their running and not started
applications, see [Spring Boot and Jakarta EE](docs/guide/user/spring.md#run-dashboard).

The status bar shows the Docker connection ("Docker 27.3.1", "Docker: connecting…",
"Docker: not connected"). Forge follows Docker's event stream, so the tree updates by itself,
and retries the connection every 10 seconds.

## Details pane

Selecting a node shows its details on the right, in tabs:

| Tab | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Dashboard | status, image, ports, mounts, networks, environment, labels; tables for compose and Kubernetes objects |
| Log | the log, following new lines; starts with the last `docker.logs.tail` lines (500) |
| Attached Console | output of compose Up/Down, builds and pulls |
| Inspection | the raw JSON (`docker inspect`) |

![Logs](docs/screenshots/services-docker-logs.png)

## Actions

The toolbar and the context menu offer what applies to the selected node:

| Node | Actions |
| --- | --- |
| Docker (not connected) | Connect, Refresh |
| Running container | Stop, Restart, Delete, Show Log, Exec (open a terminal in the container), Pull Image |
| Stopped container | Start, Delete, Show Log, Pull Image |
| Image | Pull, Delete |
| Images group | Pull Image…, Refresh |
| Volume, network | Delete |
| Compose project | Up (Run all services), Stop, Restart, Down (`docker compose down`), Show Log |
| Compose service | Up, Stop, Restart, Down, Show Log, Exec |
| Pod | Delete, Show Log, Exec (`kubectl exec`), Forward Ports… |
| Deployment | Restart Rollout, Show Log (all pods and containers) |

**Exec** opens a terminal tab in the Terminal tool window running `docker exec -it` (or
`kubectl exec -it`) with bash when the container has it, else sh. Containers started with a
TTY also offer an attached console (`docker attach`).

![Exec terminal](docs/screenshots/services-exec-terminal.png)

![Compose](docs/screenshots/services-compose.png)

![Kubernetes pod log](docs/screenshots/services-kubernetes-pod-log.png)

## Kubernetes contexts and namespaces

Above the tree, the **Context** and **Namespace** selectors pick the context to work with:
it becomes the current context in the tree (`current · <server>`), its namespace is loaded
and expanded, and manifests are applied there. The namespace list shows the context's
namespaces once they are listed. Next to the selectors Forge shows where the contexts come
from. The pick lasts for the session; the defaults are the settings below.

![Context selector](docs/screenshots/services-kube-host-contexts.png)

## Applying manifests

A YAML file with Kubernetes objects (`apiVersion` and `kind`, several documents separated by
`---`) gets a ▶ in the gutter on its first object:

| Menu item | Runs |
| --- | --- |
| Apply to '<context>' | `kubectl --context <context> [-n <namespace>] apply -f <file>` |
| Delete from '<context>' | `kubectl --context <context> [-n <namespace>] delete -f <file>` |

`-n` is the selected namespace and is only passed when no object of the file names its own
namespace. The output appears in the **Log** tab of the Kubernetes node. Applying and
deleting manifests runs the project's files against a cluster, so it is refused in Safe Mode
(see [Project trust and Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md)); so are Exec terminals and the Attached
Console of pods. Reading the cluster (the tree, logs, Inspection, port forwards) works in
Safe Mode.

![Apply a manifest](docs/screenshots/services-kube-apply.png)

## Kubernetes pods and deployments

- **Container picker**: a pod with several containers (including init containers) shows a
  container selector on its details. Log, Exec and the Attached Console use the picked container;
  the default is the one named by the `kubectl.kubernetes.io/default-container` annotation, else
  the first container. The Dashboard lists the containers' declared ports.
- **Deployment logs** follow every container of every pod that matches the deployment's
  selector, each line prefixed like `kubectl logs --prefix` (`[pod/<pod>/<container>]`).

![Container picker](docs/screenshots/services-container-picker.png)

![Deployment logs](docs/screenshots/services-deployment-logs.png)

### Port forwarding

**Forward Ports…** on a pod opens a dialog: enter `local:pod` pairs separated by commas, for
example `8080:80, 9000, :5432` (a single port forwards the same port; `:80` picks a free local
port). The pod's declared container ports are offered.

![Forward Ports dialog](docs/screenshots/services-port-forward-dialog.png)

Forge listens on `127.0.0.1:<local>` and opens one connection to the pod per accepted
connection (the Kubernetes port-forward API over WebSocket, no `kubectl` needed). Active
forwards appear in the tree (`⇄ 8080→80`) and on the pod and Kubernetes details, under **Port
Forwarding**, each with **Stop Port Forwarding**.

![Port forwards](docs/screenshots/services-port-forwards.png)

## Compose files and Dockerfiles in the editor

- `compose.yaml` / `docker-compose.yml` get a ▶ in the gutter on `services:` (**Run all
  services**) and on each service (`docker compose up` for that service).
- A `Dockerfile` gets a ▶ on its first `FROM`: **Run on 'Docker'** builds the image and runs a
  container; output appears in Attached Console.

![Compose gutter](docs/screenshots/services-compose-gutter.png)

Compose files support profiles, env files, `${VAR}` interpolation from the project's `.env`
and override files.

## Pulling images and registries

**Pull Image…** (Find Action **Docker.PullImage**, or the Images group) asks for
`repository[:tag]`, e.g. `redis:7-alpine`, and shows the progress.

![Pull image](docs/screenshots/services-pull-image.png)

Private registries: Settings | Build, Execution, Deployment | Docker | **Docker Registry**.
Add the registry (`docker.io`, `ghcr.io`, …), user name and password or access token. The
password goes to the OS keychain (service `forge-containers`); the setting
`docker.registries` only keeps `server<TAB>user`. Without accounts, public images are pulled
anonymously.

## Settings

### Build, Execution, Deployment | Docker

![Docker settings](docs/screenshots/settings-docker.png)

| Option | Setting | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Connect to Docker daemon with (`auto`, `unix`, `pipe`, `tcp`, `ssh`, `context`) | `docker.connection` | `auto` |
| SSH host: `ssh://user@host[:port]` or a `Host` alias of `~/.ssh/config` | `docker.ssh.url` | empty |
| Docker socket on the host (empty: `/var/run/docker.sock`) | `docker.ssh.socketPath` | empty |
| In remote projects, connect to Docker on the remote host | `docker.remoteProjectHost` | on |
| Docker context (`docker context ls`) | `docker.context` | empty |
| Socket path (Unix socket or named pipe; empty: the first existing default) | `docker.socketPath` | empty |
| Engine API URL (TCP) | `docker.tcp.url` | `tcp://localhost:2375` |
| Use TLS (verify the daemon certificate) | `docker.tcp.tls` | off |
| Certificates folder (`ca.pem`, `cert.pem`, `key.pem`) | `docker.tcp.certPath` | empty |
| Docker executable (compose, builds, exec) | `docker.cliPath` | `docker` |
| Show the last log lines | `docker.logs.tail` | 500 |

With `auto`, Forge uses `DOCKER_HOST` when set (also `ssh://` hosts), else the current Docker
context (`DOCKER_CONTEXT` or `currentContext` in `~/.docker/config.json`), else the platform
default socket (`/var/run/docker.sock`, Docker Desktop's `~/.docker/run/docker.sock`, rootless
`$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/docker.sock` or Podman's socket; `\\.\pipe\docker_engine` on Windows).
**Test Connection** checks the settings.

**Docker over SSH** (`ssh`): Forge connects with its own SSH client (keys from ssh-agent and
`~/.ssh`, `~/.ssh/config` aliases) and talks to the remote Docker socket through the SSH
connection; nothing is installed on the host. The host key must already be in `known_hosts`;
unknown keys are refused with their fingerprint. Compose, builds and terminals use the docker
CLI, which reaches `ssh://` hosts itself.

![Docker over SSH](docs/screenshots/settings-docker-ssh.png)

**Docker contexts** (`context`): the page lists the contexts of the Docker CLI
(`~/.docker/contexts`) with **Use**; Forge then connects to that context's endpoint.

![Docker contexts](docs/screenshots/settings-docker-contexts.png)

### Build, Execution, Deployment | Kubernetes

![Kubernetes settings](docs/screenshots/settings-kubernetes.png)

| Option | Setting | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kubeconfig file (empty: `$KUBECONFIG` or `~/.kube/config`) | `kubernetes.kubeconfig` | empty |
| Default context (empty: the kubeconfig's current-context) | `kubernetes.defaultContext` | empty |
| Default namespace (empty: the context's namespace, else `default`) | `kubernetes.defaultNamespace` | empty |
| kubectl executable (this machine: exec terminals, applying manifests) | `kubernetes.kubectlPath` | `kubectl` |
| In remote projects, use Kubernetes of the project host | `kubernetes.remoteProjectHost` | on |
| kubectl from the project host: `user@host` and the kubectl path there | `kubernetes.hostKubectlPaths` | empty (kubectl from the host's `PATH`) |

Kubernetes authentication supports CA certificates, bearer tokens, client certificates, basic
auth and exec credential plugins (as used by EKS, GKE and AKS).

**kubectl from the Project Host** lists a kubectl per remote host, e.g.
`deploy@shop.example.com` → `/usr/local/bin/kubectl` or `k3s kubectl`. The host of the open
remote project is filled in when you add an entry. Hosts without an entry run `kubectl` from
their `PATH`.

![Kubernetes settings with kubectl per host](docs/screenshots/settings-kubernetes-hosts.png)

> **Note:** port forwarding is available for Kubernetes pods, not for Docker containers.

## Remote projects

In a [remote project](docs/guide/user/remote-development.md) the project's compose files (with `.env` and
override files) are read on the host, and the compose ▶ actions and **Run on 'Docker'** of a
Dockerfile run `docker compose` / `docker build` **on the host**; the console starts with
"Running on user@host in /path".

With **In remote projects, connect to Docker on the remote host** (`docker.remoteProjectHost`,
on) the Docker node shows the host's daemon (`ssh://user@host/var/run/docker.sock`), reached
through the project's own SSH connection: no second login and nothing to set up. Exec terminals
and Attached Console then run `docker` on the host. Turn it off to use the connection configured
above; compose still runs on the host then (against the host's own daemon), while exec terminals
run on this machine.

### Kubernetes in remote projects

With **In remote projects, use Kubernetes of the project host**
(`kubernetes.remoteProjectHost`, on) Kubernetes runs where the project is, like PHPStorm's
remote development: clusters next to the host (a k3s on `127.0.0.1:6443`, a private network,
credential plugins installed there) work without copying anything to this machine.

| | In a remote project |
| --- | --- |
| Contexts | from the host's kubeconfig (`$KUBECONFIG` or `~/.kube/config` on the host), read with `kubectl config view`; the Kubernetes node says `from host deploy@shop.example.com` |
| Namespaces, pods, deployments, services, Inspection | `kubectl get … -o json` on the host |
| Logs | `kubectl logs -f` on the host |
| Exec, Attached Console | a terminal on the host running its kubectl |
| Delete pod, Restart Rollout | `kubectl delete pod`, `kubectl rollout restart` on the host |
| Forward Ports | `kubectl port-forward` on the host (on its `127.0.0.1`); every connection to `127.0.0.1:<local port>` here is tunnelled to it through the project's SSH connection. The forward shows "Forwarding via deploy@shop.example.com". |
| Apply / Delete manifests | `kubectl apply -f` / `delete -f` on the host, in the project folder |

kubectl must be installed on the host; its path is set per host under **kubectl from the
Project Host**. Turn the option off to use this machine's kubeconfig and API access in remote
projects too. Local projects always use this machine's kubeconfig.

![Kubernetes contexts from the project host](docs/screenshots/services-kube-host-contexts.png)

![Compose on the remote host](docs/screenshots/remote-finish-compose.png)

# Remote development

Forge can open a project that lives on another machine, like JetBrains Gateway. It connects over
SSH, installs a small headless **Forge agent** on the host and runs indexing, the PHP language
server, Git, terminals and run configurations **next to the files**. Only the UI runs on your
machine.

## Requirements

| Side | Needs |
| --- | --- |
| Remote host | **Linux** on x86_64 or aarch64, an SSH server, a POSIX shell, write access to `~/.cache`. PHP, Git, language servers etc. installed on the host as you would need them locally (PHP's php-lsp is built into the agent). |
| Forge | a build that bundles the agents (`pnpm release`), or agent binaries in `FORGE_REMOTE_AGENT_DIR` / an `agents/` folder next to the `forge` binary. See [Release builds](docs/guide/developer/release-builds.md). |

Nothing needs to be installed on the host in advance: Forge uploads the agent itself.

The same agent also runs **in a dev container** (over `docker exec`) and **in a WSL
distribution** (over `wsl.exe`); see [Dev Containers and WSL](docs/guide/user/dev-containers-and-wsl.md). The
Welcome screen's Remote Development section has a page for each: **SSH**, **Dev Containers** and
**WSL**. Its **Code With Me** page joins a [Code With Me](docs/guide/user/code-with-me.md#joining-a-session) session.

## Connecting

Welcome screen → **Remote Development** → **New Connection** (or **New SSH Connection…** in
Find Action).

![Remote Development on the Welcome screen](docs/screenshots/remote-welcome.png)

**Step 1 – Connect to SSH**

![New SSH Connection](docs/screenshots/remote-ssh-dialog.png)

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| SSH configuration | a saved configuration, a host from `~/.ssh/config` (with `Include`s), or **New connection** |
| Host, Port, Username | |
| Authentication type | **Password**, **Key pair (OpenSSH or PuTTY)** with an optional passphrase, or **OpenSSH config and authentication agent** (ssh-agent plus the `IdentityFile`s of `~/.ssh/config`) |
| Save password / passphrase | stored in the OS keychain (service `forge-ssh`), never in a file |

**Test Connection** shows the host's system and the latency. **Check Connection and Continue**
moves to step 2.

**Step 2 – Choose Project**: browse the host's folders (home, parent, show hidden files) and
double-click the project folder, or type its path, then **Open Project**.

![Choose the project folder](docs/screenshots/remote-folder-chooser.png)

![Project step](docs/screenshots/remote-project-step.png)

### Jump hosts and proxy commands

Hosts from `~/.ssh/config` keep their `ProxyJump` and `ProxyCommand`:

- **ProxyJump**: Forge connects through each hop in turn, tunnelling the next connection
  through the previous one; every hop's host key is checked like the target's.
- **ProxyCommand**: Forge runs the command (with `%h`, `%p`, `%r` and `%n` expanded) and speaks
  SSH over its input and output.

```text
Host shop
    HostName 10.0.0.12
    User deploy
    ProxyJump bastion.example.com
```

### Host keys

Host keys are checked against `~/.ssh/known_hosts`. An **Unknown Host** shows the key type and
fingerprint ("Are you sure you want to continue connecting?"); **Accept New Key** adds it to
`known_hosts`. A **changed** key is reported prominently ("Host Key Has Changed") and must be
confirmed explicitly before the stored key is replaced.

![Fingerprint](docs/screenshots/remote-fingerprint.png)

## The Forge agent

After connecting, Forge probes the host with one shell command (OS, architecture, home folder,
installed agent), uploads the matching agent to `~/.cache/forge-agent/<version>/` when it is
missing or differs (checked by SHA-256), and starts it in a login shell. The agent then serves
the project over the SSH channel.

Set `FORGE_AGENT_LOG=debug` in the host's environment for verbose agent logs (stderr).

## Working in a remote project

![Remote project](docs/screenshots/remote-workbench.png)

The project's root is shown as `user@host:/path`. Recent Projects keeps remote projects with an
**SSH** badge (**Container** and **WSL** for [dev container and WSL projects](docs/guide/user/dev-containers-and-wsl.md));
clicking one reconnects.

A remote project you have not trusted yet opens in Safe Mode and Forge asks "Trust and Open
Project?" right after connecting; trust is kept per host, user, port and folder, see
[Project trust and Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md#remote-projects).

![Recent remote projects](docs/screenshots/remote-open-recent.png)

| Works on the host | |
| --- | --- |
| Project view, editing, saving, file operations, file watching | yes |
| Go to File, Search Everywhere | yes |
| Git (status, commit, diff, blame, branches, log) | yes; output is parsed locally |
| Find in Files | yes, searched on the host |
| Scopes (Find in Files, Find Usages, Structural Search), the Scopes page's file tree | yes, evaluated and listed on the host |
| Structural Search and Replace | yes: the files are parsed on the host; Replace All writes through the agent |
| Analyze Stack Trace | yes: files are looked up on the host; PHP servers' path mappings and Compose bind mounts are read from the host |
| PHP index, Structure, Generate, php-lsp | yes; the agent's built-in php-lsp indexes the remote files itself |
| Catalog language servers (TypeScript, YAML, Python, …) | yes: scan, detection and the servers run on the host |
| Installing language servers (Settings) | yes: the agent downloads Node.js and the npm servers into Forge's directory on the host, with progress here |
| Laravel, Symfony and Doctrine analysis | yes, in the agent; artisan and `bin/console` run on the host |
| WebForge: npm tool window, React / Vue / Angular navigation and gutter icons | yes: `package.json` files, scripts, package managers and components are read in the agent; scripts run on the host |
| LuaForge index | yes, all Lua files are read on the host in one batch |
| StyLua (Reformat Code) | yes, StyLua runs on the host |
| Code hosts (GitLab, Forgejo, GitHub) | yes: the repository is detected with git on the host; API calls go from your machine with your tokens |
| HTTP client (`.http` files) | environment and body files are read on the host; requests are sent **from the host** through an SSH tunnel, so `localhost` URLs reach its services (Settings \| Tools \| HTTP Client \| **Send requests from**) |
| Services: compose files and Dockerfile ▶ | compose files are read on the host and `docker compose` / `docker build` run there; by default Docker of the host is used through the project's SSH connection |
| Services: Kubernetes | contexts come from the host's kubeconfig and `kubectl` runs on the host (tree, logs, exec, apply/delete manifests); port forwards are tunnelled back through the SSH connection, see [Services](docs/guide/user/services.md#kubernetes-in-remote-projects) |
| Browser Companion | files the browser reports (host paths, container paths like `/app/src/…`) open in the remote project |
| Project settings (`.forge/settings.toml`) and other `.forge/` files | yes, read and written on the host |
| Terminal | yes, a shell on the host |
| Run/Debug configurations (run) | yes, processes run on the host |
| Database tools | project data sources connect through an SSH tunnel, see [Database](docs/guide/user/database.md#remote-projects) |
| Xdebug | through a reverse SSH tunnel, see [Xdebug](docs/guide/user/debugging.md#remote-projects) |
| AI Chat (Claude Code, Gemini CLI) | the CLI runs on the host |

![Remote terminal](docs/screenshots/remote-terminal.png)

Every feature works in remote projects. Things that are about your machine stay local on
purpose: code host API calls (your tokens), the keychain and,
when you choose it, HTTP requests ("Send requests from: This machine") and Docker or Kubernetes
of this machine (see [Services](docs/guide/user/services.md#remote-projects)).

![Kubernetes contexts from the project host](docs/screenshots/services-kube-host-contexts.png)

![npm tool window of a remote project](docs/screenshots/remote-finish-npm.png)

![Compose on the remote host](docs/screenshots/remote-finish-compose.png)

![HTTP request sent from the remote host](docs/screenshots/remote-finish-http.png)

![Language server installed on the host](docs/screenshots/remote-finish-langserver.png)

## Connection status and reconnects

The status bar shows the host and latency (pinged every 5 seconds). Click it for the
connection popup.

![Status popup](docs/screenshots/remote-status-popup.png)

When the connection drops, Forge reconnects automatically with a backoff from 1 to 30 seconds
and re-attaches the project ("Reconnecting…", with the next attempt). Host key and
authentication errors stop the retries. **Reconnect to Remote Host** (Find Action) retries now.

![Reconnecting](docs/screenshots/remote-reconnecting.png)

## Saved configurations

Settings | Tools | **SSH Configurations** lists, adds, edits and removes saved configurations.
They are stored in `ssh.toml` in Forge's config folder; secrets stay in the keychain. **Parse
config file `~/.ssh/config`** (on by default) resolves `Host` aliases, jump hosts and proxy
commands from your OpenSSH config. The same configurations connect SFTP deployment servers and
SSH terminal sessions, see [Remote Host and SSH sessions](docs/guide/user/remote-host-and-ssh.md).

![SSH Configurations](docs/screenshots/remote-ssh-settings.png)

## Troubleshooting

See [Troubleshooting: remote agent upload](docs/guide/troubleshooting.md#remote-agent-upload).

# Code With Me

Code With Me lets you invite guests into the project that is open in your Forge. Everyone edits
the same files at the same time and sees the others' carets and selections. Guests use Forge
itself. Connections go straight from guest to host; no account and no Forge service is needed
(see [relay and NAT traversal](docs/guide/user/code-with-me-relay.md) for networks where that does not work).

## Hosting a session

1. Click the Code With Me icon in the toolbar (or **Tools | Code With Me | Start Session…**).
2. Pick what guests may do:

   | Level | Guests can |
   | --- | --- |
   | **Read-only** (default) | view files |
   | **Edit files** | edit files, but not use the terminal or run code |
   | **Full access** | edit files, use the terminal and run code on your machine |
   | **Custom…** | what you choose per area (see below) |

3. **Start Session** starts listening and copies the invitation link to the clipboard. Send the
   link to your guest. **Copy Session Link** in the popup copies it again.
4. **End Session** ends the session for everybody and the link stops working.

Nothing listens on your machine before you start a session.

### Custom permissions

**Custom…** opens the **Custom Permissions** dialog with one value per area:

| Area | Values |
| --- | --- |
| Files | Read-only · Edit |
| Terminal | No access · Read-only · Full access |
| Run | No access · Read-only (see output) · Full access (start, stop, rerun) |
| Version control | Read-only (status, diff, blame, log) · Full access (commit, push, checkout, …) |

Files that control what runs on your machine (run configurations, `composer.json`,
`package.json`, `Makefile`, …) can only be changed by guests with Files **Edit** and Run
**Full access**. The list is a setting, see [Files guests never see](#files-guests-never-see).

![Custom Permissions dialog](docs/screenshots/code-with-me-custom-permissions.png)

## During a session

The popup lists the participants with their permission and offers:

- **Copy Session Link** copies the invitation link again.
- **Regenerate Link** creates a new link and copies it. The old link stops working at once;
  guests who are already in the session stay.
- **Permissions ▸** changes the permission of the whole session: guests who join later get it,
  and every guest in the session gets it at once.
- **Make Everyone Follow You** asks every guest to follow you (see [Following](#following-participants)).
- **End Session** ends the session for everybody.

The **⋮** button next to a participant (or a right click on the participant) opens the
participant's menu:

- **Follow** / **Stop Following** and **Jump To** (see [Following](#following-participants)).
- **Permissions ▸** (host) changes only this guest's permission (Read-only, Edit files, Full access or
  Custom…).
- **Remove Guest** (host) disconnects the guest at once. The guest is told that the host removed them.
  Removing does not ban: with the same link the guest can ask to join again, so use
  **Regenerate Link** if they should not.

A new permission counts from the guest's next request. When files become read-only for a
guest, their open editors turn read-only and they are told so; changes they send afterwards are
refused by your Forge.

![A guest's menu in the session popup](docs/screenshots/code-with-me-guest-menu.png)

The popup works with the keyboard: **Up** and **Down** move between its entries (**Home** and
**End** jump to the first and last), **Enter** or **Space** chooses one, **Escape** closes the
popup. The same keys move through the participants in the Code With Me tool window.

![The session popup driven by the keyboard](docs/screenshots/code-with-me-popup-keyboard.png)

### Saving and changes on disk

A shared file is saved for everybody: **Save** (Ctrl+S) by the host or by a guest who may edit
files writes it on the host's disk, and every participant's tab shows the same unsaved marker.

On the host, the lines guests changed have a marker in the guest's color in the gutter, next to
the line numbers, until the file is saved; hover it to see who changed the line.

When a shared file changes on the host's disk (a `git checkout`, a formatter, an AI agent) and
it has no unsaved changes, everybody's editor takes the new text, and carets stay where they
were. If it has unsaved changes, the host gets PHPStorm's **File Cache Conflict** dialog:
"Changes have been made to … in memory and on disk."

- **Load File System Changes** replaces the shared text with the file on disk, for everybody.
- **Keep Memory Changes** keeps the shared text; it stays unsaved, and saving it overwrites the
  file on disk.
- **Show Difference** shows the file on disk next to the shared text. The choice then waits in
  a balloon, as it does when you close the dialog.

Guests see a balloon that the host is choosing which version to keep; they cannot save the file
until then. Saving it yourself as the host also keeps the memory changes, and the conflict ends
by itself when the file on disk changes back.

![The host's File Cache Conflict dialog](docs/screenshots/code-with-me-file-cache-conflict.png)

![Lines changed by Alex, marked in the host's gutter](docs/screenshots/code-with-me-guest-lines.png)

## Following participants

Every participant sees where the others are: the participant list shows the file and line each
one is in (`OrderController.php:27`) and whom they follow ("following you"), and the others'
avatars appear next to the Code With Me icon in the toolbar.

- **Follow**: click a participant in the list or their avatar in the toolbar. Forge opens their
  file and keeps their part of the file in view as they move and switch files. A banner above
  the editor says **Following Alex** in their color. Typing, clicking into the editor or opening
  another file stops following, as does **Stop** in the banner (or **Stop Following**).
- **Jump To**: in the participant's menu, opens their file at their caret once, without
  following.
- **Make Everyone Follow You** (host): every guest follows you, including guests who join later.
  The guests' banner says **Robert asked everyone to follow**; they can still press **Stop**.
  The popup shows how many guests follow you. Choose it again to stop asking.
- Guests follow the host when they join (Settings | Tools | Code With Me | **Follow the host
  when joining**).

A guest is never told the name of a file it may not see: while the host is in `.env` or another
hidden file, guests see the host without a location and following guests stay where they are.

The **Code With Me** tool window (right, while a session runs) lists the participants with the
same actions, **Stop Following** and, for the host, **Make Everyone Follow You** and the
**Session Log** tab.

All of these are also in Find Action and Settings | Keymap under Plugins | Code With Me:
**Follow Participant…** and **Jump To Participant…** (a chooser of the participants), **Stop
Following**, **Make Everyone Follow You** and **Code With Me** (the tool window). PHPStorm binds
no shortcuts to them; you can add your own.

![Following Alex](docs/screenshots/code-with-me-following.png)

![A guest follows the host after Make Everyone Follow You](docs/screenshots/cwm-guest-follow.png)

### Carets of the others

Every participant's caret and selection show in their color. The name label above a caret shows
while that participant moves or types and fades out two seconds after they stopped; hover the
caret to see the name again. The right edge of the editor (over the scrollbar) has a mark in the
participant's color where each of the others is in the file; click it to move your caret there.

![Alex's caret, name label and the mark on the right edge](docs/screenshots/code-with-me-carets.png)

## Terminal and Run

What guests see of your terminals and runs depends on their **Terminal** and **Run** permission:

| Permission | Terminal | Run |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No access | no Terminal tool window | no Run tool window |
| Read-only | watch the terminals you share | watch your runs (console and test results) |
| Full access | type in the terminals you share, open their own terminals on your machine | run, rerun and stop your run configurations, type into the console |

**Sharing a terminal (host).** Right-click a terminal tab and choose **Share with Guests** (also
**Share Terminal with Guests** in Find Action, for the active tab). Shared tabs show the
participants icon; choose it again to stop sharing. Guests see the tab with what it showed so
far (the last 2000 lines) and follow it live, at your terminal's size. When you stop sharing a
terminal, the guest's tab stays with what it showed and the line **[The host stopped sharing
this terminal]**, like a terminal whose shell ended; the guest closes it. Shared again, it
opens fresh. A shell that ends on your machine shows **[Process completed]** in the guest's
tab. To share every terminal
tab you open during a session, turn on **Settings | Tools | Code With Me | Share new terminal
tabs**.

**Guests' terminals.** A guest with Full terminal access opens new terminal tabs on your
machine: the shell is yours (your shell and settings) and starts in the project folder. The tab
shows up in your Terminal tool window as **Alex: Local**, so you always see what runs on your
machine. A guest's terminals close when the guest leaves, is removed, or loses Full terminal
access.

**Runs.** Every run of your Run tool window is shown to guests with Run access, with its console
and test tree; guests who join later see it from the start. A guest with Full run access uses the
Run widget and the Run tool window as usual: Run, Rerun and Stop act on your machine, and Forge
starts your run configuration by its name as if you clicked Run. Guests never send command
lines, and they cannot change run configurations unless they have Full access (the files that
configure what runs are protected). Debugging and Run with Coverage are not available to guests.

The session log records shared and unshared terminals, the terminals guests open and close, that
a guest typed in a terminal or a console (never the keys), and the runs guests start and stop.
Input from a guest without Full access is refused by your Forge.

![The host shares a terminal tab](docs/screenshots/code-with-me-share-terminal.png)

![A guest watches the host's shared terminal](docs/screenshots/cwm-guest-terminal.png)

![The host's test run in a guest's Run tool window](docs/screenshots/cwm-guest-run.png)

![A terminal the host stopped sharing, in the guest's window](docs/screenshots/cwm-guest-terminal-unshared.png)

![A terminal a guest opened on the host](docs/screenshots/code-with-me-guest-terminal.png)

## Session log

**Session Log…** in the popup (also in Find Action and the **Session Log** tab of the Code With
Me tool window) shows what happened in the session you
host, with the time: who joined, declined and unanswered requests, connections without a
valid link, permission changes, Regenerate Link, removed and leaving guests, files guests
saved, created, renamed or deleted, their git actions, and every request your Forge refused
(shown as warnings). Terminal keystrokes and file contents are never logged.

With **Keep a session log** on (the default, Settings | Tools | Code With Me), each session is
also written to a file in Forge's data directory, never into the project:

| OS | Folder |
| --- | --- |
| Linux | `~/.local/share/forge/code-with-me/` |
| macOS | `~/Library/Application Support/forge/code-with-me/` |
| Windows | `%APPDATA%\forge\code-with-me\` |

The file is `<date>-<session>.jsonl`, one JSON object per line. Logs older than 30 days are
deleted when you start a session.

![Session Log](docs/screenshots/code-with-me-session-log.png)

## Accepting guests

Having the link is not enough. When a guest opens it, a balloon appears and stays until you
answer:

> **Alex wants to join the session**
> Make sure the code is 482 913. With Read-only permission Alex can view files.
> **Accept** · **Decline**

The guest sees the same **verification code** while waiting. Compare the two over a call or
chat before you accept: the code is derived from both sides' keys, so somebody who got hold of
the link shows a different code than the person you invited. If the codes differ, decline.

- A guest that is declined is told so. A request that is not answered within two minutes is
  dropped and the guest is told that the host did not answer.
- A guest can have one open request at a time, and at most five requests wait at once. Further
  ones are refused without a prompt.
- Ending the session refuses everyone who is still waiting.

If you close the balloon without answering, the request stays open until it times out.

## Joining a session

1. Click the link (`forge://cwm/join?…`), or choose **Tools | Code With Me | Join Session…**
   and paste it into **Session link**. Without a project open, the Welcome screen has the same
   action under **Remote Development | Code With Me | Join Session…**. A clicked link opens
   Forge (or brings it to the front) with the dialog filled in; if that window is already in a
   session, a new window opens for it. Nothing connects before you click **Join**.
2. The dialog shows where the link leads before anything connects: the **Host** and its
   **Machine** as the link names them, the **Connection** (direct, or through the host's relay
   server) and the name you **Join as** (**Change…** opens Settings | Tools | Code With Me). If a
   project is open, it says that it is closed while you are a guest. Click **Join**. If that
   project has unsaved changes, the dialog first lists the files and asks: **Save** them,
   **Don't Save** (they stay unsaved, and are dropped only when the host's project takes the
   window), or **Cancel** to go back to the link. In Safe Mode, Save only writes the files;
   Actions on Save that run tools do not run.
3. The dialog shows **Waiting for <host> to accept…** with the **verification code** and
   **Cancel**. Tell the host the code; the host sees the same one. If the host declines or does
   not answer, the dialog says so and offers **Try Again**.
4. When the host accepts, the host's project opens in your window and you follow the host. The
   title shows `<project> — <host> (Code With Me)`. **Leave Session** in the popup or the status item
   ends it for you, and the window returns to the Welcome screen.

![Joining from the Welcome screen](docs/screenshots/code-with-me-welcome.png)

The host's project replaces the project the window had open. Everything the window showed of
that project goes with it: the Project tree shows the host's files right away, and the
problems, Find and Inspection Results tabs and the Safe Mode banner of your own project are
gone. To keep your project open, join from another window: **File | New Window** opens one on
the Welcome screen.

![The host's project after joining](docs/screenshots/code-with-me-join-joined.png)

A guest's window is always in Safe Mode, without the banner and without **Trust Project…**:
nothing of the host's project runs on your machine. Terminals and runs the host shares run on
the host (see [Terminal and Run](#terminal-and-run)).

![Join Session dialog](docs/screenshots/code-with-me-join-dialog.png)

![Unsaved changes in your own project before it closes](docs/screenshots/code-with-me-join-unsaved.png)

![Forge opened by a clicked session link](docs/screenshots/code-with-me-join-link.png)

The installers register Forge for `forge://` links (the `x-scheme-handler/forge` MIME type on
Linux, the URL protocol on Windows, the URL type on macOS). AppImages and development builds
register it when they start.

![Waiting for the host with the verification code](docs/screenshots/code-with-me-join-waiting.png)

### When the connection drops

If the connection to the host drops (Wi-Fi gone, laptop asleep, VPN reconnecting), the session
is not over:

- Your window keeps the host's project and your open files. The status bar says **Code With Me:
  Reconnecting…**, and a balloon **Connection to <host> lost** stays until the connection is
  back, with **Leave Session**. Forge tries again after 1, 2, 4 and 8 seconds and then every 15
  seconds.
- Keep typing: your edits stay in the editor and are sent when the connection is back; edits
  the others made meanwhile arrive then too, and everything merges. Saving, opening files,
  search and other requests to the host fail while the connection is down. Keys typed into a
  shared terminal or a run's console meanwhile are lost.
- Back again, you see **Reconnected to <host>.** Shared terminals and runs show what you
  missed, and the others see you where you were. The host sends the file changes you missed;
  the Project tree reads its open folders again (expansion and selection stay), and Git status,
  Find and the other views that follow file changes refresh.
- The host keeps your place (your color, permissions, terminals) for two minutes and shows you
  as **Reconnecting…** in the participant list meanwhile. After about 105 seconds without a
  connection your Forge gives up: the session ends with **The connection to the host was lost and
  could not be restored. Join again with the session link.** Edits that did not reach the host
  are lost then. If the host removed you meanwhile, you are told so.

![A guest's window while the connection is restored](docs/screenshots/cwm-guest-reconnecting.png)

![The host sees a guest reconnecting](docs/screenshots/code-with-me-guest-reconnecting.png)

Guests see the Project tree, Structure, Find, Problems, Terminal and Run (with Terminal or Run access, see [Terminal and Run](#terminal-and-run)) and Git (read-only unless the host gave
Full access). AI Chat, Database, Services, Debug and the code host tool windows are not
available in a guest's window, because they would use the host's accounts and secrets.

## Files guests never see

Secret files are invisible to guests whatever their level, in the tree, in search, in Git and
in analysis results: `.env` and `.env.*` (but not `.env.example`), private keys, certificates
and the like. The list is **Settings | Tools | Code With Me | Files guests never see**. Files larger than
**Larger files open read-only (KB)** open read-only.

Files that configure what runs on the host can be changed only by guests with Full access to
Run (with Edit files they open read-only): **Settings | Tools | Code With Me | Files only Full
access may change**. By default these are run configurations (`.forge/runConfigurations*.toml`),
`.forge/settings.toml`, `.vscode/`, `.idea/`, `.husky/`, `composer.json`, `package.json`,
`Makefile`, `artisan` and `bin/console`. The patterns work like the excluded files (`!pattern`
removes a file from the list); changes apply to sessions you start afterwards.

## Settings

Settings | Tools | Code With Me: your name in sessions, the default permission level,
whether ending a session asks for confirmation, whether guests follow the host when joining, whether new terminal tabs are shared,
whether a session log is kept, the files guests never see, the files only Full access may change
and the connection settings of the
[relay page](docs/guide/user/code-with-me-relay.md).

# Code With Me: relay and NAT traversal

Code With Me connects the guest straight to the host. Nothing is contacted besides the host's
addresses from the session link, and Forge runs no service of its own: there is no lobby, no
account and no Forge relay. When guest and host cannot reach each other (different networks,
NAT, firewalls) there are four ways out, from least to most effort:

| Situation | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| Same network or VPN | Nothing. Direct connections work, and **Discover hosts on the local network** finds the host even when its address changed. |
| Host has a public address or a port forward | Set **Port** (Settings \| Tools \| Code With Me) to a fixed UDP port and forward it on the router. |
| Both sides are behind NATs | Set up a **Relay server** (below). Forge first connects through it and then tries to open a direct path (hole punching). |
| Locked-down networks (UDP blocked, corporate firewall) | Join over a VPN such as WireGuard or Tailscale, or tunnel the UDP port (see [SSH tunnel and VPN](#ssh-tunnel-and-vpn)). |

## How a connection is made

Forge uses [iroh](https://www.iroh.computer): QUIC over UDP with TLS 1.3, where every endpoint is
identified by a public key.

1. The host starts a session. It opens a UDP socket and, if a relay server is set, connects to
   it. The **session link** contains the host's key, its addresses and, as `r=`, the relay's URL.
2. The guest dials the host's addresses **and** the relay at the same time. Direct addresses win
   when they work (LAN, port forward, VPN).
3. Otherwise the first packets travel through the relay. Both ends use that channel to exchange
   their public addresses and punch holes through their NATs (hole punching). When it works, the
   connection moves to the direct path by itself, without interruption. About nine out of ten
   connections end up direct. When it does not (symmetric NATs, UDP filters), the connection
   stays on the relay.
4. The relay only forwards packets that are **end-to-end encrypted** between guest and host. It
   sees who connects (IP addresses and the session's temporary endpoint keys) and how much data
   flows, never file contents, keystrokes or the join secret.

A new key pair is generated for every session, so links and relay logs cannot be correlated
between sessions.

## Settings

Settings \| Tools \| Code With Me.

| Setting | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Port** | UDP port for direct connections. 0 picks a free port; set a fixed one for a port forward. |
| **Listen on address** | Bind to one interface only: a VPN address, or `127.0.0.1` for tunnels. |
| **Discover hosts on the local network** | Find the host on the same network with mDNS. Nothing leaves the local network. On by default. |
| **Relay server** | URL of your own `iroh-relay`, e.g. `https://relay.example.com`. **Empty (the default): direct connections only, Forge contacts no server.** |
| **Use the public relay servers of n0** | Opt-in, off by default. n0 (number 0 computer) operates the free public iroh relays. They are rate-limited and run by a third party; they only see encrypted traffic. Ignored when a relay server is set. |
| **Relay token** (Set Token…) | The shared token of a relay that uses access control. Stored in the system keychain, never in settings files or links. |
| **Test Connection** | Connects to the relay as typed in the page and reports whether it works or why not (wrong token, certificate, unreachable). |

Notes:

- A relay URL needs `https://` (or `http://` for a relay inside a trusted network or tunnel).
  Without a scheme Forge assumes `https://`. User names, passwords and tokens do not belong
  into the URL: they would end up in session links. Use **Set Token…**.
- **The guest uses the relay of the link**, not their own setting. Guests only need their own
  settings when the relay requires a token: enter it under **Set Token…** with the same relay
  URL as in the link. A token is only ever sent to the relay it was set for.
- Guests that the link cannot reach directly and that cannot reach the relay get the error
  *The host did not answer*. Open **Test Connection** and the host's connection status first.
- Hosts that use the public relays put one of n0's relay URLs into the link. Guests then
  contact that relay because the link says so, even though they did not opt in themselves.
  Only share such links with people you would let reach that service.

## Seeing how you are connected

- **Status bar**: *Code With Me: Direct · 12 ms* or *Code With Me: Relay (relay.example.com)* for
  guests; hosts see *2 guests, direct* or *2 guests, 1 via relay*. The tooltip lists every
  participant. A warning icon appears when the relay is set but not connected.
- **Code With Me popup** (toolbar): every participant with a **Direct** or **Relay (host)**
  badge and the round-trip time, plus the state of the relay server.

A relayed connection is normal and fully encrypted, only slower (typically 20 to 100 ms more).
The badge changes to **Direct** as soon as hole punching succeeds.

![Participants with connection paths](docs/screenshots/cwm-connection-paths.png)

![Relay server settings](docs/screenshots/cwm-relay-settings.png)

## Running your own relay

A relay is the open-source `iroh-relay` server. It is a single binary, runs on any small VPS
(1 vCPU, 512 MB are plenty for a team) and needs a DNS name pointing at the machine.

Open ports:

| Port | Protocol | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 443 | TCP | HTTPS and the relay connection (WebSocket) |
| 80 | TCP | ACME HTTP challenge (Let's Encrypt) and a captive-portal probe |
| 7842 | UDP | QUIC address discovery (helps hole punching; optional) |

### With Docker Compose

`Dockerfile`:

```dockerfile
FROM rust:1-bookworm AS build
RUN cargo install iroh-relay --version "~1.3" --features server --locked --root /out

FROM debian:bookworm-slim
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ca-certificates \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
COPY --from=build /out/bin/iroh-relay /usr/local/bin/iroh-relay
ENTRYPOINT ["iroh-relay", "--config-path", "/etc/iroh-relay/relay.toml"]
```

`relay.toml`: HTTPS with an automatic Let's Encrypt certificate and a shared token:

```toml
http_bind_addr = "[::]:80"
enable_quic_addr_discovery = true

[tls]
https_bind_addr = "[::]:443"
cert_mode = "LetsEncrypt"
hostname = "relay.example.com"
contact = "admin@example.com"
cert_dir = "/var/lib/iroh-relay"

# Only clients with this token may use the relay. Several tokens are allowed.
# IROH_RELAY_ACCESS_TOKEN overrides this list with a single token.
access.shared_token = ["change-me-to-a-long-random-string"]
```

`compose.yaml`:

```yaml
services:
  relay:
    build: .
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "80:80/tcp"
      - "443:443/tcp"
      - "7842:7842/udp"
    volumes:
      - ./relay.toml:/etc/iroh-relay/relay.toml:ro
      - relay-data:/var/lib/iroh-relay
volumes:
  relay-data:
```

Generate the token with `openssl rand -base64 32 | tr -d '/+='` and start the relay with
`docker compose up -d`. Then, on every machine that uses it:

1. Settings \| Tools \| Code With Me \| **Relay server**: `https://relay.example.com`.
2. **Set Token…**: the token from `relay.toml`.
3. **Test Connection** should say *Connected to relay.example.com*.

Without Docker, install the binary with `cargo install iroh-relay --features server` and run
`iroh-relay --config-path relay.toml` from a systemd unit. For a quick test on your own
network, `iroh-relay --dev` serves plain HTTP on port 3340: use `http://<address>:3340` as the
relay server.

Other access modes in `relay.toml` (`access = "everyone"` is the default): an allow list of
endpoint keys or an HTTP callback. Keys are generated per session, so a shared token is the
practical choice for Code With Me. Rate limits can be set in a `[limits]` section; see the
[iroh-relay documentation](https://docs.rs/iroh-relay).

### Behind a reverse proxy

`iroh-relay` can run with `http_bind_addr` only (no `[tls]` section) behind a proxy that
terminates TLS, as long as the proxy forwards WebSocket upgrades. Leave out
`enable_quic_addr_discovery` then; hole punching still works, a bit less often.

## SSH tunnel and VPN

Code With Me is UDP. A plain `ssh -L` or `ssh -R` forwards TCP only, so it does not work on its
own, and tools that push UDP through a TCP stream (such as `socat`) lose the packet boundaries
QUIC needs. Two recipes work on locked-down networks.

**VPN (recommended).** Put host and guests into one WireGuard or Tailscale network. Start the
session after the VPN is up: the session link then contains the host's VPN address and the
guest connects directly. Set **Listen on address** to the VPN address if the session must not
be reachable from other interfaces. No relay is needed.

**SSH tunnel device.** OpenSSH can carry IP traffic, including UDP, over its own tunnel
(`ssh -w`). It needs root on both machines and `PermitTunnel yes` in the host's `sshd_config`:

```sh
# Guest (as root): open the tunnel to the host and give the tunnel an address.
ssh -f -N -w 0:0 root@host.example.com
ip addr add 10.99.0.2/30 dev tun0 && ip link set tun0 up

# Host (as root): the same tunnel device appears on the host.
ip addr add 10.99.0.1/30 dev tun0 && ip link set tun0 up
```

Then the host starts the session (**Listen on address** empty or `10.99.0.1`). Because the
tunnel is up, the link contains `10.99.0.1`; the guest can join straight away. Without root
access, use a VPN or a relay.

## Troubleshooting

| Message or symptom | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| *Cannot reach the relay server (… a relay token is required)* | The relay uses access control. Set the token with **Set Token…**. |
| *Cannot reach the relay server (… did not answer)* | Wrong URL, DNS, port 443 closed, or a certificate that is not valid for that name. **Test Connection** shows the details. |
| *The host did not answer* | Neither a direct path nor the relay works for this guest. Check the host's status bar for the relay state, then try a VPN. |
| Badge stays on **Relay** | Hole punching failed: usually a symmetric NAT or UDP filtering. The relay path keeps working. Open UDP 7842 on the relay and keep QUIC address discovery enabled to improve the odds. |

Source: docs/guide/user/dev-containers-and-wsl.md

# Dev Containers and WSL

Besides [SSH hosts](docs/guide/user/remote-development.md), Forge opens projects **inside a dev container** or
**inside a WSL distribution**, like PHPStorm and JetBrains Gateway. In both cases Forge starts its
headless agent (the same one it uses over SSH) in the container or the distribution and talks to
it over the stdio of `docker exec` or `wsl.exe` instead of an SSH channel. The project then opens
like a remote project: indexing, php-lsp and other language servers, Git, terminals and run
configurations all happen in the container or the distribution, with its PHP, Composer, Node.js
and tools.

## Dev Containers

A dev container is described by the project's `devcontainer.json`
([containers.dev](https://containers.dev)). Forge looks for it in the usual places:

| Location | |
| --- | --- |
| `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` | the default configuration |
| `.devcontainer.json` | in the project root |
| `.devcontainer/<name>/devcontainer.json` | one of several named configurations |

### Requirements

| Side | Needs |
| --- | --- |
| This machine | the Docker CLI (`docker`, Settings \| Build, Execution, Deployment \| Docker \| **Docker executable**, `docker.cliPath`) and a running Docker Engine (Docker Desktop, Podman with the Docker CLI, Rancher Desktop, …) |
| The container | Linux on x86_64 or aarch64 with `/bin/sh`; nothing else: Forge copies its agent in |
| Forge | a build that bundles the agents, as for SSH (see [Remote development](docs/guide/user/remote-development.md#requirements)) |

### Create a dev container

- Welcome screen → **Remote Development** → **Dev Containers** → **New Dev Container**, then
  choose the project folder, or
- in an open local project: **Create Dev Container and Mount Sources…** (Find Action), or the
  dev container icon in the gutter of `devcontainer.json`.

![Dev Containers on the Welcome screen](docs/screenshots/devcontainers-welcome.png)

The dialog lists the folder's configurations and shows what the selected one does: how the
container is made (image, Dockerfile or Docker Compose service), the workspace folder in the
container, the remote user, forwarded ports, `postCreateCommand` / `postStartCommand` and the
features.

![Create Dev Container and Mount Sources](docs/screenshots/devcontainers-config.png)

**Build Container and Continue** asks "Trust and Open Project?" for an untrusted folder first:
building the image and the lifecycle commands run the project's code. Forge then runs the
Docker CLI and streams every step, command line and line of output into the build log:

1. `docker pull` the image, `docker build` the Dockerfile (with `build.args`, `build.target`),
   or `docker compose up -d --build` the service with Forge's override file (labels, extra
   mounts, `containerEnv`, the keep-alive command),
2. `docker run -d` with the sources mounted (`workspaceMount`, default
   `type=bind,source=<folder>,target=/workspaces/<folder name>`), `mounts`, `containerEnv`,
   `runArgs`, `containerUser` and the forwarded ports published on `127.0.0.1`,
3. `onCreateCommand`, `postCreateCommand` and `postStartCommand` with `docker exec` as the
   remote user in the workspace folder (strings run with `/bin/sh -c`, arrays without a shell,
   objects one after the other),
4. the agent is copied into the container (`~/.cache/forge-agent/<version>/` of the remote
   user) and started; the workspace folder opens as the project.

![Build log](docs/screenshots/devcontainers-build-log.png)

**Stop** cancels the build (the running `docker` process ends). A failed step shows its exit
code; **Retry** runs it again.

![Gutter icon in devcontainer.json](docs/screenshots/devcontainers-gutter.png)

### What Forge reads from devcontainer.json

The file may contain `//` and `/* */` comments and trailing commas (JSONC). The editor treats
it as JSON with comments.

| Property | Support |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | the container's name in Forge (default: the folder name) |
| `image` | pulled, then run |
| `build.dockerfile`, `build.context`, `build.args`, `build.target` (and the old `dockerFile` / `context`) | built with `docker build`; paths relative to `devcontainer.json` |
| `dockerComposeFile` (one or several), `service`, `runServices` | `docker compose up`; the compose files mount the sources |
| `workspaceFolder`, `workspaceMount` | the project folder in the container and the sources' mount |
| `forwardPorts` | numbers are published on `127.0.0.1:<port>`; `service:port` entries are listed only |
| `onCreateCommand`, `postCreateCommand`, `postStartCommand` | run after creating / on every start |
| `remoteUser`, `containerUser` | the user of the agent, terminals and commands / of the container |
| `containerEnv`, `remoteEnv` | the container's environment / the agent's (`${containerEnv:…}` entries are left to the container) |
| `mounts` | strings in `--mount` syntax or `{ source, target, type }` objects |
| `runArgs`, `overrideCommand` | extra `docker run` arguments; keep the container alive with a sleep loop (default for image and Dockerfile) |
| `features` | **listed only**: Forge does not install features yet and says so in the build log |
| `${localWorkspaceFolder}`, `${localWorkspaceFolderBasename}`, `${containerWorkspaceFolder}`, `${containerWorkspaceFolderBasename}`, `${localEnv:NAME[:default]}`, `${devcontainerId}` | replaced |

### Your dev containers

The Dev Containers page lists every container Forge created (Docker labels
`forge.devcontainer.id` and the Dev Containers CLI's `devcontainer.local_folder` /
`devcontainer.config_file`). Click a container to open it (a stopped one is started first), or
use its buttons:

| Button | Does |
| --- | --- |
| Start / Stop | `docker start` (then `postStartCommand`) / `docker stop` |
| Rebuild | removes the container and builds it again without cache (the dialog opens with **Rebuild Container**) |
| Delete | `docker rm -f`; the sources stay on your machine |

Recent Projects show dev container projects with a **Container** badge; opening one starts its
container, or offers to build it again when it is gone. The status bar shows
`Dev Container: <name>`; when the agent ends (container stopped or restarted) Forge starts it
again with a backoff of 1 to 30 seconds and re-attaches the project.

![A project in a dev container](docs/screenshots/devcontainers-project.png)

## WSL

On Windows, Forge opens projects that live inside a WSL distribution and runs its agent there
(`wsl.exe -d <distro> --exec …`), so files are read at Linux speed and PHP, Composer, Git and
the language servers are the distribution's.

- Welcome screen → **Remote Development** → **WSL** lists the distributions of `wsl.exe -l -v`
  (state, WSL version, the default one; Docker Desktop's internal distributions are hidden).
  Choose one, then the project folder in the distribution's file system.
- **Open** a folder under `\\wsl$\<distro>\…` or `\\wsl.localhost\<distro>\…`: Forge opens it
  in that distribution instead of reading it over the network share.

![WSL distributions](docs/screenshots/wsl-distros.png)

![Choose a folder in the distribution](docs/screenshots/wsl-folder-chooser.png)

The project is shown as `\\wsl.localhost\<distro>\home\…` and kept in Recent Projects with a
**WSL** badge. Trust is kept for that path, see
[Project trust and Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md#remote-projects).

Paths are mapped between the two views as WSL does:

| Windows | Linux (in the distribution) |
| --- | --- |
| `C:\Users\me\shop` | `/mnt/c/Users/me/shop` |
| `\\wsl$\Ubuntu\home\me\shop`, `\\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu\home\me\shop` | `/home/me/shop` |

### Terminal › WSL

In a local project on Windows, the arrow next to **+** in the Terminal tool window offers a
`WSL: <distro>` entry per distribution: a shell in the distribution
(`wsl.exe -d <distro> --cd <project folder>`), started in the project folder when it is on a
Windows drive.

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| "Docker is not available" on the Dev Containers page | start Docker Desktop / the Docker Engine, or set the Docker executable in Settings \| Build, Execution, Deployment \| Docker |
| "The Forge agent for Linux … is not part of this build" | use a release build or build the agents with `pnpm --dir app/ui agents` (static musl binaries, they run in any Linux container) |
| A feature from `features` is missing in the container | install it in the Dockerfile; Forge lists features but does not install them yet |
| "… is not available in Safe Mode" when building | trust the folder: the build runs the project's code |
| WSL page says "WSL is only available on Windows" | WSL projects need Windows with WSL installed (`wsl --install`) |

Source: docs/guide/user/deployment.md

# Deployment

Forge deploys project files to a server like PHPStorm's **Tools | Deployment**: you configure
servers once per project, then upload, download, compare and sync files or folders. Files can
be uploaded automatically every time you save.

![Deployment settings](docs/screenshots/deployment-settings.png)

## Servers

Settings | Build, Execution, Deployment | **Deployment** (or Tools | Deployment |
Configuration…) lists the project's servers. **+** adds one of these types:

| Type | Connects with |
| --- | --- |
| **SFTP** | an SSH configuration from Settings | Tools | SSH Configurations, so host keys, `~/.ssh/config` aliases, keys, the ssh-agent, `ProxyJump` and passwords work as in [Remote development](docs/guide/user/remote-development.md) |
| **FTP** | host, port (21), user name and password, or an anonymous login; passive mode is on by default |
| **FTPS** | FTP over explicit TLS (`AUTH TLS`); the server certificate must be valid for the host |
| **Local or mounted folder** | a folder on this machine: a local web server's document root, a mounted network share, a build folder |

The ★ button (**Use as Default**) makes a server the project's **default server**: the actions
"…to Default Server" and automatic upload use it. The first server you add becomes the default.

### Connection tab

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| SSH configuration | SFTP only. **…** opens SSH Configurations. Trust an unknown host key there with Test Connection first. |
| Host, Port, Username, Password, Anonymous login, Passive mode | FTP and FTPS. The password is stored in the OS keychain (service `forge-deploy`, account `ftp://user@host:port`). |
| Root path | The folder on the server every deployment path is relative to, e.g. `/var/www/shop`. Empty: the login folder. **Autodetect** fills in the login folder. |
| Folder | Local servers: the target folder. A folder inside the project is never uploaded into itself; the project folder itself is refused. |
| Web server URL | `https://shop.example.com`; with the web paths of the mappings it gives each file's URL. |

**Test Connection** connects with the values in the form (also a password you have not saved
yet) and checks that the root path exists.

### Mappings tab

Each mapping says where a project folder goes:

| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Local path | a project folder, empty for the project root |
| Deployment path | relative to the root path; `/` is the root path itself |
| Web path | relative to the web server URL |

The longest matching local path wins, so `public` → `/htdocs` and `public/assets` →
`/cdn/assets` can live side by side. Without mappings the project root is deployed to the
root path. Paths with `..` are never mapped.

### Excluded Paths tab

**Add Local Path** excludes a project folder or file (e.g. `storage`, `node_modules`), **Add
Deployment Path** a path on the server (e.g. `/public/uploads`, user content that must not be
overwritten or deleted). Excluded paths are never uploaded, downloaded, compared or deleted.

The configuration is saved in the project as `.forge/deployment.toml`, without passwords, so it
can be shared with the team.

## Uploading and downloading

Tools | Deployment and **Deployment** in the Project view's context menu work on the files and
folders selected in the Project view, or on the file in the editor:

| Action | Shortcut | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Upload to *default server* | | uploads to the default server |
| Upload to… | `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+X` (macOS `Cmd+Alt+Shift+X`) | asks for the server first |
| Download from *default server* / Download from… | | copies the deployed files into the project |
| Compare with Deployed Version | | opens the diff viewer: the deployed file on the left, the project file (editable) on the right |
| Sync with Deployed to… | | compares a folder with its deployed copy, see below |
| Delete on *default server* | | deletes the deployed files and folders (after a confirmation); the root path itself is never deleted |
| Automatic Upload (Always) | | switches automatic upload between Always and Never for this project |

Folders are transferred with everything in them. Files and folders matching "Exclude items by
name" (`.git`, `.idea`, `.DS_Store`, `.forge`, … by default) and excluded paths are skipped.

![Deployment in the Project view](docs/screenshots/deployment-upload-menu.png)

When the target of a file is newer than the source and differs from it ("Warn when uploading
over newer file"), Forge does not overwrite it and asks first: **Overwrite** transfers those
files too.

## File Transfer tool window

Every upload, download and delete appears in the **File Transfer** tool window (bottom
stripe): a line per operation with its time, server and result ("3 files transferred
(12.4 KB), 40 skipped"), and below it every transferred, deleted or failed file with its
deployment path. **Show Skipped** also lists files that were up to date, excluded or not
mapped. **Cancel** stops a running transfer after the current file; **Clear All** removes the
finished operations. Automatic uploads are marked *automatic*.

![File Transfer tool window](docs/screenshots/deployment-file-transfer.png)

## Sync with Deployed

Sync with Deployed to… opens the folder diff of a project folder (left) and its deployed
folder (right) in an editor tab, like Compare Directories: equal files, different files and
files on one side only, with filters for each state. Double-click (or `Ctrl+D`) a file to see
its diff; **Upload** (→) and **Download** (←) copy the selected file or folder to the other
side. What counts as different is "Sync with Deployed compares by" in the options: contents
and size (the default; files of equal size are read on both sides), size, or size and
timestamp.

![Sync with Deployed](docs/screenshots/deployment-sync.png)

## Options

Settings | Build, Execution, Deployment | Deployment | **Options** (Tools | Deployment |
Options…):

| Option | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exclude items by name | `.svn;.cvs;.idea;.DS_Store;.git;.hg;.forge` | `;`-separated, `*` and `?` work |
| Overwrite up-to-date files | off | off: files whose deployed copy has the same size and is not older are skipped |
| Preserve files timestamps | on | the copy gets the source's modification time (FTP servers need `MFMT`) |
| Delete target items when source ones do not exist | off | uploading or downloading a folder deletes what exists only on the target |
| Create empty directories | off | |
| Warn when uploading over newer file | Compare timestamp & size | or Compare content, or No |
| Sync with Deployed compares by | Contents and size | or Size, or Size and timestamp |
| Upload changed files automatically to the default server | Never | **Always** (every save, also automatic saves when switching windows), **On explicit save action** (`Ctrl+S`, Save All) or **Never** |

The keys are `deployment.*` (see the [settings reference](docs/guide/reference/settings.md)); like in
PHPStorm they are usually set for the project.

## Safe Mode

Uploading, downloading and comparing only copy files; they never run project code, so you can
deploy an untrusted project you opened in [Safe Mode](docs/guide/user/project-trust.md). **Automatic upload is
off in Safe Mode**: the servers and the option come from the project's own `.forge` files, and
an untrusted project must not upload anything (possibly with your SSH configurations) without
you choosing to.

> **Note:** Deployment works with projects on this machine. In a [remote
> project](docs/guide/user/remote-development.md) the files already are on the server; the Deployment actions
> report that they are not available there.

## Browse Remote Host

Tools | Deployment | **Browse Remote Host** opens the **Remote Host** tool window with the
files of a server: a lazy tree with the mapped folders highlighted, Edit Remote File (a
temporary copy uploaded back on save, with a check for changes on the server), Download from
Here, Upload to Here, Compare with Local Version, New File / New Directory, Rename, Delete and
Copy Path. See [Remote Host and SSH sessions](docs/guide/user/remote-host-and-ssh.md); the same page describes
SSH terminal sessions to the SFTP servers of the project (Tools | Start SSH Session…).

![Remote Host tool window](docs/screenshots/remote-host-tree.png)
